Following Trump's election as US President, the global economy faces greater uncertainty. Not only did the election result come as a surprise to the market, but the related market reaction was also unexpected. In particular, expectations that measures such as Trump's tax reform, increased infrastructure spending, and deregulation would boost US economic growth drove up global stock markets. After the new US administration takes office, US policy direction may undergo fundamental changes in two aspects — a shift from monetary easing to fiscal expansion, and a shift from globalisation to anti-globalisation — which may have far-reaching implications for the global economic landscape. However, the tax cut measures that the market anticipates from Trump may fail to produce the expected stimulus effect on US economic growth. In particular, with US economic activity now close to its economic potential, fiscal stimulus measures may only bring a mild cyclical boost to US economic growth, while intensifying the upside risks to US inflation. Although it remains uncertain whether the US Federal Reserve (the Fed) will therefore significantly accelerate the pace of monetary policy tightening, long-term bond yields have already risen markedly, partly reflecting market expectations of increasing inflation risks. At the same time, the rise of trade protectionism would create a "lose-lose" situation for the US and the rest of the world. Increased trade barriers would lead to market distortions that harm overall interests, hamper global trade, reduce the efficiency of global supply chains, and pose downside risks to the global economic outlook. Meanwhile, political instability remains a major risk and adverse factor, particularly for the still-weak recovery of the European economy. For emerging market economies, the risk of capital outflows arising from an accelerated pace of US interest rate hikes and further appreciation of the US dollar has risen. This could weigh on economic growth and intensify the risk of rapid capital outflows. In fact, amid expectations that the Trump administration will implement large-scale fiscal expansion and concerns about a sharp rise in energy prices, the market has repriced inflation risks, causing long-term bond yields to rise significantly across the board in both advanced economies and many emerging market economies. Following Trump's unexpected election as US President, uncertainty over US policy has increased accordingly. Although market attention has focused on the short-term benefits arising from the potentially implemented large-scale fiscal policies and business-facilitation measures, US economic activity is now close to its economic potential, and fiscal stimulus measures may only provide a mild cyclical boost to US economic growth, while further intensifying the upside risks to inflation. More importantly, the risks facing emerging market economies are increasing amid capital outflow pressures brought about by the faster pace of US interest rate hikes and a stronger US dollar, while the trade protectionist measures that the US may adopt will also threaten global trade flows. In East Asia, real economic activity improved slightly in the second half of 2016, and export volumes have also increased recently. However, against the backdrop of US interest rate hikes, US dollar appreciation, and possible US protectionist measures, financial markets are likely to remain volatile, and the downside risks to economic growth are rising. On the Chinese Mainland, overall economic growth accelerated marginally in the second half of 2016, supported by robust growth in infrastructure investment and improved private-sector business spending. The Mainland economy continues to rebalance, with the tertiary industry expanding steadily, but the continued advancement of economic structural adjustment as well as changes in China-US trade relations may increase the uncertainty of the short-term economic outlook. Given the government's determination to curb rising property prices, if the real estate market continues to cool, the contribution of the real estate industry to economic growth this year may also decline. On the external front, although the renminbi remained stable against the China Foreign Exchange Trade System (CFETS) currency basket during the reporting period, capital outflow pressures increased towards the end of 2016 amid US dollar appreciation and US interest rate hikes, and subsequently appeared to ease slightly in early 2017. Following Trump's unexpected election as US President, global financial markets reacted strongly, with the market in particular anticipating that policies such as Trump's tax reforms, large-scale increases in infrastructure spending, and deregulation would boost US economic growth and inflation, stimulating a rally in major stock markets (Chart 2.1). As a result, market expectations of US inflation and US interest rate hikes heated up, causing US Treasury bond yields to surge and the US dollar to strengthen. Chart 2.1 Stock market indices of selected advanced economies. However, the tax cuts that the market expects from Trump may fail to have the positive impact on US economic growth that the market anticipates. Although a shift in economic policy toward reliance on fiscal easing measures would help alleviate the heavy burden borne by monetary easing policy, given the current stage of the US economic cycle, whether now is the appropriate time to implement fiscal easing measures is debatable. Although US economic growth has slowed somewhat in recent quarters, the output gap has gradually narrowed, and the February unemployment rate was also in line with the Federal Reserve's estimated natural unemployment rate of 4.7%, reflecting that US economic activity is already close to its economic potential. The US economy is currently in an expansionary cycle, and the fiscal multiplier would be lower than during a recession (see, for example, Auerbach and Gorodnichenko (2012))1. In fact, recent estimates of the US Laffer curve indicate that tax cuts on either labour or capital could lead to reduced tax revenue (see, for example, Trabandt and Uhlig (2012))2. In any case, with the reduction of excess capacity, any further measures to boost economic growth, even if their actual impact on economic growth is limited, may also push up inflation. Meanwhile, other factors such as rising oil and commodity prices, as well as potential trade protectionist measures including the Border Adjustment Tax currently under consideration, may also intensify the upside risks to US inflation. Even as the risk of rising US inflation increases, the Federal Reserve remains prudent about tightening US monetary policy and tends to maintain an ultra-accommodative monetary policy stance. However, long-term bond yields have risen, partly reflecting increased US inflation risks. Since the US election, although market forecasts for the future federal funds rate have been revised upward to close to the median of the Federal Reserve's forecasts for 2017 and early 2018, they remain far below the Federal Reserve's long-term forecasts (Chart 2.2). As a result, a faster pace of US interest rate hikes may trigger the risk of significant market volatility. Although financial markets have focused on the short-term benefits of potentially implemented expansionary fiscal policies and business-facilitation measures driving stronger US economic growth, long-term risks remain, including damaging protectionist trade policies and further rises in US Treasury (government bond) yields. In fact, the Trump administration may fulfil its campaign promises and adopt trade protectionist measures. Increased trade barriers would cause market distortions that harm overall welfare, hinder global trade flows, reduce the efficiency of global supply chains, and pose downside risks to the global economic outlook. Chart 2.2 Future federal funds rate forecasts: Federal Reserve versus market. In Europe, political instability remains a major risk and drag on Europe's economic recovery. Although the economic environment in the euro area has gradually improved, with fourth-quarter real gross domestic product growing at a moderate 1.7% year on year, only slightly below the third quarter's 1.8% year-on-year increase, relative to the stronger recovery of the US economy, economic activity in the euro area still remains only slightly above pre-global financial crisis levels (Chart 2.3). Since the UK's decision to leave the EU last summer, the market has been concerned that the euro area will eventually break apart. Although Italy's economic and political situation appears to have become more stable after forming a new government and implementing measures to rescue the banking sector, against the backdrop of the Brexit negotiations and rising anti-establishment sentiment, the upcoming elections in Germany and France (and possibly Italy) may become political flashpoints. Partly due to increased political uncertainty, sovereign bond yields in Europe have continued to climb, and corporate bond spreads have also widened, a situation that is especially pronounced in peripheral countries, potentially creating a vicious cycle for the real economy and possibly putting pressure on real business investment in the euro area. Chart 2.3 Real gross domestic product of major advanced economies. In Japan, real gross domestic product in recent quarters has been revised upward, with the year-on-year growth rate in the fourth quarter of 2016 rising to 1.6%, the fastest pace since the third quarter of 2015, and the economic recovery is stronger than previously expected. However, partly due to structural problems in the labour market, wage growth has been slow, resulting in weak consumption growth. At the same time, the recent rapid depreciation of the yen means that the downside pressure on "new core" goods inflation caused by the earlier appreciation of the yen is about to begin to fade. Coupled with a stronger-than-expected recovery, this indicates that the short-term inflation outlook has improved, and although "new core" inflation (excluding fresh food and energy) fell to 0.1% in December, it is expected to bottom out and rebound. Nevertheless, in the face of long-term and structural headwinds, growth may remain slow, and inflation expectations remain at around 0.5%–0.6%, below the level when Abenomics was introduced in early 2014, so the risk that the inflation rate fails to reach the Bank of Japan's medium-term target of 2% still exists. For other countries, especially emerging market economies, since the US reduced imports after the global financial crisis, and the US may implement protectionist policies, the benefits brought by faster US economic growth through the trade channel may be smaller. Meanwhile, the faster pace of US interest rate hikes and further US dollar appreciation will lead to tighter financial conditions, exacerbating downside economic risks. This may weigh on economic growth and increase the risk of rapid capital outflows. In fact, the market expects the Trump administration to pursue large-scale fiscal expansion, coupled with concerns about surging energy prices, and has therefore repriced inflation risks, causing long-term bond yields to rise significantly across the board in advanced economies as well as many emerging market economies. Faster growth in private consumption and buoyant public-sector building and construction activities drove Hong Kong's economic growth to accelerate slightly in the second half of 2016. Amid increasing uncertainties in the external environment, economic growth in 2017 is expected to be moderate. Benefiting from stable import prices and moderate local growth momentum, inflationary pressure is expected to remain contained. Hong Kong's economic growth quickened slightly in the second half of 2016. Seasonally adjusted real Gross Domestic Product (GDP) grew by 1.2% quarter-on-quarter in the fourth quarter, slightly higher than the 0.8% growth rate in the third quarter (Chart 3.1). Partly due to improved consumer confidence and robust labour market conditions, private consumption grew at a faster pace, becoming the main driver of GDP growth. Supported by infrastructure projects such as the third runway of the Hong Kong airport, building and construction activities also became buoyant. However, as corporate capital expenditure was weak, the contribution of overall investment expenditure to GDP growth narrowed. On the external front, both exports and imports of goods accelerated in tandem with rising intra-regional trade flows (Chart 3.2).²² Trade-related and transport services drove further growth in exports of services, while imports of services rebounded partly on the back of strong travel demand by local residents. Net exports continued to drag on GDP growth. Chart 3.1 Real GDP growth rate and contributions of major expenditure components Chart 3.2 Real exports and imports The labour market remained tight. The seasonally adjusted unemployment rate stayed at 3.4% in the first three quarters, before edging down slightly to 3.3% in the fourth quarter (Chart 3.3). In fact, the unemployment rates of several major industries declined in the second half, including the retail, accommodation and food services sectors, partly because the slowdown in the retail sector had stabilised. Total employment reached a new high of 3.824 million persons in February 2017, while the labour force participation rate remained stable at around 61%. Chart 3.3 Unemployment rate and total employment Real economic growth in 2017 is expected to remain moderate. On the external front, amid uncertainties in the global macroeconomic and financial environment, global economic and trade growth may continue to be moderate. Coupled with the strong US dollar pushing up the real effective exchange rate of the Hong Kong dollar, Hong Kong's export performance will be restrained. On the domestic front, although stable employment and income conditions will support consumption, private consumption is expected to grow moderately, weighed down by rising interest rates. With increased housing supply and the commencement of several infrastructure projects, building and construction activities should grow steadily, but the subdued business sentiment and rising interest rates will restrain corporate capital expenditure. The Government currently forecasts real GDP growth in 2017 to be in the range of 2 to 3%, while the average forecast of private-sector analysts is 2.0%. The economic growth outlook is subject to numerous uncertainties, with those from the external environment being particularly significant. Policy uncertainties under the new US administration will cloud the global economic outlook, and the potential emergence of trade protectionist policies will pose headwinds to global trade flows. The Brexit process and elections in several major European countries may also lead to volatility in asset markets and affect fund flows involving the Hong Kong dollar. In addition, the normalisation of US interest rates will tighten local monetary conditions and exert downward pressure on the real economy and asset prices. Since the second half of 2016, although local inflation has gathered momentum on a quarter-on-quarter basis in recent months, it has remained moderate overall. On a year-on-year basis, the underlying Composite Consumer Price Index stayed stable at 2.1% from the second half of 2016 to January this year (Chart 3.4). The annualised three-month underlying inflation rate, which reflects inflation momentum, accelerated from 0.9% in the third quarter to 3.0% in the fourth quarter, before easing slightly to 2.4% in January. The rise in inflation momentum was mainly due to increases in the prices of tradable goods and housing rentals (Chart 3.5). In particular, tradable goods price inflation rose from a negative figure in the third quarter to 3.0% in the fourth quarter, driven mainly by the prices of basic foodstuffs and clothing and footwear. Meanwhile, since the third quarter, as the decline in private residential rentals narrowed and public housing rentals were raised in September 2016, the housing rental component of the Composite Consumer Price Index rose, before easing slightly in January (Chart 3.6). Chart 3.4 Different indicators reflecting consumer price inflation Chart 3.5 Consumer price inflation by major components Chart 3.6 Rental component of the Composite Consumer Price Index and market rentals In the near term, with weak import prices and moderate local cost pressures, inflationary pressure is expected to remain contained. As the strong Hong Kong dollar has, to some extent, offset the impact of the rebound in global commodity prices, imported inflation will remain low (Chart 3.7). On the domestic side, the output gap is estimated to have remained close to zero in the fourth quarter of 2016, which should help ease business cost pressures and thereby contain inflation in the services components. Despite the tight labour market, wage increases in recent quarters have been mild, with real wages per capita rising by 1.1% in the first half of 2016 before falling by 0.4% in the third quarter (Chart 3.8). Given the persistent uncertainties in the external environment leading to cautious business sentiment, against this backdrop, increases in labour costs should be contained. In addition, as retail sales performance has been lacklustre in recent months, increases in retail property rentals are expected to be moderate. Furthermore, the impact of the earlier softening in private residential rentals will gradually emerge, which will also help ease inflationary pressure. Overall, the year-on-year inflation rate for 2017 as a whole is expected to decline, with the Government forecasting an underlying inflation rate of 2.0% for the year, lower than the 2.3% in 2016. Chart 3.7 Commodity and import prices Chart 3.8 Unit labour cost and real wages per capita The inflation outlook faces both upside and downside risks. On the downside, if inflation in the US accelerates under the Trump administration, this could lead to a faster-than-expected pace of US interest rate hikes, which may push up local mortgage rates and increase the downward pressure on property prices and housing rentals. At the same time, the appreciation of the Hong Kong dollar may keep import prices weak while also weakening Hong Kong's attractiveness to visitors to Hong Kong. On the upside, if the global economic expansion is faster than expected, it may accelerate Hong Kong's economic growth and push up demand-driven international commodity prices, thereby exerting upward pressure on local inflation. In addition, the increased statutory minimum wage will take effect on 1 May 2017, which could lead to a further rise in inflation, but the actual impact of this cost-push inflation will depend on the extent to which wage costs are passed on to consumer prices.

In early 2017, the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate strengthened somewhat in line with other Asian currencies, but as market expectations of a US rate hike in March rose from mid-February onwards, the Hong Kong dollar began to show signs of weakening. At the same time, amid uncertainties surrounding the new US administration, the Brexit process, and elections in EU member states, fund flows may become more volatile. In addition, increased investment demand from Mainland investors for Hong Kong dollar assets may create inflow pressure on the Hong Kong dollar. Although northbound trading exceeded southbound trading in scale in the early stage after the launch of the Shenzhen-Hong Kong Stock Connect in December, two-way equity investment fund flows between the Mainland and Hong Kong under the scheme are expected to increase gradually. Despite rising US dollar interest rates and financial market volatility, Hong Kong's monetary conditions remained accommodative in the second half of 2016 and in recent months. The Hong Kong dollar monetary base remained sizeable, rising a further 1.7% in the second half, driven by growth in Certificates of Indebtedness and government-issued notes and coins in circulation (Chart 4.5). As the Convertibility Undertaking was not triggered, the sum of the Aggregate Balance and outstanding Exchange Fund Bills and Notes remained broadly at the high level of HK$1,222.7 billion. Of this, owing to an additional issuance of HK$49 billion of Exchange Fund Bills to meet banks' strong demand for liquidity management, the Aggregate Balance contracted while outstanding Exchange Fund Bills and Notes rose correspondingly. As a major component of Hong Kong dollar M3, Hong Kong dollar deposits recorded faster growth of 6.6% in the second half (Chart 4.7), mainly driven by stronger local economic activity and increased transaction demand arising from a pickup in IPO activity. Analysed by counterpart assets, the growth in Hong Kong dollar M3 mainly reflected increases in Hong Kong dollar loans and banks' net foreign currency assets (Chart 4.6), which respectively reflected money derived from credit expansion and net Hong Kong dollar fund inflows to the non-bank private sector. By contrast, other foreign currency deposits contracted a further 10.3%, mainly due to a decline in renminbi deposits. Overall, total deposits with authorized institutions grew at a faster pace of 6.2% in the second half of 2016, with full-year growth of 9.1%. Chart 4.7 Deposit growth. Amid expectations of US interest rate normalisation, banks' wholesale funding costs rose in the fourth quarter of 2016. Global financial markets turned volatile again at the beginning of the year as markets reassessed inflation risks in the US. In February, global equity markets fell sharply from their late-January highs, completely offsetting the significant gains recorded earlier in the year, while the benchmark 10-year US Treasury yield also rose to a four-year high. Over the past two years, global equity markets rose persistently amid low volatility because markets had expected the economic environment to continue delivering solid growth, with inflation and interest rates remaining at ideally low levels. However, this expectation is now facing risks from tightening global monetary conditions, rising trade protectionist sentiment, and heightened geopolitical tensions. The Hong Kong dollar exchange rate softened, but markets continued to function in an orderly manner. In the second half of 2017, overall loans continued to increase, but at a more moderate pace. Property prices and transaction volumes, after experiencing a modest slowdown in the middle of last year, both rebounded in the fourth quarter of 2017. Looking ahead, the renewed volatility in global and local financial markets may add volatility to Hong Kong's fund flows. Given the uncertainties in financial markets, as well as the ongoing normalisation of US monetary policy and persistent geopolitical risks, banks should remain vigilant about greater interest rate volatility and potential capital outflow risks. In particular, given the continued rise in corporate leverage levels and the elevated household debt burden, banks should assess the potential impact on asset quality should interest rates rise more than expected. After the Chicago Board Options Exchange Volatility Index (VIX) had hovered at low levels for more than two years, global financial markets turned volatile again at the beginning of the year. Global equity markets fell sharply from their late-January highs, with the S&P 500 Index at one point declining by more than 10%, completely offsetting the significant gains recorded in early January. Market sentiment shifted, owing to signs that the global economic recovery could exert pressure on long-subdued US wages and prices, which could in turn prompt the Federal Reserve to accelerate the pace of its interest rate hikes. The benchmark 10-year US Treasury yield also rose to a four-year high. The prolonged rally in global equity markets over the past two years had been premised on market expectations that economic conditions would remain favourable. In the second half of 2017, global economic growth momentum continued to strengthen, with economic activity in advanced and emerging market economies picking up in tandem. Towards the end of the year, the US Congress passed a tax reform package that included tax cuts and a comprehensive overhaul of corporate and personal tax rules, leading markets to anticipate that the US's strong economic recovery would receive additional cyclical stimulus in the near term. Despite the strengthening of activity, core inflation in major advanced economies remained mild, further reinforcing market expectations that global interest rates would stay low for a prolonged period. Against this backdrop, global asset markets rose significantly in 2017, with US equity markets in particular repeatedly setting new record highs. However, as the US reported stronger-than-expected wage growth data for January, global equity markets reassessed inflation risks. Following the short-term financial market volatility, the risk of tightening global monetary conditions may continue to cast a shadow over the global economic outlook. In the US, the economy has now reached its output potential, and the anticipated cyclical stimulus to domestic demand from tax cuts could accelerate a rebound in inflation, thereby prompting the Federal Reserve to tighten monetary policy at a faster pace. Meanwhile, as the tax cuts lead to a rising fiscal deficit, the US may issue more Treasury bonds in the future, which is expected to add upward pressure on long-term bond yields at a time when the Federal Reserve continues to advance the normalisation of its balance sheet. Outside the US, growth momentum in other major advanced economies has strengthened, leading markets to expect that their central banks may scale back the size of their quantitative easing programmes. If implemented, this would lead to a synchronised tightening of global monetary conditions. Policy and event risks arising from international political and geopolitical tensions could also cast a shadow over the outlook for global economic growth. The US government appears increasingly inclined to adopt trade protectionist measures to shield domestic industries from competition, with recent examples including the announcement of import tariffs on solar panels, washing machines, steel, and aluminium. These moves have raised concerns about whether its trading partners would respond with retaliatory measures. In addition, should geopolitical tensions escalate unexpectedly, global trade could be affected and volatility in global financial markets could intensify. Given the above-mentioned uncertainties in the global economic outlook, whether the currently elevated valuations in global asset markets can be sustained remains in question. From a fundamental perspective, it remains to be seen whether the cyclical growth in global demand and the anticipated rise in the fiscal deficit arising from US tax cuts will push up the natural rate of interest (R*); in addition, the Federal Reserve's balance sheet normalisation is expected to lead to a rise in the term premium, which may push up long-term interest rates and thereby be unfavourable to asset market valuations. In East Asia, economies in the region were also in an ideal environment of solid growth and mild inflation. Amid the favourable economic performance and optimistic outlook, fund inflows also accelerated, with financial markets rising simultaneously. However, this favourable outlook faces downside risks owing to a range of factors: tightening global liquidity as major central banks synchronously advance monetary policy normalisation; the US government's pursuit of inward-looking trade policies; heightened geopolitical tensions; and the possibility that offshore US dollar liquidity could become tight as US corporations repatriate profits to the US on a large scale in response to the one-off "deemed repatriation" provision under the country's tax reform. Should credit and financial markets face any shocks, this could trigger a reversal of fund flows, with more highly leveraged sectors and economies being the most vulnerable to the impact of tightening financial conditions. In Mainland China, the economy performed well in the second half of 2017, supported by factors such as robust consumption, strong infrastructure, and a rebound in industrial spending towards the end of the year. At the same time, signs of the rise of the "new economy" became increasingly evident, with sectors such as high value-added manufacturing and services demonstrating strong business expansion momentum over the past few quarters. Looking ahead, the near-term economic growth outlook remains positive, though uncertainties persist. In particular, it remains to be seen to what extent the rapid growth of the "new economy" can help offset the short-term pressure on growth arising from the further advancement of structural reforms. The Mainland authorities announced in 2018 that they would continue to adopt a proactive fiscal policy stance, which could help cushion adverse developments in the economy when necessary. During the review period, some progress was made in both structural reforms and the control of systemic risks. In particular, with the introduction of tightening measures, the Mainland property market showed signs of cooling during the review period, most notably in first-tier cities. At the same time, as banks tightened loan approval standards, banks' exposures to enterprises in industries with excess capacity remained under control, while shadow banking activities also slowed amid financial deleveraging. In addition to the above positive developments, our analysis also suggests that the efficiency of capital allocation in Mainland China appears to have improved. In particular, the borrowing constraints faced by state-owned enterprises with weaker repayment capacity appear to have tightened, possibly owing to weakened support provided by local governments (for details, please refer to Box 2 on page 28). On the external front, amid a stabilising economic situation and diminishing risks, capital outflow pressure remained mild for most of 2017. Hong Kong's economy maintained its sequential growth momentum in the second half of 2017. Real Gross Domestic Product grew by 3.8% for the full year of 2017, the fastest pace in nearly six years. Owing to favourable employment and income conditions and rising asset prices, private consumption continued to grow solidly in the second half of 2017. Overall investment spending also rebounded on the back of increased corporate capital expenditure. On the external front, benefiting from the improvement in global trade growth and the gradual recovery of inbound tourism, Hong Kong's export performance improved further. Nevertheless, as imports grew faster than exports, net exports of goods continued to drag on GDP growth, while net exports of services made a positive contribution to GDP growth. Economic growth is expected to remain solid in 2018, with private consumption, building and construction activity, and exports continuing to support economic growth. Given that Hong Kong dollar interest rates will eventually rise, Box 3 examines the impact of a higher mortgage repayment burden on private consumption. The Government and market consensus forecasts real GDP growth for 2018 at 3 to 4% and 3.0%, respectively. However, Hong Kong's growth outlook is still affected by numerous uncertainties and risks, including the external environment mentioned above, the economic performance of Mainland China amid tightening financial conditions, and movements in Hong Kong's asset markets. Although the unemployment rate fell to a nearly 20-year low of 2.9%, local inflationary pressures remained under control. Nonetheless, sequential inflation momentum showed signs of edging up in recent months, with prices of both traded goods and services rising. Looking ahead, underlying inflation may edge up slightly to a still-mild level, partly reflecting the pass-through effect from rising rents on newly signed private residential leases. As liquidity conditions eased and interest rate arbitrage activities became active again, the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate softened once more from December 2017. At the beginning of 2018, despite turbulence in global financial markets (particularly equity markets), the Hong Kong dollar remained broadly stable. The Hong Kong dollar exchange rate weakened further in early March 2018, but the Convertibility Undertaking was not triggered. This was mainly due to funding demand from IPO fundraising activities and banks' cautious approach to liquidity management towards the year-end. The synchronised strengthening of the global economy since late 2016 has shown no signs of abating. Improved growth prospects propelled global stock markets steadily higher throughout 2017 and into early 2018. However, as the market reassessed US inflation risks, global equity markets experienced a sell-off and sharp volatility in February, marking the end of the calm that had prevailed in financial markets over the previous two years. Looking ahead, the risk of tightening global financial conditions, together with a range of policy and event risks, will continue to cast a shadow over the global outlook. Amid a tight labour market, US tax cuts could accelerate a cyclical rebound in inflation, prompting the Federal Reserve to quicken the pace of monetary policy tightening. As the Federal Reserve continues to advance the normalisation of its balance sheet, increased US Treasury issuance to fund the tax cuts may add to upward pressure on long-term bond yields. The shadow of rising trade barriers, along with any unexpected escalation of geopolitical tensions, could also threaten the nascent recovery in global trade. In East Asia, real economic growth continued to climb in the second half of 2017, buoyed by strong export performance and steady domestic demand. Nevertheless, while the economic outlook is optimistic, it also faces a variety of downside risks, such as a possible larger-than-expected tightening of global monetary conditions, US inward-looking trade policies, and geopolitical tensions. Should these downside risks materialise, they would also heighten the risk of a reversal in capital flows. Policymakers are confronting multiple challenges: on one hand, they must guard against the risks facing economic growth, while on the other, they must limit the impact of prolonged accommodative financial conditions on inflation and on the fragility of balance sheets. In Mainland China, economic performance was strong in the second half of 2017. During the review period, some progress was made in structural reforms and in curbing systemic risks. The near-term growth outlook remains positive, but uncertainties persist, and this will depend in part on the extent to which the rapid growth of the "new economy" can offset the short-term pressure on growth arising from the further advancement of structural reforms. With economic conditions stabilising and risks receding, capital outflow pressures remained moderate for most of 2017. As the momentum of cyclical economic improvement has become increasingly entrenched since late 2016, growth in advanced and emerging market economies accelerated in tandem in 2017. Among the major advanced economies, the United States saw steady increases in investment and exports, driven by upbeat private-sector sentiment and a substantial depreciation of the US dollar, while the euro area and Japan also recorded a broad-based cyclical recovery. Exports of emerging market economies also benefited from the stabilisation of global commodity prices and rising import demand in the major advanced economies. In the near term, following the passage of tax reform in the United States, investment and consumption are expected to be further boosted by reductions in corporate and personal income taxes. In view of the current cyclical upswing and the expansionary effects of US tax reform, the International Monetary Fund forecast in January that global economic growth would accelerate from an estimated 3.7% in 2017 to 3.9% in 2018 (Chart 2.1). Chart 2.1 Real GDP growth forecasts. As growth momentum in the euro area and Japan strengthened, the market expected global monetary policy divergence to narrow; combined with a more optimistic global growth outlook, this spurred a rise in risk appetite and capital inflows into emerging market economies, thereby putting the US dollar under pressure. Although the Federal Reserve raised interest rates three times during the year and began to advance balance sheet normalisation, the US dollar index still recorded a decline of nearly 10% in 2017. At the same time, despite the broad-based acceleration in economic growth, core inflation in the major advanced economies remained weak and below their central banks' targets, leading the market to expect until recently that global interest rates would remain low (Chart 2.2). Against this backdrop, global stock markets moved steadily higher throughout 2017 and into early 2018, with the S&P 500 Index repeatedly hitting record highs, pushing the cyclically adjusted price-to-earnings ratio to 33.8 in January 2018, the highest since the "dot-com bubble" of early 2000. Chart 2.2 Core inflation in major advanced economies. However, since the second half of 2017, market concerns that tax cuts would lead to a fiscal deficit and rising inflation caused US long-term Treasury yields to climb steadily, casting doubt on whether the increasingly elevated valuations in asset markets could be sustained. As the United States reported a higher-than-expected increase in average hourly earnings for January 2018, the market reassessed US inflation risks, triggering a correction in global stock markets in early February 2018. The S&P 500 Index at one point fell more than 10% from its high on 26 January, fully erasing the significant gains at the start of the year, and remained under pressure after the US government announced a new round of trade protection measures in early March. The benchmark 10-year US Treasury yield also rose to a four-year high in mid-February. Market volatility surged sharply, with the Chicago Board Options Exchange Volatility Index spiking at one point to a two-year high of 37.3, marking the end of the persistently narrow trading environment of the previous two years (Chart 2.3). Chart 2.3 Chicago Board Options Exchange Volatility Index (VIX). Looking ahead, following the short-term stock market volatility, US inflation risks, the risk of rising US long-term bond yields, and the possibility that other major central banks may tighten monetary policy could all lead to a tightening of global monetary conditions, thereby casting a shadow over the global economic outlook. First, with regard to US inflation risks, the recently passed tax reform includes several provisions expected to provide a short-term cyclical stimulus to private consumption and investment. The key measures involved in the tax reform include: (1) lowering corporate and personal income tax rates; (2) temporarily allowing full expensing of capital investment; and (3) a one-off "deemed repatriation" provision that helps reduce US companies' incentive to park their overseas earnings abroad. Although it remains uncertain how the tax cuts will affect domestic demand and inflation, with the US economy now having reached its output potential, the tax cuts could push US output beyond its potential, thereby leading to an overheating of the economy and a cyclical rebound in inflation. If inflationary pressures rise more than expected, this may prompt the Federal Reserve to quicken the pace of monetary policy tightening. At present, the trajectory of the federal funds rate expected by financial markets is flatter than the projections released by the Federal Reserve. However, should inflation rebound unexpectedly, the risk of an abrupt repricing of rate-hike expectations cannot be ruled out (Chart 2.4). Chart 2.4 Federal funds rate forecasts. Second, given that the tax reform could worsen the fiscal deficit, US Treasury issuance is expected to increase going forward. As the Federal Reserve continues to advance its balance sheet normalisation programme, this is expected to lead to a rise in the term premium; in this context, increased US Treasury issuance could add to upward pressure on long-term bond yields. In addition, as the market increasingly anticipated the likelihood of the US passing the tax cut package, US inflation expectations have risen steadily since the second half of 2017 (Chart 2.5). As a result, the benchmark 10-year US Treasury yield, after hovering at low levels for most of 2017, has risen by more than 70 basis points since the third quarter, partly reflecting market concerns over increased Treasury supply pressures and rising inflation expectations. Chart 2.5 Five-year, five-year forward inflation expectations. Furthermore, a key question is whether the natural rate of interest (R*), a major component of long-term interest rates, will remain at low levels over the long term, as most people expect. Although estimates of R* vary, it is generally believed to have fallen substantially since the global financial crisis (Chart 2.6). Nonetheless, owing to (1) an expected decline in the national savings rate resulting from a rising fiscal deficit, and (2) the possibility that corporate tax cuts and more favourable tax treatment of capital expenditure may raise the investment rate, US R* may face upward risks in the future. A rise in R*, together with the expected increase in the term premium arising from Federal Reserve balance sheet normalisation, could signal that long-term interest rates will rise, thereby creating headwinds for asset market valuations. Driven by robust domestic demand and improved export performance, the Hong Kong economy maintained solid growth momentum in the second half of 2017. Economic growth is expected to remain solid in 2018. The economic outlook for Hong Kong is still subject to numerous uncertainties and risks, including the normalisation of monetary policy by major central banks, the stability of global financial markets, rising protectionist sentiment, and the escalation of geopolitical tensions. In the near term, while local inflationary pressures should remain mild, certain upside risks persist. The Hong Kong economy maintained its growth momentum in the second half of 2017. Seasonally adjusted real gross domestic product grew by 0.8% quarter-on-quarter in both the third and fourth quarters, broadly comparable to the average growth rate of 0.9% in the preceding two quarters (Chart 3.1). Compared with the first half of the year, private consumption continued to grow steadily and remained one of the main drivers of GDP growth. Consumption growth was solid, owing to favourable employment and income conditions, continued upbeat consumer sentiment, and the positive impact of rising asset prices through the wealth effect. Although building and construction activity weakened, business capital expenditure increased, causing overall investment expenditure to rise notably in the final quarter after broadly stable performance over three quarters. On the external front, benefiting from improved global trade growth and a gradual recovery in inbound tourism, Hong Kong's export performance improved further (Chart 3.2). Nonetheless, as imports grew faster than exports, net exports of goods continued to drag on GDP growth, while net exports of services made a positive contribution to GDP growth. Chart 3.1 Real GDP growth rate and contributions of major expenditure components. Chart 3.2 Real imports and exports. The sustained economic growth momentum drove an increase in employment in the second half of 2017. Total employment rose by about 0.7% during the period to over 3.85 million persons, with the most notable gains in the construction sector, the financing and business services sector, and the public administration, social and personal services sector. As real GDP growth outpaced employment growth, labour productivity showed signs of further improvement. Economic growth is expected to remain solid in 2018. On the external front, Hong Kong's export performance will continue to benefit from an improving global economic growth outlook and a gradual recovery in inbound tourism. On the domestic front, private consumption is expected to keep growing, mainly owing to favourable labour market conditions. In view of the eventual rise in Hong Kong dollar interest rates, Box 3 examines the impact of a higher mortgage debt-servicing burden on private consumption. As for local fixed capital formation, building and construction activity should grow steadily, benefiting from increased housing supply and the continued commencement of infrastructure projects. Although an improving economic environment will stimulate business capital expenditure, a possible increase in interest rates may have a negative impact. The Government forecasts real GDP growth of 3% to 4% in 2018, while growth forecasts by international institutions and private-sector analysts range from 2% to 4%. However, Hong Kong's growth outlook remains subject to numerous uncertainties and risks, including the external environment mentioned in the preceding sections, the economic performance of Mainland China amid tightening financial conditions, and the developments in Hong Kong's asset markets. Local inflationary pressures remained under control in the second half of 2017, but sequential inflation momentum has shown signs of a slight pickup in recent months. On a year-on-year basis, the underlying Composite Consumer Price Index rose by 1.7% and 1.6% in the third and fourth quarters respectively, broadly comparable to the average increase of about 1.7% in the first half of the year. However, the annualised three-month underlying inflation rate, which reflects inflation momentum, edged up to 2.8% in January 2018 (Chart 3.3). Within this, prices of both tradable goods and services increased. The rebound in rentals of newly signed private residential leases since mid-2016 may also have added to inflation momentum to some extent (Chart 3.4). In addition, labour cost pressures have remained mild over recent quarters (Chart 3.5). Chart 3.3 Different indicators reflecting consumer price inflation. Chart 3.4 Rental component of the Composite CPI and market rentals. Chart 3.5 Unit labour cost and wage per person. As global inflation remains mild and local cost increases are stable, Hong Kong's inflationary pressures are expected to remain mild in 2018, but the underlying inflation rate may gradually pick up from the eight-year low of 1.7% in 2017. For example, owing to the pass-through effect from the growth in newly signed private residential rentals, inflationary pressures may increase somewhat in the second half of 2018. Market consensus forecasts overall inflation at a mild 2.2% in 2018, while the Government forecasts an underlying inflation rate of 2.5%. Although the inflation outlook is mild, upside risks persist. On the external front, should global inflation or commodity prices record larger-than-expected increases, this could add to local inflation momentum. On the domestic front, the labour market has tightened further recently, with the seasonally adjusted unemployment rate falling from 3.4% in 2016 to 2.9% in December 2017—the first time it has dropped below 3% in nearly 20 years (Chart 3.6). The current output gap is estimated to be close to zero, and a significant tightening of the labour market could exert additional upward pressure on inflation. Chart 3.6 Unemployment rate. Following the low interest rates after the 2008 global financial crisis, the mortgage debt of Hong Kong households increased. As the normalisation of US dollar interest rates proceeds, Hong Kong dollar interest rates will eventually follow US dollar interest rates upward, and the future mortgage debt-servicing burden of households will increase accordingly, thereby dragging on household consumption. Therefore, this Box examines the impact of an increased mortgage debt-servicing burden on private consumption in Hong Kong. The mortgage debt-servicing burden refers to the ratio of mortgage debt-servicing payments (i.e. interest payments plus loan principal amortisation) to income. Chart B3.1 illustrates the role of the mortgage debt-servicing burden in the transmission of interest rate shocks to private consumption. In addition to the substitution effect, income effect, and the wealth and collateral effects arising from changes in asset prices as discussed in general economic theory, in the presence of a mortgage debt-servicing burden, interest rate shocks also affect private consumption by altering mortgage interest payments and thereby changing households' disposable income. This impact will be amplified as the outstanding mortgage loan amount increases. In addition, the amount of loan principal amortisation varies with changes in the outstanding mortgage loan amount, which also affects private consumption by altering households' disposable income. Chart B3.1 Determinants of private consumption. To measure the impact of the mortgage debt-servicing burden on private consumption, we estimate the outstanding mortgage debt-servicing ratio (OMDSR) based on outstanding mortgage debt. Unlike the currently used mortgage debt-servicing burden indicator, which applies only to newly originated mortgage debt, the OMDSR covers all outstanding mortgage debt of overall households, which is more closely related to aggregate private consumption. Broadly following the methodology used by the Bank for International Settlements, we measure the OMDSR using the standard formula for fixed instalment payments: where Dt is the amount of outstanding residential mortgage loans in the banking sector, Yt is the total income of owner-occupier households (proxied by the median income of owner-occupier households multiplied by the number of owner-occupier households), and rt and st are, respectively, the average interest rate and term of outstanding mortgage loans. To assess whether the OMDSR can reliably measure the mortgage debt-servicing burden of the entire household sector, it is worthwhile to compare the OMDSR with two commonly used debt-servicing burden indicators. Chart B3.2 shows the estimated OMDSR from 1985 to mid-2017, along with the median mortgage payment and loan repayment to income ratio estimated by the Census and Statistics Department based on the quinquennial Population Census. In the early 2000s, both ratios exhibited a downward trend, consistent with the reduction in overall household mortgage borrowing after the bursting of the 1997 property bubble and the substantial decline in mortgage interest rates over the same period. Despite the substantial rise in property prices after the global financial crisis, these two ratios remained stable, owing to the macroprudential measures imposed by the HKMA on bank mortgage lending, which curbed overall household mortgage leverage. In addition, the lengthening of the term of newly originated mortgage loans also reduced the actual amount of mortgage payments. Chart B3.2 OMDSR and the median mortgage payment and loan repayment to income ratio. We also compare the OMDSR with banks' debt-servicing ratio, which is the actual debt-servicing to income ratio of banks' new mortgage applicants. As shown in Chart B3.3, the OMDSR is lower than banks' debt-servicing ratio, partly because the OMDSR covers not only new mortgages but also existing mortgages. As existing mortgages were taken out when property prices were lower, their payments are correspondingly lower than those of new mortgages. Therefore, the outstanding mortgage debt-servicing burden indicator that covers both existing and new mortgages (i.e. the OMDSR) is lower than the debt-servicing burden indicator for new mortgages (i.e. banks' debt-servicing ratio). In addition, banks' debt-servicing ratio is higher partly because banks, in compliance with the HKMA's prudential regulatory requirements, include non-mortgage loan repayments when calculating the debt-servicing ratio. After the global financial crisis, both the OMDSR and banks' debt-servicing ratio remained stable, mainly owing to the HKMA's implementation of prudential regulation on mortgage lending, which set a cap on banks' debt-servicing ratio, a measure that also helped stabilise the OMDSR. Chart B3.3 OMDSR and banks' debt-servicing ratio for new mortgages. Overall, the OMDSR is broadly consistent with commonly used debt-servicing burden indicators, but the OMDSR has greater timeliness and is able to reflect the burden of overall outstanding mortgage debt rather than just the burden of newly originated mortgage debt. Therefore, we believe that the OMDSR can be used to assess the impact of the mortgage debt-servicing burden on private consumption. To assess the impact of the mortgage debt-servicing burden on private consumption in Hong Kong, we estimate an error-correction model following the methodologies of Lai and Lam (2002) and Kang (2016). In this model, the long-term relationship between real private consumption (proxied by real average private consumption per household) and its determinants is represented in the short-term equation by an error-correction term. Based on existing theoretical and empirical evidence, we take real income (proxied by median household income and deflated by the Composite CPI), real housing and financial wealth (proxied respectively by residential property prices and the Hang Seng Index, and deflated by the Composite CPI), and the OMDSR as the long-term determinants of private consumption.

The Hong Kong dollar exchange rate weakened, while the local interbank market continued to function in an orderly manner. In the second half of 2017, total loans continued to increase, but the pace of growth slowed compared with the first half of the year. Looking ahead, as the normalisation of US monetary policy continues, Hong Kong dollar interest rates may face greater upward pressure. Should sentiment in global financial markets shift abruptly, the volatility of fund flows may increase. In the second half of 2017, the Hong Kong dollar spot exchange rate against the US dollar traded between 7.799 and 7.827 (Chart 4.1). The Hong Kong dollar spot exchange rate strengthened briefly during the period from September to November 2017 and remained at a level close to 7.80. This was mainly due to increased funding demand arising from initial public offering (IPO) activities and banks' cautious attitude towards liquidity management ahead of month-ends and the year-end, which led to tighter liquidity conditions, thereby slowing down interest rate arbitrage activities and increasing the unwinding of Hong Kong dollar short positions. As the tightness in Hong Kong dollar liquidity eased somewhat, and with rising commercial demand for US dollars towards the year-end, the Hong Kong dollar spot exchange rate softened again in mid-December 2017. Moving into 2018, despite increased volatility in global financial markets (particularly equity markets), the Hong Kong dollar continued to function in an orderly manner. During the reporting period, the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate against the US dollar weakened, but the Convertibility Undertaking was not triggered (Chart 4.2). Chart 4.1 Hong Kong dollar exchange rate; Chart 4.2 Fund flow indicators. The nominal effective exchange rate index of the Hong Kong dollar fluctuated slightly in the second half of 2017, but recently faced greater downward pressure as the US dollar weakened further (Chart 4.3). This was largely in line with the movement of the US dollar against most major currencies. As the inflation differential between Hong Kong and its trading partners was small and had a limited impact on the real effective exchange rate index, the real effective exchange rate index of the Hong Kong dollar continued to track closely the movements of the nominal effective exchange rate index. Chart 4.3 Nominal and real effective exchange rates. Portfolio investment by non-residents recorded inflows in the second half of 2017. The latest balance of payments statistics showed that both resident and non-resident equity securities investment recorded inflows in the third quarter, reflecting improved economic prospects in the region and optimistic market sentiment (Table 4.A). Non-resident debt securities investment recorded inflows in the third quarter of 2017, offsetting the outflow of debt investment by residents. A survey of global mutual funds also showed that, as the market held an optimistic view on economic prospects and corporate earnings, both equity and debt investment recorded inflows in the fourth quarter of 2017. In the most recent weeks, the survey data indicated that, despite corrections in global financial markets, equity investment still recorded inflows, while bond investment recorded slight outflows (Chart 4.4). Chart 4.4 Market survey of equity- and bond-related fund flows. Looking ahead, as the normalisation of US monetary policy continues, the negative interest rate spread between the Hong Kong dollar and the US dollar will widen, which may lead to increased arbitrage activities. Therefore, the possibility that the weak-side Convertibility Undertaking of the Hong Kong dollar will be triggered should not be ruled out. This is a normal process under the Linked Exchange Rate System. At the same time, given that the pace of US monetary policy normalisation remains uncertain, and that global macro-financial conditions and market sentiment are changing rapidly, the volatility of Hong Kong dollar fund flows and the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate may increase. The HKMA will continue to safeguard the stability of the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate in accordance with the Currency Board mechanism. Although the US Federal Reserve raised interest rates and continued to shrink its balance sheet, Hong Kong's monetary conditions remained accommodative in the second half of 2017 and in the recent period. The Hong Kong dollar Monetary Base rose further by 1.4% in the second half of 2017, mainly driven by the growth in Certificates of Indebtedness issued for the issuance of banknotes (Chart 4.5). As the Convertibility Undertaking was not triggered, the total of the Aggregate Balance and outstanding Exchange Fund Bills and Notes remained largely unchanged in the second half of the year, staying at about HK$1,226.8 billion. Among these, the Aggregate Balance contracted somewhat, while outstanding Exchange Fund Bills and Notes increased correspondingly. This was due to the additional issuance of Exchange Fund Bills (totalling HK$80 billion) to meet banks' strong demand in liquidity management. Moving into 2018, despite the correction in the stock market, the Monetary Base remained stable. Chart 4.5 Components of the Monetary Base. Meanwhile, the Hong Kong dollar money supply grew further in the second half of 2017, but the pace of growth slowed. The growth of Hong Kong dollar broad money supply (Hong Kong dollar M3) slowed from 8.9% in the first half of the year to 2.5% in the second half. As the major component of Hong Kong dollar M3, Hong Kong dollar deposits rose slightly by 2.2% in the second half of the year (Chart 4.7). Among these, demand deposits grew faster in the second half of the year, partly due to the buoyant asset markets and rising investment demand. An analysis of the corresponding assets showed that, on the one hand, the growth of Hong Kong dollar M3 was supported by the strong growth of Hong Kong dollar loans (Chart 4.6), while on the other hand it was dragged down by the net outflow of Hong Kong dollar funds from the non-bank private sector and the contraction of banks' net foreign currency assets. Chart 4.6 Changes in Hong Kong dollar M3 and its corresponding assets. On the other hand, the growth of foreign currency deposits was mixed. Partly reflecting the depreciation of the US dollar against most major currencies, the growth rate of US dollar deposits fell from 3.0% in the first half of the year to 2.4% in the second half (Chart 4.7). By contrast, other foreign currency deposits, after declining continuously for more than two years, rebounded significantly by 8.4% in the second half of the year. This was mainly driven by the recent rebound in renminbi deposits. As the growth of Hong Kong dollar and US dollar deposits slowed, total deposits with authorized institutions increased slightly by 3.0% in the second half of the year, compared with a growth of 5.6% in the first half. For 2017 as a whole, total deposits grew moderately by 8.7%, broadly similar to 2016. Chart 4.7 Deposit growth. During the period from September to December 2017, funding demand arising from IPO activities increased, while banks adopted a cautious attitude towards liquidity management ahead of month-ends and the year-end, which exerted upward pressure on Hong Kong dollar interbank rates (Chart 4.8). Compared with six months earlier, the overnight and three-month Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rates (HIBORs) rose by 14 and 50 basis points respectively, climbing to 0.25% and 1.26% in December (based on monthly averages). The negative interest rate spread between the one-month to three-month Hong Kong dollar and US dollar interbank rates also narrowed correspondingly. Chart 4.8 Hong Kong dollar and US dollar interbank rates. Meanwhile, the Hong Kong dollar yield curve shifted upward but flattened, broadly in line with the movement of the US dollar yield curve. In the second half of the year, the yield on three-year Hong Kong Government Bonds rose by 63 basis points to close at 1.52% at the end of 2017, while the yield on ten-year Hong Kong Government Bonds rose by a smaller extent, up 33 basis points, to close at 1.83% at the end of 2017 (Chart 4.9). Chart 4.9 Government bond yields, composite interest rate, and average lending rate for new mortgages. Moving into 2018, the Hong Kong dollar interbank market continued to function in an orderly manner. As the year-end funding demand subsided, Hong Kong dollar interbank rates fell back in early January. Since then, despite corrections in global and local stock markets, Hong Kong dollar interbank rates have remained largely stable. The overnight and three-month HIBORs closed at 0.43% and 1.08% respectively at the end of February 2018. At the retail level, although banks' lending rates rose along with the surge in HIBORs, banks' funding costs generally remained low as the deposit base remained large. Despite intense competition in the mortgage lending business, banks' average lending rate for new mortgages rose gradually by 36 basis points to 2.16% in December (Chart 4.9), broadly following the upward trend of the one-month HIBOR. On the other hand, the composite interest rate, which measures the Hong Kong dollar funding cost of retail banks, although rising briefly in October due to increased funding demand from IPO activities, remained soft for most of the second half of the year and closed at 0.38% at the end of December. Looking ahead, as the normalisation of US monetary policy continues, and as other major economies may initiate interest rate normalisation, Hong Kong dollar interest rates may face greater upward pressure. At the same time, fluctuating global market sentiment and rapidly changing macro-financial conditions may increase the volatility of fund flows. Nevertheless, the large Hong Kong dollar Monetary Base can serve as a buffer, helping to moderate any overly rapid increase in Hong Kong dollar interest rates. In addition, banks' prudent liquidity management and access to the Discount Window also help curb excessive volatility in interbank rates. Bank credit grew strongly throughout 2017. The loan growth rate reached as high as 10.2% in the first half of the year, then slowed to 5.3% in the second half (Chart 4.10). In the second half of 2017, the growth of both loans for use in Hong Kong and loans for use outside Hong Kong slowed. By currency, owing to the favourable local economic environment and the relatively low funding cost of the Hong Kong dollar, Hong Kong dollar loans continued to grow rapidly by 9.5% in the second half of the year, while foreign currency loans rose only slightly by 0.1%. Among these, the growth of US dollar loans slowed to 1.8%, partly due to the rise in US dollar funding costs. For 2017 as a whole, total loans recorded strong growth of 16.1%, compared with 6.5% in 2016. Chart 4.10 Loan growth. Loans for use in Hong Kong (including trade financing) grew at a slower pace, falling from 9.4% in the first half of the year to 5.6% in the second half, with mixed performance across major sectors (Chart 4.11). Loan growth for the construction industry and for property development and investment slowed in the second half of the year, partly because since June 2017 the authorities have required banks to strengthen the risk management of loans to property developers. Although merchandise trade and retail sales improved further, loans for trade financing and the transportation sector recorded only relatively modest growth, while loans for the wholesale and retail sector recorded a decline. In contrast, loan growth for financial and finance-related enterprises remained strong, partly reflecting the steady expansion of the financial services industry. Chart 4.11 Domestic loan growth by selected sector. Household debt grew by 6.5% in the second half of 2017, compared with a growth of 5.0% in the first half. Within household debt, personal loans (including credit card advances and other personal-use loans) grew at a further accelerated pace, rising by 12.4% in the second half of the year.

Benefiting mainly from the growth in net interest income, the profitability of retail banks improved in the second half of 2017 compared with the same period in 2016. The capital and liquidity positions remained sound. After experiencing strong growth in the first half of 2017, credit growth slowed in the second half, while asset quality remained sound by historical standards. Despite the significant rise in the Hong Kong dollar interbank offered rate (HIBOR), retail banks' Hong Kong dollar funding costs remained low due to low retail deposit rates. However, banks should be vigilant about the risks of increased interest rate volatility and possible capital outflows amid the normalisation of US monetary policy, as well as geopolitical risks. Given the continued rise in corporate leverage levels and the high level of household debt burden, banks should assess the potential impact on asset quality of an interest rate increase exceeding expectations. To enhance banks' resilience against systemic risks, Hong Kong's countercyclical capital buffer ratio will be raised to 2.5% with effect from 1 January 2019.  In the second half of 2017, retail banks' overall pre-tax operating profit grew by 13.6% compared with the same period a year earlier. This was mainly attributable to a substantial increase in net interest income and a reduction in loan impairment provisions, which was sufficient to offset the decrease in non-interest income. However, as assets grew faster than earnings, the return on assets of retail banks edged down slightly from 1.17% in the first half to 1.15% in the second half of 2017. Nevertheless, the return on assets in the second half of 2017 was still higher than the 1.11% recorded in the same period of 2016 (Chart 5.1). For the full year of 2017, retail banks' overall pre-tax operating profit grew by 15.8%, while the return on assets rose from 1.09% in 2016 to 1.16%. Empirical evidence suggests that the improvement in net interest margin was consistent with the rise in the average spread of Hong Kong dollar corporate loans in the Hong Kong syndicated loan market (Chart 5.3). The consolidated capital adequacy ratio of locally incorporated authorised institutions remained well above the international minimum standard, indicating that the Hong Kong banking sector's capital remained strong. At the end of December 2017, the total capital ratio increased to 19.1% from 18.7% at the end of June (Chart 5.6), while the Tier 1 capital ratio also rose to 16.6%, of which 15.4% was Common Equity Tier 1 capital.  Chart 5.6 Capital of locally incorporated authorised institutions  The HKMA recently issued a consultation paper to consult on the rules for setting out loss-absorbing capacity requirements applicable to authorised institutions under the Financial Institutions (Resolution) Ordinance. While enhancing authorised institutions' loss-absorbing capacity helps reduce the likelihood of a financial crisis and thereby benefits society, it inevitably also generates costs. Box 5 conducts a cost-benefit assessment of the potential impact of the loss-absorbing capacity requirements on Hong Kong. Our assessment indicates that the implementation of the loss-absorbing capacity requirements will bring net benefits to the Hong Kong economy.  As measured by the Liquidity Coverage Ratio requirement under Basel III, the banking sector's liquidity position remained sound during the review period. The average Liquidity Coverage Ratio of Category 1 institutions rose from 144.2% in the second quarter of 2017 to 155.1% in the fourth quarter (Chart 5.7), well above the statutory minimum requirement of 80% applicable to 2017. Although the average Liquidity Maintenance Ratio of Category 2 institutions declined slightly from 49.7% in the second quarter of 2017 to 49.4% in the fourth quarter, it remained well above the statutory minimum requirement of 25%. The ample liquidity of authorised institutions shows that the Hong Kong banking sector is able to withstand a liquidity shock arising from possible capital outflows from Hong Kong.  Chart 5.7 Liquidity Coverage Ratio  The Net Stable Funding Ratio, as one of the Basel III liquidity standards, was implemented in Hong Kong on 1 January 2018. The requirement aims to reduce banks' medium- to long-term funding risk by requiring banks to maintain sufficient stable funding sources to finance their business activities. Specifically, Category 1 institutions must maintain a Net Stable Funding Ratio of not less than 100% at all times.  Customer deposits remained the main source of funding for authorised institutions, reflecting the stable funding structure maintained by the banking system. At the end of December 2017, customer deposits as a proportion of the total liabilities of all authorised institutions remained largely the same as six months earlier, at 56.2% (Chart 5.8). In the second half of 2018, the global economy continued to grow. However, while the US economy grew steadily, growth momentum in other regions slowed. Among the advanced economies, growth in Japan and several major eurozone countries slowed, and inflation remained low. The slowdown in global trade flows and the significant fall in oil prices both posed cyclical headwinds to emerging market economies. In view of the slowing global growth momentum, the International Monetary Fund in January lowered its global growth forecasts for 2019 and 2020 by 0.2 and 0.1 percentage points respectively compared with its October 2018 forecasts. Amid a dimmer growth outlook and escalating trade frictions, global equity markets experienced significant volatility at the end of 2018. The US Treasury yield curve flattened to levels not seen since the global financial crisis, triggering market concerns over an imminent US recession. However, US economic fundamentals remained sound, and the likelihood of a recession in the short term was low. Nonetheless, the global economic outlook remained full of uncertainties. In the US, although mild inflation gave the Federal Reserve room to pause rate hikes, the Fed's policy leaning towards being data-dependent also signalled that financial markets could become more sensitive to subsequently released data, particularly data that could prompt monetary policy tightening, such as rising US inflation. Meanwhile, the outcomes of the trade negotiations between the US and China, as well as between the US and the EU, remained uncertain. In the UK, whether a solution to avoid a "hard Brexit" could be achieved remained an open question. During the review period, the global economy continued to grow, but its growth momentum weakened under the combined influence of special and cyclical headwinds, particularly noticeably in regions outside the United States. In view of the dimming growth outlook, the US Federal Reserve adjusted its monetary policy stance, emphasising that decisions would be "data-dependent" and require "patience", and no longer providing forward guidance on further interest rate hikes. As the Federal Reserve's policy leans towards being data-dependent, financial markets may become more sensitive to subsequently released data, and may regard monetary policy as having become more uncertain. Meanwhile, global trade policy uncertainties and intensifying geopolitical risks may continue to cast a shadow over the global economic outlook. In East Asia, as signs of a slowdown in the US interest rate hike cycle emerged, coupled with the stabilisation of the US dollar, financial markets have been largely stable since the end of 2018. However, due to the deteriorating external environment—namely the unresolved China-US trade conflict and weakening growth in advanced economies—the region may face a broad-based slowdown. On the Mainland of China, growth momentum further slowed in the second half of 2018, and amid the China-US trade conflict and the financing difficulties faced by small enterprises, uncertainty over the growth outlook has risen. As a result, policymakers have adopted more targeted measures to stabilise the economy and support the private sector and small enterprises. Facing these challenges, policymakers will need to strike a careful balance between continuing to guard against and control systemic risks and supporting businesses and the real economy. In the second half of 2018, the global economy continued to grow broadly. However, although the US economy remained generally robust, some signs of a slowdown had emerged. There were also clear signs that growth momentum in regions outside the United States had slowed. A number of country-specific shocks—including natural disasters in Japan, the implementation of new automobile emission standards in Germany, the surge in Italian sovereign bond yields due to the fiscal standoff with the European Union, and social unrest in France—all weighed on economic activity in advanced economies (Chart 2.1). In addition, a cyclical slowdown in global import growth emerged, posing headwinds to industrial production in emerging market economies (Chart 2.2). The sharp fall in oil prices in the fourth quarter also posed new challenges to emerging market economies that export commodities. In view of the weakening growth momentum in the second half of 2018, the International Monetary Fund lowered its 2019 global growth forecast by 0.2 percentage points to 3.5% in January. In the fourth quarter, owing to the slowing global growth momentum, intensifying trade policy uncertainties, market concerns over the sustainability of US corporate earnings growth, and the Federal Reserve's statements that monetary policy would continue to tighten, global equity markets underwent a substantial correction. As financial market sentiment deteriorated, the US Treasury yield curve flattened to levels not seen since the global financial crisis, prompting some market participants to worry that the United States was heading towards a recession (Chart 2.3). Chart 2.3 The 10-year and 3-month US Treasury yield spread and the probability of a US recession. Nevertheless, the likelihood of a recession in the United States in the near term is very low. US economic fundamentals remain sound, and in particular the tight labour market is expected to continue to support private consumption. At the same time, the US output gap is estimated to have only returned to positive territory last year, making it less likely that economic overheating would prompt the Federal Reserve to tighten monetary policy substantially. However, possibly taking into account the significant tightening of financial conditions since the fourth quarter, senior Federal Reserve officials began in early January to emphasise that monetary policy would be data-dependent, and pointed out that mild inflationary pressures allowed them to remain "patient" in determining future monetary policy adjustments. In addition, following its meeting in January, the Federal Open Market Committee no longer provided forward guidance on further rate hikes, and announced that it "would be prepared to adjust any of the details for completing balance sheet normalisation in light of economic and financial developments". This shift triggered a rebound in global equity markets (Chart 2.4). Despite the Federal Reserve's recent "dovish" signals, the outlook for US monetary policy remains fairly uncertain, hinging on inflation and other developments. Inflationary pressures have so far been mild, giving the Federal Reserve room to advance monetary normalisation gradually. Inflation expectations have remained stable in recent years, supporting the view that it "can be patient" (Chart 2.5). Moreover, as Federal Reserve Chairman Powell pointed out in January, the US economic outlook faces multiple headwinds, including slowing growth in regions outside the United States and trade policy uncertainty. In view of these developments, the Federal Reserve may need to adopt a more cautious monetary policy stance. Chart 2.5 Market-based and survey-based indicators of US inflation expectations. However, the tight labour market is expected to continue to support the overall performance of the US economy. In this environment, wage growth may accelerate, which usually signals that future inflation may intensify (Chart 2.6). Therefore, the market's expectation, which has essentially ruled out the possibility of a Federal Reserve rate hike in 2019, may be overly optimistic (Chart 2.7).
