In sum, a prolonged pause in Federal Reserve rate hikes is not a foregone conclusion. To reduce policy mistakes, the Federal Reserve has increasingly emphasised that its decisions would be data-dependent, as a risk management strategy. It can therefore be inferred that financial markets may become more sensitive to subsequently released data, particularly data that could prompt monetary policy tightening. The monetary policies of other major central banks are also uncertain. In the euro area, the European Central Bank ended its asset purchase programme in December, while continuing to reinvest, in full, the principal repayments of maturing securities under the asset purchase programme, and reiterated its forward guidance of keeping policy rates unchanged at least through the summer of 2019. However, the European Central Bank lowered its short-term growth assessment in January, describing the risks to the growth outlook as having "moved to the downside". The impact of this downgrade in the European Central Bank's economic growth assessment on monetary policy remains to be seen. In Japan, the Bank of Japan indicated at its most recent policy meeting that it would ease its monetary policy stance when necessary amid increasing downside risks. However, the resistance to further monetary policy easing may be considerable, as its effectiveness has been questioned and the drawbacks of maintaining an ultra-low interest rate environment over the long term have become increasingly apparent—for example, as persistently low yields continued to weigh on profitability, the capital ratio of regional banks fell from 10.6% in 2015 to 9.7% in 2018. Therefore, the Bank of Japan has very limited room to adjust monetary policy in the near term. Apart from the uncertainties relating to the global monetary policy outlook, the uncertain outcome of future trade negotiations and intensifying geopolitical risks are two other major sources of risk facing the global economic outlook. In early December, the US government announced that it would not raise tariffs on imported goods from China within 90 days, and extended the deadline again at the end of February, but whether the two sides can reach a long-term trade agreement remains to be seen. Meanwhile, the trade negotiations between the United States and the European Union have made almost no progress at this stage. As the outcomes of these trade negotiations remain uncertain, they may continue to cast a shadow over the global economic outlook. Policy and geopolitical risks are also quite prominent. In the United States, disagreements between the two parties over border security funding led to a 35-day federal government shutdown from late December 2018 to late January 2019. Although the impact of the shutdown on economic growth should be short-lived, tensions between the Trump administration and the Democratic-controlled House of Representatives may lead to more policy gridlock in the future. In the United Kingdom, after Prime Minister May's Brexit deal was overwhelmingly rejected in mid-January, risks relating to Brexit and its knock-on effects surged, and whether a plan could be devised at the last minute to avoid a disruptive "hard Brexit" remains unknown. Elsewhere, geopolitical tensions in the Middle East—such as the reimposition of US sanctions on Iran—may also create uncertainties for oil prices, thereby affecting the global growth outlook. In East Asia, financial markets, after fluctuating repeatedly in the first three quarters of last year, largely stabilised in the fourth quarter. The US dollar has stabilised since October, and there have been signs that the Federal Reserve is being patient regarding further rate hikes, easing the currency depreciation and capital outflow pressures faced by East Asian economies. A number of currencies in the region rose slightly against the US dollar in the fourth quarter, while portfolio investment flows returned to net inflows (Chart 2.8). Chart 2.8 East Asia: currency indices and fund flows. Despite the stability of financial markets, there are increasing signs that the region will face a broad-based slowdown. As the China-US trade conflict weakened global trade momentum, export growth in the region declined, causing real gross domestic product growth in most East Asian economies to slow in the second half of last year. Indeed, the new export orders sub-index of the Purchasing Managers' Index (which reflects short-term external trade performance) of several economies in the region has fallen into contractionary territory since the fourth quarter, signalling that short-term growth momentum may slow further (Chart 2.9). Chart 2.9 The new export orders index of the Markit Purchasing Managers' Index of East Asian economies. In an environment of slowing growth, coupled with the recent fall in oil prices, inflationary pressures in East Asia have eased (Chart 2.10). Chart 2.10 East Asia: headline inflation rate and oil prices. As the recent inflationary pressures and upward pressure on the US dollar have both been relatively mild, East Asian central banks have had no urgent need to raise interest rates, which has alleviated the policy dilemma of choosing between promoting economic growth and curbing inflation and capital outflows. However, as private sector debt in some East Asian countries remains high by emerging market standards, central banks still face the challenge of financial imbalances (Chart 2.11).

The China-US trade conflict gradually intensified in the second half of 2018: the US imposed 25% tariffs on goods imported from Mainland China worth US$34 billion and US$16 billion on 6 July and 23 August respectively. In immediate response to these two measures, Mainland China imposed 25% tariffs on an equivalent value of US goods. On 24 September, the US further escalated by imposing 10% tariffs on goods imported from Mainland China worth US$200 billion. Mainland China immediately responded by imposing tariffs of 5% to 10% on US goods worth US$60 billion. Since then, the two countries have entered negotiations to avoid further tariffs. As Hong Kong has always been an entrepôt between these two economies, the imposition of tariffs will inevitably have a direct impact on Hong Kong through trade channels. Therefore, the China-US trade dispute has important implications for Hong Kong's macroeconomic and financial stability. This Box reviews Hong Kong's recent merchandise trade performance and explores its near-term outlook. We will also attempt to use more granular data to distinguish the traded goods directly affected by the tariffs, so as to examine the impact of the tariffs more closely. In order to analyse the impact of the tariffs, we first extracted data on six groups of Hong Kong re-export goods, which were respectively affected by the various rounds of tariffs described in the previous section. In the first two rounds of tariffs, the US mainly imposed tariffs on capital goods and semi-finished products, while Mainland China mainly targeted agricultural products, chemicals, medical equipment, and energy equipment. In the third round of tariffs, the range of affected goods was expanded to cover more consumer goods. For brevity, we name the goods affected by these three rounds of tariffs List 1, List 2, and List 3 respectively. After collecting these more granular trade data, we focus on analysing the year-on-year changes in the value of Hong Kong's re-exports to adjust for the impact of seasonal factors. In addition, readers should be cautious when analysing the September 2018 data, as trade activity in that month was disrupted to some extent by super typhoon Mangkhut. Overall, the analytical results in this section should only be regarded as preliminary evidence of the impact of the tariffs. The Hong Kong dollar exchange rate strengthened in September and November, partly reflecting the unwinding of carry trades amid liquidity tightening driven by anticipated seasonal funding demand. Entering 2019, the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate gradually weakened, partly due to corporations repatriating funds raised from initial public offerings (IPOs) and the market re-establishing carry trade positions, and it triggered the weak-side Convertibility Undertaking in March. Nevertheless, trading of the Hong Kong dollar remained smooth and orderly. Hong Kong interbank interest rates (HIBOR) rose broadly in the second half of 2018, reflecting expectations of US interest rate hikes and seasonal funding demand, before easing in January 2019. Looking ahead, in the face of uncertainties such as ongoing China-US trade frictions, Brexit negotiations, and the increasingly unpredictable pace of US monetary policy normalisation, fund flows for the Hong Kong dollar may become more volatile. Should the interest rate spread between the Hong Kong dollar and the US dollar remain wide, market carry trade activities may persist, causing the Hong Kong dollar to continue to be on the weak side for some time and potentially triggering the weak-side Convertibility Undertaking again, which is in line with the design of the Linked Exchange Rate System.  Following the triggering of the weak-side Convertibility Undertaking in late August, the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate moved away from 7.8500 and traded between 7.8062 and 7.8499, until it triggered the weak-side Convertibility Undertaking again a total of four times up to March 2019 (as of 19 March) (Chart 4.1). The Hong Kong dollar exchange rate rose briefly in September, partly reflecting the unwinding of carry trades amid liquidity tightening, but it then declined gradually in October. The Hong Kong dollar stabilised again after November, due to the unwinding of carry trades resulting from liquidity tightening driven by year-end funding demand. Entering 2019, the spot exchange rate weakened, partly reflecting corporations repatriating funds raised from IPOs and the market re-establishing carry trade positions. As the interest rate spread between the Hong Kong dollar and the US dollar widened after the year-end, market participants engaged in carry trade activities buying US dollars and selling Hong Kong dollars, driving the Hong Kong dollar to weaken gradually, and the weak-side Convertibility Undertaking was triggered again in March. Despite the triggering of the weak-side Convertibility Undertaking, trading of the Hong Kong dollar remained smooth and orderly. The Aggregate Balance stayed at around HK$76 billion since August (Chart 4.2), and slightly declined to HK$70.9 billion after the weak-side Convertibility Undertaking was triggered in March (as of 19 March). The funds flowing out of the Hong Kong dollar since April 2018 only accounted for a small portion of the approximately HK$1 trillion that had flowed in since 2008.  Chart 4.1 Hong Kong dollar exchange rate Chart 4.2 Fund flow indicators  The nominal effective exchange rate index of the Hong Kong dollar broadly tracked movements in the US dollar and continued to rise during the review period (Chart 4.3). As the inflation rate differential between Hong Kong and its trading partners was very small and thus had limited impact on the real effective exchange rate index of the Hong Kong dollar, the trend of the real effective exchange rate index broadly followed that of the nominal effective exchange rate index.  Chart 4.3 Nominal and real effective exchange rates  The latest balance of payments statistics show that portfolio investment continued to record outflows in the third quarter of 2018. Amid weak market sentiment and heightened volatility in the equity market, outflows of local residents' equity securities investment accelerated, more than offsetting the inflows of non-resident portfolio investment in the third quarter (Table 4.A). By contrast, debt securities investment by both local residents and non-residents recorded inflows in the third quarter. Looking ahead, in the face of uncertainties such as ongoing China-US trade frictions, Brexit negotiations, and the increasingly unpredictable pace of US monetary policy normalisation, fund flow volatility may intensify. In addition, the significant negative interest rate spread between the Hong Kong dollar and the US dollar may stimulate carry trade activities, leading to fund outflows. Under the Linked Exchange Rate System, the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate may weaken, and the weak-side Convertibility Undertaking may be triggered again. Both fund outflows and the possible triggering of the weak-side Convertibility Undertaking are part of the normal operation of the Linked Exchange Rate System.  Despite the ongoing US interest rate normalisation process and the multiple triggering of the weak-side Convertibility Undertaking between April and August, the monetary conditions in Hong Kong remained accommodative in the second half of 2018. The Hong Kong dollar Monetary Base contracted slightly by 0.7% in the second half of the year, standing at HK$1,632.9 billion at the end of 2018 (Chart 4.4). The contraction in the Monetary Base was mainly due to the triggering of the weak-side Convertibility Undertaking in August 2018, which caused the Aggregate Balance to decrease from HK$109.5 billion at the end of June 2018 to HK$76.4 billion at the end of 2018, while the Certificates of Indebtedness, government-issued currency notes and coins in circulation, and outstanding Exchange Fund Bills and Notes increased slightly. The Hong Kong dollar Monetary Base remained broadly stable in the first two months of 2019, with the Aggregate Balance showing no significant change since August. Subsequently, due to the triggering of the weak-side Convertibility Undertaking in March, the Aggregate Balance declined slightly to around HK$70.9 billion (as of 19 March).  Chart 4.4 Components of the Monetary Base  As for the broader Hong Kong dollar money supply indicators, the growth in money supply generally slowed in the second half of the year, partly reflecting increased uncertainties in the macroeconomic and financial environment. Hong Kong dollar broad money supply (Hong Kong dollar M3) grew by 3.6% in the first half of the year, but only increased slightly by 0.1% in the second half (Chart 4.5). As the major component of Hong Kong dollar M3, Hong Kong dollar deposits showed little change compared with the end of June (Chart 4.6). Among Hong Kong dollar deposits, demand deposits and savings deposits declined, partly due to the reduction in investment-related transactions in the second half of the year; on the other hand, time deposits continued to record strong growth as deposit interest rates were raised. Analysis of the corresponding assets shows that the growth of Hong Kong dollar M3 slowed due to changes in banks' capital and reserves (recorded under "net other items").  Chart 4.5 Changes in Hong Kong dollar M3 and its corresponding assets  The growth of foreign currency deposits accelerated in the second half of the year. US dollar deposits grew strongly by 8.8% in the second half of the year as banks raised their preferential US dollar deposit rates and attracted more deposits, thus becoming the main driver of the growth in foreign currency deposits (Chart 4.6). Other foreign currency deposits grew slightly by 1.4% in the second half of the year, among which renminbi deposits continued to record growth. Overall, the total deposits of authorized institutions grew moderately by 3.3% in the second half of the year, slightly faster than the 1.6% increase in the first half.  Chart 4.6 Deposit growth  Despite the still-large scale of the Hong Kong dollar Monetary Base and deposits, Hong Kong dollar interbank interest rates began to face some upward pressure in the second half of 2018, mainly reflecting US interest rate hikes. Seasonal liquidity demand occasionally pushed up short-term interbank interest rates, causing the latter to be more volatile than long-term interbank interest rates (Chart 4.7). The 3-month and 12-month HIBOR averaged 2.32% and 2.74% respectively in December, about 30 basis points higher than the June averages. Entering 2019, as seasonal demand subsided, Hong Kong dollar interbank interest rates declined overall. The averages of the 3-month and 12-month HIBOR fell to 1.65% and 2.39% respectively in February.  Chart 4.7 Hong Kong dollar and US dollar interbank interest rates  The Hong Kong dollar yield curve shifted downward in the second half of 2018, broadly following the movements of the US dollar yield curve. Compared with the end of June 2018, the yields on 3-year and 10-year Hong Kong Government Bonds fell by 45 and 37 basis points respectively, to 1.56% and 1.83% at the end of February 2019 (Chart 4.8).  Chart 4.8 Government bond yields, composite interest rate, and average lending rate for new mortgages  During the review period, the composite interest rate, which measures the average Hong Kong dollar funding cost of retail banks, rose slightly. Reflecting changes in interbank and deposit funding costs, the composite interest rate rose from 0.62% at the end of June to 0.89% at the end of December 2018, before easing to 0.83% at the end of January 2019 (Chart 4.8). Given the rise in funding costs, following the upward adjustment of the target range for the US federal funds rate in September, retail banks raised their Best Lending Rates by 12.5 to 25.0 basis points. After the target range for the US federal funds rate was raised again in December, retail banks did not make further adjustments to their Best Lending Rates. On the other hand, the average lending rate for new mortgages rose in tandem with the Best Lending Rate, standing at around 2.45% at the end of January 2019. Looking ahead, the trend of US dollar interest rates, fund flows, and local financial market activities (such as IPO subscription activities) will continue to be the main drivers of Hong Kong dollar interest rates. Given the still-large Hong Kong dollar Monetary Base and the large holdings of Exchange Fund Bills and Notes by the banking system, the pace of increase in Hong Kong dollar interest rates should be relatively moderate, as banks can use the Exchange Fund Bills and Notes as collateral to borrow Hong Kong dollar funds through the Discount Window.  Against the backdrop of intensifying China-US trade frictions, both the offshore renminbi and onshore renminbi exchange rates recorded depreciation against the US dollar since the beginning of 2018 (Chart 4.9). However, amid the optimism driven by the resumption of high-level China-US trade negotiations, the offshore and onshore renminbi exchange rates stabilised in November. Meanwhile, the spread between the onshore renminbi and the offshore renminbi was not significant during the review period.  Chart 4.9 Onshore and offshore renminbi exchange rates  At present, the ongoing China-US trade frictions have not yet had a significant impact on the funding conditions in the offshore interbank market. As liquidity conditions remained broadly stable, the overnight offshore renminbi Hong Kong interbank interest rate (CNH HIBOR) stayed below 4% for most of the review period, rising only occasionally under the influence of seasonal factors (Chart 4.10). The 3-month offshore renminbi interbank interest rate hovered around 4% between September and December 2018, before falling to 3.02% at the end of February 2019, which may reflect the recent monetary easing measures introduced by the People's Bank of China. Nevertheless, it remains to be seen how the progress of the China-US trade negotiations will affect the liquidity in the offshore renminbi interbank market in 2019. Benefiting mainly from an increase in net interest income, the profitability of retail banks continued to improve in the second half of 2018 compared with the same period in 2017. Their capital and liquidity positions also remained robust. Reflecting the upward pressure on Hong Kong dollar interbank interest rates and retail deposit rates amid US interest rate normalisation, the overall Hong Kong dollar funding cost of retail banks rose notably, but remained at a relatively low level. Amid an uncertain external environment, bank credit contracted moderately in the second half of 2018. Nonetheless, credit growth has shown signs of stabilising since November, and asset quality remained sound by historical standards. Looking ahead, the Hong Kong banking sector will face multiple headwinds arising from persistent uncertainty over Sino-US trade relations, a global economic slowdown, an increasingly uncertain pace of the US monetary policy tightening cycle, and geopolitical risks. Given that corporate leverage has continued to rise, banks should stay vigilant to the impact on the credit risk of their corporate loan exposures should the external environment deteriorate further.  The overall pre-tax operating profit of retail banks grew by 14.3% compared with the same period in 2017, while the return on assets also rose from 1.14% to 1.23% (Chart 5.1). This strong performance was driven mainly by a substantial increase in net interest income, which was sufficient to offset the increase in loan impairment allowances and operating expenses. For 2018 as a whole, the overall pre-tax operating profit of retail banks grew by 19.4%, while the return on assets rose from 1.16% in 2017 to 1.27%. Chart 5.1 Retail banks' profitability. The net interest margin of retail banks widened further to 1.67% in the fourth quarter, compared with 1.5% in the same period last year (Chart 5.2). Chart 5.2 Retail banks' net interest margin. Largely reflecting further US interest rate hikes and a reduction in interbank Hong Kong dollar liquidity following the triggering of the weak-side Convertibility Undertaking in August 2018, Hong Kong interbank funding costs continued to face upward pressure in the second half of 2018. Specifically, the three-month Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rate rose by 23 basis points in the second half of 2018 (Chart 5.3). As banks generally raised time deposit rates to secure stable long-term funding, Hong Kong dollar retail deposit rates also rose during the review period. In addition, following the US rate hike decision at the end of September, banks raised their Best Lending Rate and correspondingly raised their savings deposit rates. Given the rise in both wholesale and retail funding costs, the composite interest rate (a measure of the average cost of Hong Kong dollar funds of retail banks) rose from 0.62% in June 2018 to 0.89% in December, but remained at a relatively low level by historical standards. Chart 5.3 Interest rates. (a) Period-end figures. (b) Period-average figures for newly approved loans.  More broadly, the overall Hong Kong dollar and US dollar funding costs of Hong Kong's licensed banks continued to trend upward. In the second half of 2018, banks' average overall Hong Kong dollar and US dollar funding costs rose by 36 basis points, following a rise of 40 basis points in the first half (the red line in Chart 5.4). Chart 5.4 Licensed banks' Hong Kong dollar and US dollar funding costs and maturity. The cumulative increase in the Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rate outpaced the increase in Hong Kong banks' overall funding costs, which may have a positive effect on retail banks' HIBOR-based mortgage loans, which the industry has also been actively promoting over the past few years. However, future improvements in net interest margin may become more limited, as most HIBOR-based mortgage loans have already reached the cap rate benchmarked against the Best Lending Rate. As the timing of future increases in the Best Lending Rate remains unclear, amid US interest rate normalisation, the continued upward trend in banks' funding costs may weigh on the overall net interest margin. Looking ahead, increased uncertainty in the external environment may cloud banks' profit outlook. In particular, against the backdrop of slowing global economic growth, persistent uncertainty over Sino-US trade relations may dampen business confidence and reduce demand for bank credit. Should this lead to a significant decline in loans and a deterioration in asset quality, it may weigh on banks' profitability.  The capital base of Hong Kong's banking sector remained strong, well above international minimum standards. At the end of 2018, the consolidated total capital ratio of locally incorporated authorized institutions rose further to 20.3% (Chart 5.5). The Tier 1 capital ratio also increased to 17.9%, of which 16.0% was Common Equity Tier 1 capital. Chart 5.5 Capital base of locally incorporated authorized institutions. 1. As such, capital ratios from March 2013 onwards are not directly comparable with data up to December 2012. In addition to the risk-based capital adequacy ratio, Basel III also introduced a non-risk-based leverage ratio requirement to constrain excessive leverage in the banking system. The minimum leverage ratio requirement took effect in Hong Kong in 2018, and the leverage ratio of locally incorporated authorized institutions remained at a sound level of 8.0% at the end of December 2018, exceeding the statutory minimum of 3% (Chart 5.6). As measured by the Liquidity Coverage Ratio requirement under Basel III, the liquidity position of the banking sector remained sound during the review period. The average Liquidity Coverage Ratio of Category 1 institutions rose from 156.6% in the second quarter of 2018 to 167.6% in the fourth quarter (Chart 5.7), well above the statutory minimum requirement of 90% applicable in 2018. The average Liquidity Maintenance Ratio of Category 2 institutions also rose from 51.3% in the second quarter to 54.3% in the fourth quarter, likewise well above the statutory minimum requirement of 25%. Chart 5.7 Liquidity Coverage Ratio. 1. Consolidated positions. 2. Quarterly average figures. The Net Stable Funding Ratio, one of the Basel III liquidity standards, showed that the funding positions of authorized institutions were stable. The average Net Stable Funding Ratio of Category 1 institutions remained at a high level of 135.6% in the fourth quarter of 2018 (Chart 5.8), well above the statutory minimum requirement of 100%. The average Core Funding Ratio of Category 2A institutions remained at a high level of 134.3%, also exceeding the statutory minimum requirement of 50% applicable in 2018. The ample liquidity and sound funding positions of authorized institutions indicate that Hong Kong's banking sector is capable of withstanding various liquidity shocks. At the end of 2018, the proportion of customer deposits in the total liabilities of all authorized institutions rose slightly from 54.5% six months earlier to 55.7% (Chart 5.9). Against the backdrop of persistent uncertainty over the Sino-US trade conflict, tightening global financial liquidity, and slowing global economic growth, credit growth slowed markedly in the second half of 2018. However, credit growth has shown signs of stabilising since November 2018. On a half-yearly basis, total loans and advances of all authorized institutions fell by 0.9% in the second half of 2018, following a 5.3% increase in the first half (Chart 5.12). This decline was due to a slowdown in the growth of domestic loans (including loans for use in Hong Kong and trade financing) and a fall in loans for use outside Hong Kong. Domestic loan growth slowed to 0.1% in the second half, while loans for use outside Hong Kong contracted by 3.0% over the same period, compared with increases of 5.3% and 5.2% respectively in the preceding six months. The coronavirus outbreak that erupted in early 2020 has simultaneously hit both demand and supply, posing challenges to the global economy that differ from those of previous crises. Although major central banks and some governments have rolled out stimulus measures since early March to counter the economic shock brought about by the pandemic, financial markets remained volatile and global financial conditions have tightened. Despite the uncertainties in the external and local environments, Hong Kong's foreign exchange and money markets continued to operate smoothly and in an orderly manner. Amid a stronger Hong Kong dollar exchange rate, a stable Aggregate Balance, and moderate growth in total deposits, no significant outflow of funds from the Hong Kong dollar or the Hong Kong banking system was observed during the review period. After moderately rebounding in the first half of 2019, the growth of total loans slowed in the second half of the year. The residential property market has generally softened since mid-2019, though its trend has been somewhat volatile. Looking ahead, the Hong Kong banking sector will continue to face a number of downside risks, including uncertainties arising from the spread of the coronavirus, future China-US trade relations, geopolitical tensions, and local social incidents. Given the persistent rise in corporate leverage levels and personal debt burdens, banks should prudently assess the impact on the asset quality of their loan portfolios should these risk factors intensify.  Since the fourth quarter of 2019, global economic growth has shown preliminary signs of stabilising, benefiting from major central banks stepping up monetary easing, the easing of China-US trade tensions, and the reduced risk of a "no-deal Brexit" in the United Kingdom. However, since late January, the number of global coronavirus infection cases has continued to rise, sparking market concerns and triggering sharp volatility in global financial markets. To address the evolving risks of the pandemic, several major central banks slashed interest rates significantly and expanded liquidity tools, while some governments also introduced targeted measures to support the real economy. Nonetheless, amid rising credit spreads and plunging equity markets, global financial conditions have tightened. Looking ahead, downside risks to the global economic outlook have increased. The coronavirus outbreak will hit global economic activity, and the extent of the impact on the economy will depend on the severity and persistence of the pandemic. In the medium term, relations between the United States and its major trading partners may once again turn tense, while trade negotiations between the United Kingdom and the European Union following Brexit may also prove difficult.  Weak global demand continued to weigh on economic growth in the East Asia region.¹ The region's exports to major destinations such as the United States, European economies, and Mainland China remained weak in the second half of 2019. Some of the region's major telecommunications equipment exporters recently reported growth in their earnings, but whether the technology product cycle will rebound broadly remains to be seen. Financial markets reacted positively to the China-US Phase One trade agreement announced in December 2019, and the trade truce reduced to some extent the uncertainties surrounding global trade. Nevertheless, East Asia will continue to face adverse factors such as weak corporate earnings and high private-sector leverage ratios. Meanwhile, the coronavirus outbreak has raised concerns that the region's economy may come under further pressure amid persistently weak growth. Travel bans imposed by a number of economies in the region may hit Asia's tourism industry, particularly those economies that are more reliant on the export of tourism services. As the region's supply chains are closely linked to those of Mainland China, the manufacturing sector may also be affected by the outbreak.  As for Mainland China, economic growth continued to slow in the second half of 2019 due to weak domestic and external demand. Looking ahead, although the signing of the China-US Phase One trade agreement helps to temporarily reduce the external uncertainties facing the Mainland economy, downward pressures persist in the face of the coronavirus outbreak, the ongoing economic rebalancing, and the impact of the global economic slowdown. The Central Economic Work Conference held in December 2019 set stabilising the economy as the priority for 2020, while also placing emphasis on controlling financial risks. The latest consensus forecast indicates that Mainland economic growth will slow to 5.2% in 2020. During the review period, the Mainland authorities continued to announce targeted monetary and fiscal policies to support the private sector, particularly small private enterprises. Despite these measures, some media reports and market analysts have pointed out that private industrial enterprises may have faced a decline in shareholders' equity in recent years, which has been regarded as a sign of a "retreat of the private sector". Box 2 examines the drivers of equity changes among Mainland industrial enterprises using 2018 listed company data, and finds that private or small enterprises are not inherently more prone to downsizing or "retreat". While the study finds that negative earnings are the largest driver, other factors, particularly structural factors, are also worth noting (for details, please refer to Box 2).  Local economic activity contracted significantly in the second half of 2019. Real Gross Domestic Product declined continuously over the past three quarters, indicating that the local economy has entered a recession. Dragged down by this, the economy contracted by 1.2% for the whole of 2019, worse than the 2.9% growth in 2018, and marked the first annual contraction since 2009. The slowdown in local demand, particularly the contraction in private consumption, was the main factor dragging down GDP in the second half of 2019. Local social incidents seriously affected consumption activity, resulting in a weak economic outlook and thereby dampening consumer and business confidence. With the renewed escalation of China-US trade frictions, the slowdown in global economic growth, and the serious decline in inbound tourism, Hong Kong's external trade performance remained sluggish. Given that the economy is facing significant headwinds, the Government rolled out several rounds of economic stimulus measures between August and December 2019. In order to provide banks with greater room to step up their support for the local economy and to help smooth out the economic cycle, the HKMA announced on 14 October that it would lower the Countercyclical Capital Buffer ratio for banks from 2.5% to 2.0%, thereby allowing banks to release an additional HK$200 billion to HK$300 billion in lending capacity to enterprises, particularly small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs).  Economic performance in 2020 is expected to face considerable challenges, and the pandemic has recently posed significant downside risks. As sectors such as retail, accommodation services, food services, tourism, and transportation have yet to recover from the disruption caused by the social incidents, the pandemic will deliver a double blow to these sectors. However, a series of countercyclical measures announced in the 2020/21 Budget can provide relief to households and enterprises (particularly SMEs), including the disbursement of a one-off cash payout to adult permanent residents and the provision of concessionary low-interest loans with a 100% government guarantee to enterprises under the "SME Financing Guarantee Scheme". On 16 March 2020, the HKMA further lowered the Countercyclical Capital Buffer ratio for banks from 2.0% to 1.0%, which will provide banks with greater room to step up their support for the local economy, particularly for sectors and individuals facing greater short-term pressure as a result of the pandemic. Analysing by the components of GDP, private consumption and investment are likely to remain weak owing to fragile consumer and business confidence. Although government consumption will support economic growth, public investment expenditure is expected to be relatively subdued as some major infrastructure projects are completed. On the external front, the China-US Phase One trade agreement is expected to have a slight positive impact on the local economy in the short term. However, weak global economic growth and trade activity will continue to weigh on Hong Kong's external trade performance. In particular, the coronavirus outbreak may cause disruptions to supply chains in the region and a slowdown in cross-border economic activities (such as tourism), thereby constraining Hong Kong's export performance. The Government forecasts real GDP growth in 2020 to be between -1.5% and 0.5%, while the average growth forecast of international institutions and private-sector analysts is -1.5%. This weak economic outlook is affected by numerous uncertainties and risks, including the slowdown in global economic growth, China-US trade relations, Mainland China's economic performance, and local social incidents.  The labour market came under greater pressure in the second half of 2019 and early 2020, with total employment declining, the unemployment rate rising, and the real wage index falling year on year. Specifically, the unemployment rate rose from a multi-year low of 2.8% in June 2019 to 3.7% in February 2020, partly reflecting the impact of the social incidents and the pandemic outbreak on the retail, accommodation, and food services sectors. Looking ahead, given the weak economic outlook and the coronavirus outbreak, the unemployment rate will climb further. Box 3 will explore in greater detail the recent developments and short-term outlook of the labour market.  Local inflationary pressures continued to accumulate up to the third quarter of 2019, mainly owing to the impact of rising fresh pork prices; thereafter, as economic activity weakened, inflationary momentum gradually slowed. Owing to weak economic conditions, the consolidation of private residential rents, and moderate imported inflation, inflation is expected to ease in the short term. Market consensus forecasts headline inflation in 2020 to be between 0.6% and 3.7%, while the Government forecasts underlying inflation at 2.5%.  Supported by increased Hong Kong dollar demand related to equities (including initial public offerings), the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate gradually strengthened from mid-October 2019. Entering December, the upward momentum of the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate strengthened further, partly due to buoyant IPO activity and partly due to the unwinding of Hong Kong dollar short positions prompted by tightening liquidity towards year-end. After the Lunar New Year holidays, liquidity conditions eased somewhat, and the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate softened slightly towards the end of February. Overall, Hong Kong dollar trading continued to be smooth and orderly during the review period, and the Convertibility Undertaking was not triggered. The Aggregate Balance remained stable at around HK$54 billion. Since the fourth quarter of 2019, short-term Hong Kong dollar interbank rates have been volatile, reflecting seasonal liquidity demand as well as increased capital market activities such as IPOs. Box 4 examines how market attention to future IPO activity affects the three-month HIBOR. Meanwhile, the composite interest rate rose gradually from 0.94% at the end of July 2019 to 1.01% at the end of January 2020, reflecting banks' continued increases in preferential deposit rates to attract deposit funds. As some banks raised the interest rate caps set with reference to the Best Lending Rate, the average interest rate on new mortgages rose to around 2.6% in October, but as the Best Lending Rate in the market was lowered from November, the average interest rate on new mortgages edged down slightly to around 2.5% by January 2020.  Amid a stronger Hong Kong dollar exchange rate, a stable Aggregate Balance, and moderate growth in total deposits, no significant outflow of funds from the Hong Kong dollar or the Hong Kong banking system was observed during the review period. However, we need to monitor the impact of any further worsening of the coronavirus pandemic amid the uncertain external environment. With Hong Kong's ample foreign exchange reserves and robust banking system, the HKMA has the ability, resources, and determination to cope with fund outflows and to maintain Hong Kong's monetary and financial stability. Towards the end of 2019, global economic activity showed signs of stabilisation, raising market hopes for a global economic recovery. However, since late January 2020, the continued rise in coronavirus infection cases worldwide has dashed these hopes of recovery, deepening investors' concerns over a global economic recession and triggering a sell-off in global financial markets. To counter the economic shock, major central banks and some governments have rolled out stimulus measures since early March. In view of the spread of the epidemic, the downside risks to the global economic growth outlook have increased. In East Asia, weak global demand since the second half of 2019 has cast a shadow over the outlook of economies in the region. The coronavirus outbreak is expected to weigh on economic growth in the region in the near term, with the tourism industry being particularly hard hit. On the other hand, the East Asian region also continues to face the challenges of weak corporate earnings and elevated private-sector leverage ratios. As for Mainland China, economic growth continued to slow in the second half of 2019 due to weak domestic and external demand. Looking ahead, although the signing of the Phase One trade agreement between China and the US helps to temporarily reduce external uncertainties, downside pressures persist amid the impact of the coronavirus outbreak, the ongoing economic rebalancing and the global economic slowdown, while the authorities' monetary and fiscal policy responses will provide some buffer. Amid persistent trade tensions and policy uncertainty, the manufacturing sector and investment remained sluggish, and global economic growth stayed weak in the second half of 2019. Nevertheless, economic growth showed preliminary signs of stabilisation early in the final quarter (Chart 2.1), partly benefiting from the earlier accommodative policies of the US Federal Reserve and the European Central Bank, as well as the easing of global trade tensions following the signing of the "Phase One" trade agreement between China and the US. However, since late January, the continued rise in coronavirus infection cases worldwide and the subsequent economic shock they brought raised market concerns, and a wave of sell-offs emerged in global financial markets (Chart 2.2). Given that Mainland China is a major global export destination and occupies an important position in the global supply chain, when the epidemic disrupts production activities on the Mainland and drags down its economic growth, it will create significant spillover effects that may spread across the globe (Chart 2.3). However, financial markets still face immense sell-off pressure, leading to a significant tightening of global financial conditions, which may in turn intensify the downside pressure on the global economy (Chart 2.4). Chart 2.4 Bloomberg Advanced Economies Financial Conditions Index. Apart from the developments of the epidemic, other downside risks and uncertainties also loom over the global economic outlook. In particular, regarding trade tensions, although policy risks have declined after China and the US reached the Phase One trade agreement, subsequent negotiations may prove difficult as many thorny structural issues remain to be resolved. In Europe, trade negotiations between the EU and the UK are not expected to go smoothly, thereby prolonging post-Brexit uncertainties. In addition, oil prices have plummeted since March, which will exert pressure on major oil-exporting emerging economies. In East Asia, owing to sluggish global demand, real economic activity remained weak in the second half of 2019. Exports from the East Asian region to major destinations such as the US, European economies and Mainland China remained weak in the second half of 2019 (Chart 2.5). Although there are preliminary signs that the downcycle in technology products in the region is bottoming out and rebounding — including reports by major electronics companies in the region of improved earnings towards the end of 2019 6 — whether there is a genuine rebound in the region's technology product exports remains to be seen. Chart 2.5 East Asia: Merchandise exports to major destinations. Persistently weak economic growth and trade uncertainties have also weighed on investor sentiment, with total fixed capital investment in most East Asian economies declining in 2019 (Chart 2.6), which may affect the region's potential economic growth in the long run. In order to support economic growth in an environment of moderate inflation, the central banks of Indonesia, the Philippines and South Korea further lowered their policy rates in the second half of the year after cutting rates in the first half of 2019, while the Bank of Thailand also lowered its policy rate for the first time since 2015. Chart 2.6 East Asia: Gross fixed capital formation. The coronavirus outbreak has raised concerns that economies in the region may come under further pressure amid persistently weak growth. As many economies in the region have imposed entry and exit restrictions on Mainland China, the tourism industry has borne the brunt, with economies more reliant on Mainland Chinese visitors and tourism service exports being more heavily affected by this epidemic (Chart 2.7). A prolonged and intensified epidemic would also affect supply chains in the region that are closely linked with Mainland China. Chart 2.7 East Asia: Tourism exports and Chinese visitors. In the near term, this epidemic will continue to affect economic activity and investor sentiment. Drawing on the experience of the 2003 SARS outbreak, these effects may be temporary, but the actual situation will depend on the severity and extent of the spread of the epidemic and the effectiveness of government actions to contain the outbreak. Meanwhile, East Asian economies also face multiple headwinds. First, although the market expects corporate earnings to deteriorate in the near term (Chart 2.8), accommodative global monetary conditions encourage yield-seeking activities, thereby pushing up asset prices without fundamental support. As a result, stock markets in the region are more susceptible to shifts in investor sentiment. Chart 2.8 Expected earnings of constituent stocks of benchmark stock indices. Second, weak corporate earnings and economic growth may make it more difficult for private-sector institutions in the region to repay debt. Although declining local interest rates can provide breathing space for indebted corporates and households, they may also sow the seeds of further debt accumulation. Moreover, as discussed in Box 1, when more index-tracking funds flow into the region's financial markets, the risk of a debt overhang among private-sector institutions may also intensify, although this impact may be confined to corporates with more solid financial foundations and their long-term borrowings. Third, in terms of external factors, East Asian economies may also face increased risks amid an increasingly protectionist US trade policy. Despite the recent progress in the China-US Phase One trade agreement, China-US trade tensions persist as fundamental trade issues between the two countries remain. As shown by the continued increase in the trade surpluses of several economies in the region with the US (Chart 2.9), multinational corporations may continue to seek additional supply channels outside China-centred supply chains in order to circumvent tariffs. As of November 2019, the cumulative trade surplus of nine emerging Asian economies (excluding China) with the US had risen to about US$167 billion. If the trade surpluses with the US continue to widen, the relevant Asian economies may become the next targets of the trade war; for example, the US government imposed hefty tariffs of up to 456% on steel imports from Vietnam in July 2019. 7 In view of this, despite the China-US trade truce, the region's trade outlook remains highly uncertain. Chart 2.9 Merchandise trade surpluses with the US. Over the past decade, intensified integration of international financial markets has led to a significant increase in global cross-border portfolio investment flows. A recent study shows that up to 70% of these cross-border investment flows are driven by index-driven funds. 8 Index-driven funds include not only funds that closely track investment indices (commonly referred to as passive funds) but also actively managed funds that reference investment indices. 9 By introducing overseas investors that the relevant economies would otherwise be unable to attract or reach, these funds help drive the development of financial markets in emerging market economies. Thus, such funds enable emerging market economies to diversify their investor base, which helps the long-term growth and stability of the markets. However, is there really such a thing as a free lunch? In the case of passive bond funds, the market is concerned that such funds' investment may weaken the financial discipline of the corporate bond issuers in which they invest, thereby leading to elevated leverage levels among the relevant corporates. 10 In addition, some argue that the growth of index-driven funds in recent years has intensified the volatility of global portfolio investment flows, making emerging market economies — which are already highly sensitive to global factors and influenced by other common factors — even more vulnerable. 11 This Box assesses the impact of index-driven investment on financial stability with respect to these two propositions. Passive bond funds allocate their investment funds to the relevant bonds according to the weights of the constituent bonds in the benchmark index. Therefore, relative to actively managed bond funds, the mechanical investment decisions adopted by passive bond funds may reduce issuers' incentive to act in the fund investors' interests. 13 Worse still, from a financial stability perspective, such behaviour may fuel excessive borrowing, posing significant credit and solvency risks to the corporate sector of emerging market economies, whose leverage ratios have risen sharply since the global financial crisis (Chart B1.1). Chart B1.1 Corporate leverage in emerging market economies. Using the weights of emerging market economy corporates in a mainstream index tracking emerging market economy corporate bonds as a proxy for the extent to which their bonds are invested in by passive bond funds, 14 we find that an increase in such investment would push up the long-term (rather than short-term) leverage ratios of the corporate issuers of the relevant bonds. The solid blue bars in Chart B1.2 represent the estimated impact. In addition to driving the development of the emerging market economy corporate bond market, the expanded long-term bond investor base brought about by passive bond funds also benefits the development of emerging market economy corporates. We also find that the above effect has a significant impact only on emerging market economy corporates with more solid fundamentals (in particular, stronger solvency and lower leverage ratios) (the solid green bars in Chart B1.2). Facing higher financial distress costs, highly leveraged or less solvent corporates appear not to fall further into a debt trap as a result of passive bond fund investment. In sum, the above research shows that the growth of passive bond fund investment may not necessarily substantially increase the solvency risks of the corporate sector in emerging market economies.

The Hong Kong economy contracted in the second half of 2019 and entered its first recession since 2009, as private consumption weakened, investment spending fell and export performance was lacklustre. Economic performance in 2020 is expected to face considerable challenges, while the coronavirus epidemic has also recently posed significant downside risks. The economic outlook is being affected by numerous uncertainties and risks, including the slowdown in global economic growth, the Sino-US trade relationship, the economic performance of Mainland China and the development of local social incidents. In view of the various headwinds facing the economy, the unemployment rate is likely to rise further in 2020. Local inflationary pressure is expected to ease somewhat, though its outlook faces potential risks on both the upside and downside. The Hong Kong economy contracted markedly in the second half of 2019. On a year-on-year basis, real Gross Domestic Product (GDP) contracted by 2.8% and 2.9% in the third and fourth quarters respectively (Table 3.A). Dragged down by the economic contraction in the second half of the year, the economy contracted by 1.2% for the whole year, worse than the 2.9% growth in 2018, and also the first annual contraction recorded since the global financial crisis in 2009. Figure 3.1 Real GDP growth rate and the contributions of major expenditure components. On a quarter-on-quarter basis, economic activity slowed markedly in the second half of the year (Figure 3.1). Specifically, real GDP fell successively by 0.4%, 3.0% and 0.3% in the second, third and fourth quarters, indicating that the economy had entered a recession. On the domestic front, private consumption was the main factor dragging down GDP in the third quarter. Local social incidents severely affected consumption activities, thereby weakening the economic outlook and denting consumer confidence, so private consumption contracted markedly starting from the third quarter.33 As economic uncertainties increased and the business sentiment worsened, total investment spending remained weak and dragged down GDP in the fourth quarter.34 On the external front, with the intensification of Sino-US trade frictions, weakening global economic growth and a sharp drop in the number of visitor arrivals to Hong Kong, Hong Kong's external trade performance remained sluggish (Figure 3.2).35 Under the influence of the sharp contraction in the export of services, net exports dragged down GDP in the third quarter, but provided support to GDP growth in the fourth quarter, partly reflecting an improvement in the visible trade balance. Figure 3.2 Real imports and exports. In view of the substantial headwinds facing the economy, the Government introduced multiple rounds of measures between August and December 2019 to alleviate the financial burden of the public, safeguard employment, and support enterprises, in particular small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) as well as severely affected sectors, such as retail, catering services, transport and tourism.36 In order to give banks greater room to step up their support to the local economy and help smooth the economic cycle, the HKMA announced on 14 October a reduction of banks' countercyclical capital buffer ratio from 2.5% to 2.0%, thereby enabling banks to release an additional HK$200 billion to HK$300 billion in lending capacity to enterprises, including SMEs. Hong Kong's economic performance in 2020 is expected to face considerable challenges, while the epidemic has also recently posed significant downside risks. As some sectors have yet to recover from the damage caused by the social incidents, the epidemic will deal a double blow to these sectors. Nevertheless, a series of countercyclical measures announced in the 2020/21 Budget can provide assistance to households and enterprises (especially SMEs), including the distribution of a one-off cash payment to adult permanent residents and the provision of concessionary low-interest loans with a 100% government guarantee to enterprises under the "SME Financing Guarantee Scheme".37 On 16 March 2020, the HKMA further lowered banks' countercyclical capital buffer ratio from 2.0% to 1.0%, which will give banks greater room to step up their support to the local economy, in particular sectors and individuals that are under greater pressure in the short term due to the impact of the epidemic. Analysed by GDP components, private consumption and investment are likely to remain weak owing to fragile consumer and business confidence. Although government consumption will underpin economic growth, public investment spending is expected to be relatively subdued as some major infrastructure projects are completed. On the external front, the Sino-US Phase One trade agreement is expected to have a slight positive impact on the local economy in the short term.38 However, weak global economic growth and trade activities will continue to weigh on Hong Kong's external trade performance. In particular, the coronavirus outbreak may lead to disruptions in regional supply chains and a slowdown in cross-boundary economic activities (such as tourism), thereby constraining Hong Kong's export performance. The Government forecasts real GDP growth of between -1.5% and 0.5% in 2020, while the average growth forecast of analysts from international institutions and the private sector is -1.5%. This weak economic outlook is affected by the numerous uncertainties and risks described in the preceding chapters. The labour market faced greater pressure in the second half of 2019 and at the beginning of 2020. The seasonally adjusted unemployment rate rose from a multi-year low of 2.8% in June 2019 to 3.3% in December 2019, and climbed further to 3.7% in February 2020 (Figure 3.3). Among these, the unemployment rate in the retail, accommodation and catering services sectors rose to a near-decade high of 6.1%, partly reflecting the severe blow caused by the social incidents.39 As economic momentum weakened, total employment fell by 0.5% year-on-year in the second half of 2019 and continued to decline to 3,768,800 in February 2020. Among these, the decline in employment mainly came from the trade, wholesale, retail, accommodation, catering services and construction sectors. Real wages also fell by 0.3% year-on-year in the third quarter. Looking ahead, in view of the weak economic outlook mentioned above, the labour market will continue to face more challenges, and the unemployment rate is very likely to climb further. Box 3 will explore the recent developments and short-term outlook of the labour market in greater detail. Figure 3.3 Labour market conditions. Local inflationary pressure continued to build up until the third quarter of 2019, mainly owing to the impact of rising fresh pork prices; thereafter, as economic activity weakened, inflationary momentum gradually slowed. On a year-on-year basis, the underlying Composite Consumer Price Index grew by 3.3% in the third quarter, and the increase eased slightly to 3.0% in the fourth quarter. The 3-month-on-3-month annualised underlying inflation rate, which reflects inflationary momentum, also softened from a high of 4.7% in August 2019 to 2.1% in January 2020. The slowdown in inflationary momentum was due to reduced price pressures on various components of the Consumer Price Index. In terms of traded goods, underlying food inflation remained notable owing to rising fresh pork prices, but price pressures on consumer goods such as clothing and footwear, and durable goods, remained mild. In terms of services, as the growth of newly signed private residential rentals slowed earlier, the growth of the rental component of the Consumer Price Index also showed a downward trend (Figure 3.5). Labour cost pressures rose slightly but remained at mild levels in the most recent quarters (Figure 3.6). Figure 3.4 Different indicators reflecting consumer price inflation. Figure 3.5 Rental component of the Composite Consumer Price Index and market rentals. Figure 3.6 Unit labour cost. Local inflationary pressure is expected to ease somewhat in the short term. On the domestic front, the weak economic conditions and the widened negative output gap will continue to exert downward pressure on local inflation. As private residential rentals continue to slow, the housing rental component of inflation should ease further. On the external front, import inflation is expected to remain mild owing to weak global economic growth and soft energy prices. The market consensus forecasts that the headline inflation rate in 2020 will range between 0.6% and 3.7%, while the Government forecasts an underlying inflation rate of 2.5% and a headline inflation rate of 1.7%. This inflation outlook is affected by risk factors on both the upside and downside. On the one hand, given that the estimated negative output gap has widened since the third quarter of 2019, if the economy deteriorates more severely than expected (for example, due to a prolonged coronavirus epidemic), inflation may be further suppressed. On the other hand, if the disruption to fresh pork supply becomes more severe, it will pose upward pressure on inflation. Despite the marked slowdown in the Hong Kong economy, the unemployment rate in the first nine months of 2019 still remained at a low level of 2.8-2.9%. It was only as the social incidents persisted that the unemployment rate climbed more noticeably to 3.3% at the end of 2019. Affected by the coronavirus epidemic, the labour market will face greater headwinds in 2020. Against this backdrop, this Box analyses the recent developments and short-term outlook of the labour market, including exploring why the overall labour market remained largely resilient in the first three quarters of 2019 (with the unemployment rate barely changing), and what implications this has for future developments. This article also examines some risk factors that may lead to a sharp rise in the unemployment rate. It is worth noting that, partly because adjusting labour demand entails costs, the unemployment rate is a lagging indicator. In fact, the unemployment rate tends to lag the year-on-year growth rate of real GDP by about two to three quarters (Figure B3.1). This lagging nature can explain why the unemployment rate remained low at around 2.9% when real economic activity deteriorated sharply in the third quarter. Figure B3.1 Real GDP growth rate and unemployment rate. In terms of labour demand, although the Sino-US trade tensions and local social incidents dealt heavy blows to employment in the trade, and retail and tourism-related sectors respectively, some major sectors were still able to support the overall labour market. Specifically, employment in the financial, business, public administration, social and personal services sectors continued to grow in 2019, partly offsetting the impact of the decline in employment in the trade and retail sectors (Figure B3.2). Despite the economy entering a recession, Hong Kong's financial system remained robust, and financial activities in areas such as fintech development and new share listings were also very active. These factors may all help support the employment market in the financial and business services sectors. In addition, the public administration, social and personal services sectors, including education, healthcare and social work activities, appear to be less sensitive to the economic cycle. Correlation analysis shows that, while employment in many sectors is highly correlated with real GDP, employment in the public administration, social and personal services sectors reacts more neutrally to the economic cycle. In other words, even if the economy slows, employment in these sectors may not be greatly affected by cyclical factors. Figure B3.2 Changes in employment by sector in 2019. In terms of labour supply, the labour force participation rate40 fell from 61.2% in 2018 to 60.5% in 2019, providing a cushion against the rise in the unemployment rate. Figure B3.3 shows the various demand and supply factors affecting the change in the unemployment rate (blue line). As shown in the chart, the labour force participation rate (green bars) exerted downward pressure on the unemployment rate in 2019.41 On the other hand, the increase in employment in the first half of 2019 (purple bars) also helped restrain the unemployment rate. However, as the economy contracted markedly in the second half of the year, the decline in employment exerted upward pressure on the unemployment rate. Taken together, although employment declined during the economic recession, the lower labour force participation rate helped ease the pressure of the rising unemployment rate in the second half of 2019. The Hong Kong dollar exchange rate has strengthened since October, with the upward momentum strengthening further in December, keeping the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate on the strong side of the Convertibility Undertaking range in recent months. The strong demand for the Hong Kong dollar came partly from equity-related demand and partly from the unwinding of short Hong Kong dollar positions prompted by tighter liquidity towards the end of the year. Overall, the Hong Kong foreign exchange and money markets continued to operate in a smooth and orderly manner. Despite the uncertain external environment, in which the coronavirus outbreak affecting market sentiment could lead to increased volatility in fund flows, Hong Kong has ample foreign exchange reserves and a robust banking system, and is therefore capable of withstanding the pressure of capital outflows without affecting the city's financial stability. Supported by increased equity-related demand for the Hong Kong dollar (including initial public offerings), the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate has gradually strengthened since mid-October (Chart 4.1). Entering December, the upward momentum of the Hong Kong dollar strengthened further, and from mid-December through February, the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate remained on the strong side of the Convertibility Undertaking range. The strengthening of the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate was due partly to buoyant initial public offering activity and partly to the unwinding of short Hong Kong dollar positions prompted by tighter liquidity towards the end of the year. After the Lunar New Year holidays, liquidity conditions eased somewhat, and the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate softened slightly, closing at 7.7956 on 28 February. Overall, during the review period, Hong Kong dollar trading continued to be smooth and orderly. As neither the strong-side nor the weak-side Convertibility Undertaking was triggered during the review period, the Aggregate Balance remained unchanged at around HK$54 billion (Chart 4.2). Chart 4.1 Hong Kong dollar exchange rate. Chart 4.2 Aggregate Balance and outstanding Exchange Fund Bills and Notes. The nominal effective exchange rate index of the Hong Kong dollar broadly tracked the movement of the US dollar and edged up during the review period (Chart 4.3). As the inflation differential between Hong Kong and its trading partners was very small and therefore had limited impact on the real effective exchange rate index of the Hong Kong dollar, the movement of the real effective exchange rate index broadly followed that of the nominal effective exchange rate index. Chart 4.3 Nominal and real effective exchange rates. In gauging Hong Kong's fund flows, it is essential to distinguish between two distinct but interrelated concepts of fund flows: (1) Hong Kong dollar fund flows; and (2) cross-border fund flows. Hong Kong dollar fund flows focus on the currency dimension of fund flows and are useful for assessing monetary stability, particularly under the Linked Exchange Rate System. On the other hand, cross-border fund flows focus on the movement of funds across geographical regions through the Hong Kong banking system, which is useful for assessing the stability of Hong Kong's overall financial system. The two concepts of fund flows require different monitoring indicators. In monitoring Hong Kong dollar fund flows, attention should be paid to the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate and the Aggregate Balance. If the public or investors convert large amounts of their Hong Kong dollar assets into foreign currency assets, the demand for the Hong Kong dollar will naturally decline, causing the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate to weaken. Under the Linked Exchange Rate System, if the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate weakens to the weak-side Convertibility Undertaking rate of HK$7.85 to US$1, the HKMA stands ready to buy Hong Kong dollars at banks' request, and the Aggregate Balance will subsequently decrease. Since April 2019, the Aggregate Balance has remained broadly unchanged, and the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate has been on the strong side of the Convertibility Undertaking range in recent months, so no significant outflow from the Hong Kong dollar was observed during the review period. In monitoring cross-border fund flows, total bank deposits in Hong Kong are a useful indicator. When there are large capital outflows from the Hong Kong banking system, bank deposits will inevitably decrease. During the review period, total deposits grew at a moderate pace, indicating that there was no significant cross-border capital outflow. Hong Kong's foreign exchange and money markets continued to operate in a smooth and orderly manner, indicating that the impact of the coronavirus outbreak on the city's monetary environment remained limited. Nevertheless, we need to closely monitor the risks arising from the coronavirus outbreak. Hong Kong has ample foreign exchange reserves and a robust banking system, and the HKMA has the ability, resources and determination to cope with capital outflows and maintain Hong Kong's monetary and financial stability. Despite the uncertain external environment and the local economic slowdown, Hong Kong's monetary environment remained relatively accommodative during the review period. The Hong Kong dollar Monetary Base remained large, rising by 4.0% since the end of June to HK$1,689.4 billion at the end of January 2020 (Chart 4.4). As the Convertibility Undertaking was not triggered during this period, the Aggregate Balance remained broadly unchanged at around HK$54 billion. Other components of the Monetary Base, including outstanding Exchange Fund Bills and Notes, Certificates of Indebtedness, and government-issued notes and coins in circulation, rose steadily. Chart 4.4 Components of the Monetary Base. During the review period, broad measures of Hong Kong dollar money supply remained broadly stable. The Hong Kong dollar broad money supply (Hong Kong dollar M3) grew by 3.5% in the first half of 2019 and subsequently edged up by 0.2% over the seven-month period since the end of June 2019. Analysis by counterpart assets shows that the growth of Hong Kong dollar M3 since the end of June mainly reflected an increase in banks' net foreign currency assets, as well as a rise in the Monetary Base (through the increase in Certificates of Indebtedness and government-issued notes and coins in circulation) (Chart 4.5). Over the seven-month period since the end of June 2019, Hong Kong dollar deposits (the main component of Hong Kong dollar M3) remained broadly unchanged (Chart 4.6). Within Hong Kong dollar deposits, time deposits continued to grow moderately, partly reflecting the rise in Hong Kong dollar deposit rates. Chart 4.5 Changes in Hong Kong dollar M3 and counterpart assets. Over the seven-month period since the end of June 2019, foreign currency deposits grew moderately by 2.3% (Chart 4.6), driven mainly by US dollar deposits, which increased by 3.5% over this period. Other foreign currency deposits fell by 1.0% over the same period, with renminbi deposits recording a slight decline in Hong Kong dollar terms. Overall, total deposits with authorized institutions grew steadily by 1.2% since the end of June. Supported by the increase in total deposits, Hong Kong's total broad money supply also rose at a relatively stable pace, with total money supply M2 and M3 increasing by 1.6% and 1.5% respectively since the end of June (Chart 4.7). As monthly monetary statistics may fluctuate due to various short-term factors (such as seasonal and IPO-related fund demand, as well as business- and investment-related activities), the statistics should be interpreted with care. Chart 4.6 Deposits with authorized institutions by currency. Chart 4.7 Total broad money supply (M2). Although the monetary environment remained relatively accommodative, short-term Hong Kong dollar interbank interest rates fluctuated, reflecting seasonal liquidity demand and the increase in capital market activity since the fourth quarter of 2019—particularly the buoyant initial public offering activity in the Hong Kong stock market. The Hong Kong dollar overnight interbank interest rate experienced relatively large fluctuations at times in late October and mid-November (Chart 4.8).⁴⁴ During the review period, other short-term Hong Kong dollar interbank interest rates generally rose. Subscriptions for large new share listings can exert significant pressure on overnight interbank rates, and Box 4 shows through empirical analysis that market attention on future initial public offering activity can also affect the 3-month Hong Kong dollar interbank interest rate. This situation arises if market participants anticipate the future subscription deadlines of large new share listings in advance and prepare medium-term funds ahead of time for early positioning. Chart 4.8 Hong Kong dollar and US dollar interbank interest rates. As for the Hong Kong dollar yield curve, it moved downward in line with the US dollar yield curve. Compared with the end of June 2019, the yield on 10-year Hong Kong Government Bonds fell by 60 basis points to 1.04% on 28 February 2020 (Chart 4.9). Meanwhile, the yield on 3-year Hong Kong Government Bonds fell by 50 basis points to 1.00% over the same period. Chart 4.9 Government Bond yields, composite interest rate and average lending rate for new mortgages. As for the retail level, the composite interest rate, which reflects the average cost of Hong Kong dollar funds for retail banks, gradually rose from 0.94% at the end of July 2019 to 1.01% at the end of January 2020. This increase mainly reflected banks' continued raising of preferential deposit rates to attract deposit funds, which in turn pushed up the Hong Kong dollar weighted deposit rate. At the end of October 2019, following the downward adjustment of the target range for the US federal funds rate, a number of retail banks lowered their best lending rates by 12.5 basis points. As a result, the best lending rates of retail banks are currently in the range of 5.00% to 5.50%. On the mortgage lending front, for Hong Kong dollar interbank interest rate–based mortgage loans, major banks raised the ceiling set with reference to the best lending rate, so the average lending rate for new mortgages in October rose to around 2.63%.⁴⁵ As best lending rates in the market have been lowered since November, the average mortgage lending rate accordingly declined slightly to 2.53% in January 2020. In response to the evolving risks posed by the coronavirus outbreak to US economic activity, and to support the US Federal Reserve in achieving its policy objectives, the Federal Reserve cut the target range for the federal funds rate by a total of 150 basis points to 0–0.25% on 3 March (US time) and 15 March (US time). Although Hong Kong dollar interbank interest rates track US dollar interest rates in the long run, short-term Hong Kong dollar interbank interest rates may be affected by local factors that could influence the demand for the Hong Kong dollar, such as local new share listing activity. As the Aggregate Balance of the banking system has decreased since April 2018, the sensitivity of Hong Kong dollar interbank interest rates to changes in the supply of and demand for Hong Kong dollar funds may have increased. However, this does not mean that the current Aggregate Balance level of HK$54 billion is insufficient to meet the demand for interbank payment settlement. In fact, Hong Kong's interbank market has been operating in an orderly manner. Should liquidity become tight in the short term, banks can make use of the liquidity facilities provided by the HKMA. In view of the possible escalation of the China-US trade conflict, the offshore and onshore renminbi exchange rates weakened significantly in late August and September 2019, with the offshore renminbi falling against the US dollar to a ten-year low of 7.19 on 2 September (Chart 4.10).
