Amid increasing uncertainties in the global and local economic environment, the profitability of Hong Kong's retail banks recorded a slight decline in the second half of 2019. Nevertheless, the capital and liquidity positions of Hong Kong's banking sector remained strong and robust by international standards. Asset quality remained at a healthy level by historical standards. Although the growth of total loans slowed somewhat in the second half of last year, it still outpaced deposit growth over the same period during the review period. Correspondingly, the average loan-to-deposit ratios of all authorized institutions in all currencies, as well as the Hong Kong dollar loan-to-deposit ratio, both increased. However, given the stable level of the aggregate balance in the banking system and the broadly steady deposits, the liquidity position of the banking sector remained sound. Looking ahead, Hong Kong's banking sector will continue to face a number of downside risks, including uncertainties arising from the spread of the coronavirus, the future course of Sino-US trade relations, geopolitical tensions, and local social incidents. Given the continued rise in corporate leverage levels and personal debt burdens, banks should prudently assess the impact on the asset quality of their loan portfolios should these risk factors potentially intensify.  In the second half of 2019, the overall pre-tax operating profit of retail banks[59] fell slightly by 1.5% compared with the same period in 2018. Correspondingly, the return on assets dipped slightly to 1.13% in the second half of 2019, lower than the 1.23% recorded in the same period of 2018 (Chart 5.1). Although the net interest margin of retail banks narrowed slightly from 1.67% in the second half of 2018 to 1.63% in the same period of 2019 (Chart 5.2), the net interest income of retail banks continued to record moderate growth during the review period. However, both loan impairment provisions and operating expenses of retail banks increased, resulting in a slight decline in profitability. Chart 5.1 Profitability of retail banks. Chart 5.2 Net interest margin of retail banks.  Despite the US federal funds target rate being cut three times by 25 basis points each in the second half of 2019, the Hong Kong dollar wholesale funding market has not yet shown significant downward pressure so far. On the contrary, affected by a number of local factors (including seasonal funding demand, increased liquidity demand due to large initial public offerings, and relatively tight interbank market liquidity conditions), short-tenor Hong Kong dollar interbank interest rates have been on an upward trend since the fourth quarter of 2019. At the same time, longer-tenor Hong Kong dollar interbank interest rates remained broadly stable during the review period, with the three-month Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rate staying at 2.43% as at the end of 2019, close to the level six months earlier (the blue line in Chart 5.3). At the retail level, since the Hong Kong dollar savings deposit rate remained close to zero, retail banks had limited scope to cut rates in line with the US after it lowered its policy rate.[60] On the other hand, as Hong Kong dollar liquidity in the banking system tightened during the review period, banks continued to compete for long-term stable deposit funding.[61] Reflecting the increase in the weighted funding cost of Hong Kong dollar deposits, the composite interest rate (an indicator measuring the average Hong Kong dollar funding cost of retail banks) rose gradually from 0.95% six months earlier to 1.09% at the end of 2019, though it remained at a relatively low level by historical standards (the green line in Chart 5.3). From a more comprehensive perspective, since the decline in the US dollar funding cost of Hong Kong's licensed banks offset the slight rise in their Hong Kong dollar funding cost, the average overall Hong Kong dollar and US dollar funding cost of Hong Kong's licensed banks fell slightly by 14 basis points in the second half of 2019 (Chart 5.4). During the review period, banks' net interest income benefited from the slight decline in their overall funding cost and the relatively high level of Hong Kong dollar interbank interest rates, providing support to the profitability of the banking sector during the same period. Looking ahead, a number of downside risk factors in the external and local environments will continue to cast a shadow over banks' profitability outlook. Relevant factors include uncertainties arising from the spread of the coronavirus, the future direction of Sino-US trade relations, and the escalation of geopolitical tensions. The intensification of these risk factors could dampen the already weak momentum of global economic growth and reduce demand for bank credit. Given the widespread adoption of accommodative monetary policies by major central banks, the global low interest rate environment may persist, which could exert pressure on banks' future net interest margins. At the local level, the local social incidents since mid-2019 have continued to weigh on business investment and market confidence. Against the backdrop of an already weak economic environment, if the situation persists or even further intensifies in the future, it could worsen the outlook for credit demand and banks' asset quality.  In terms of overall market developments, following the granting of eight virtual banking licences by the Hong Kong Monetary Authority, Hong Kong's banking sector has begun to launch virtual banking services. Although the short-term impact may remain moderate given the currently limited business scale of virtual banks, their long-term impact may depend on whether existing banks accelerate the adoption of financial technology to maintain competitiveness. The results of Box 5 show that the extent to which Hong Kong banks adopt financial technology is statistically correlated with improvements in their cost efficiency and enhancements in their profitability. The rollout of COVID-19 vaccines has brought hope for reopening economies and boosted global growth prospects. Coupled with continued fiscal and monetary easing, financial markets have repeatedly hit new highs. However, the global outlook remains clouded by uncertainties, and the pace of recovery across economies is expected to be uneven. In the medium term, the decoupling of financial markets from the real economy, high debt levels, and the long-lasting economic scars caused by the pandemic will be the challenges facing policymakers ahead. The Hong Kong dollar foreign exchange and money markets continued to operate smoothly and in an orderly manner. The Hong Kong dollar traded close to the strong-side Convertibility Undertaking level, driven mainly by equity-related demand. During the review period, total deposits increased, with no signs of significant fund outflows from Hong Kong's banking system. Partly reflecting the weak economic activity and lower credit demand resulting from the recurring pandemic, total loans in the banking sector declined slightly in the second half of the year, though a slight increase was still recorded for 2020 as a whole. Meanwhile, the residential property market remained largely stable. Looking ahead, uncertainties over the pace of economic recovery and persistent geopolitical risks will continue to pose challenges to Hong Kong's banking sector. In particular, as the pandemic may weaken the repayment ability of corporates and households, the banking sector should continue to closely monitor the impact of relevant downside risk factors on asset quality. Global economic growth rebounded in the third quarter of 2020 as economies reopened, but COVID-19 infection numbers rose again from the fourth quarter, causing global growth to slow once more. Nonetheless, following the breakthrough in vaccine development at the end of 2020, markets expect the pandemic to eventually end, which would facilitate the return of the global economy to normal and accelerate growth. Coupled with continued fiscal and monetary easing, global financial markets rose to new highs in early 2021, even as signs of decoupling from the real economy began to emerge. Against this backdrop, uncertainties will continue to cloud the global economic outlook. Whether vaccines can be widely distributed remains to be seen. Meanwhile, supply bottlenecks and the earlier aggressive easing policies could lead to higher-than-expected inflation, which in turn could require central banks to reduce monetary easing earlier than anticipated, bringing an end to the market's expectation of a "lower-for-longer" monetary policy. In the long run, policymakers will need to assess the costs and benefits of extending relief measures and address the many economic legacies triggered by the pandemic, including high global debt and long-lasting economic scarring. In the East Asian region, gross domestic product growth improved in the second half of 2020, supported by a rebound in export demand. With increased risk appetite, portfolio investment inflows into the region picked up, and search-for-yield activity re-emerged. Despite these positive developments, East Asia still faces persistent uncertainties brought about by the pandemic. First, in the global competition for vaccine procurement, the region's less developed economies may lag behind advanced economies in achieving herd immunity, hindering the recovery of their tourism and services sectors. Second, uncertainties may arise regarding vaccine supply, coverage, or efficacy, and together with weakening government fiscal positions in the region, this could dampen market sentiment and trigger a reversal of fund flows. As for Mainland China, the pace of economic recovery accelerated in the second half of 2020 as consumption activity gradually returned to normal. With local demand rising slightly and goods exports expanding further, seasonally adjusted real gross domestic product began to rebound in the third quarter, ending five consecutive quarters of contraction. The year-on-year contraction in real gross domestic product also narrowed significantly from 9% in the first half of 2020 to around 3% in the second half. Nevertheless, for 2020 as a whole, real gross domestic product fell by 6.1%, the largest decline on record and, following the 1.2% contraction in 2019, the first-ever consecutive two-year decline in history. The latest gross domestic product data by sector show that consumption- and tourism-related sectors contracted more severely than the overall economy under the pandemic. To address the ongoing pandemic, the Government launched two more rounds (the third and fourth) of the Anti-epidemic Fund in the second half of 2020 to help sectors and members of the public affected by the pandemic and to enhance Hong Kong's capacity to combat the epidemic. The Government also announced additional counter-cyclical measures in the recent 2021/22 Budget to boost the economy, including the issuance of a one-off HK$5,000 electronic consumption voucher and the provision of a 100% guaranteed personal special loan scheme for the unemployed. Given that widespread vaccination takes time, the local economy will still face significant challenges in early 2021. With breakthroughs in vaccine development, markets expected that the COVID-19 pandemic would eventually come to an end and that the global economy could accelerate its growth thereafter. Coupled with the expectation of a "lower-for-longer" global monetary policy, investors were undeterred by the resurgence of the pandemic in late 2020, and financial markets rose to new highs in early 2021. However, the keen expectations of financial markets have become disconnected from a macroeconomic environment that remains full of challenges. Should the strength of the economic recovery fall short of expectations, or should policy support be withdrawn earlier than anticipated (for example, due to inflation exceeding expectations), asset prices could become volatile. Looking ahead, policymakers will have to grapple with the difficult question of when to withdraw policy support, as well as address the many problems left behind by the pandemic, including elevated debt levels and long-term economic scarring. The persistent uncertainties of the pandemic continue to cast a shadow over the economic recovery in East Asia, and the region's slower-developing emerging market economies may face greater challenges in vaccine procurement and distribution. Any setbacks in the progress of vaccination programmes could reverse the current optimistic sentiment, rendering capital inflows and financial markets unstable. As for Mainland China, with consumption activity gradually returning to normal, the pace of economic recovery quickened in the second half of 2020. Looking ahead, the outlook for economic growth remains full of uncertainties, depending to a large extent on the development of the pandemic and changes in China-US tensions. Accordingly, the government announced that it would continue to maintain a supportive policy stance, while emphasising the importance of controlling systemic risks.  Benefiting from the purchasing power unleashed by the reopening of economies, most major economies recorded better-than-expected real GDP growth in the third quarter of 2020. However, since the fourth quarter, COVID-19 infection figures have climbed again, prompting governments around the world to reinstate lockdowns and social distancing measures, and global growth momentum weakened once more. In late 2020, more transmissible variants of the virus emerged and subsequently spread across the world, making the situation even more severe. Nonetheless, with breakthroughs in vaccine development and the approval of multiple vaccines for use in late 2020, markets expected the pandemic to eventually come to an end, with the global economy returning to normal and accelerating its growth. Another force underpinning the global economic recovery came from continued policy stimulus, including major central banks' commitment to a "lower-for-longer" monetary policy amid weak inflation, as well as continued fiscal easing measures in major advanced economies, particularly the fiscal stimulus packages passed by the US Congress in December 2020 and March 2021. Correspondingly, in January 2021 the International Monetary Fund revised its forecast for global GDP growth in 2021 upward to 5.5%, 0.3 percentage points higher than the forecast made in October 2020 (Chart 2.1).  Chart 2.1 Real GDP growth forecasts made by the International Monetary Fund in January 2021 and October 2020  Against this backdrop, optimistic market sentiment strengthened, and share prices of cyclical sectors that typically benefit from economic recovery rose, driving global stock prices and valuations to new highs in early 2021 (Chart 2.2).  Chart 2.2 12-month forward price-to-earnings ratios of major stock indices  However, while financial markets performed strongly, the macroeconomic situation remained full of challenges, and the disconnect between the two could lead to volatility in asset markets in the face of multiple risks. First, the prospects for bringing the pandemic under control depend on whether vaccines can be widely distributed, which remains to be seen. As of mid-March 2021, the overall global vaccination rate remained low (Chart 2.3). Although there are global mechanisms (such as COVAX) to promote more equitable distribution of vaccines, the problem of low vaccination rates in lower-income emerging market economies is expected to be even more severe due to limited vaccine supply. If the pandemic is not brought under control as hoped, various economies may need to extend social distancing and other restrictive measures, thereby dampening the prospects for global recovery.  Chart 2.3 Proportion of population having received at least one dose of vaccine in selected economies (as of 15 March 2021)  Second, the rebound in financial markets is built on continued monetary and fiscal policy support, particularly the "lower-for-longer" monetary policy. However, there is a risk that support measures could be withdrawn faster than expected. For example, under the combined effects of supply bottlenecks, strong money and liquidity growth, and aggressive fiscal easing, inflation expectations in the United States and Europe have already heated up (Chart 2.4). If future inflation proves stronger than expected, central banks may need to scale back the size of their monetary easing policies, and inflation data exceeding expectations could also lead to greater volatility in financial markets.  Chart 2.4 5-year/5-year inflation-linked swap rates in the United States and the euro area  Third, there is significant uncertainty surrounding future China-US relations. The wave of China-US "decoupling", particularly in the financial and technological fields, has intensified since the outbreak of the pandemic. And given the increasingly hardline attitude of both the Democratic and Republican parties in the US towards Mainland China, this trend may not be reversed under the Biden administration. An unexpected escalation of China-US tensions could trigger financial market turmoil in the future.  Looking ahead, policymakers will need to face the difficult question of whether and when to withdraw pandemic support measures. Although withdrawing these measures prematurely could jeopardise the economic recovery and cause a "cliff effect", these measures are costly in the long run, including imposing fiscal burdens and delaying the necessary reallocation of resources after the pandemic—for example, allowing "zombie companies" whose business models are no longer viable to survive on continued government support. In addition, policymakers must also address the many problems left behind by the pandemic. First, due to declining corporate revenues and surging government spending, global debt levels rose sharply in 2020 (Chart 2.5). Although the problems brought about by the surge in debt may not be imminent given that global interest rates are currently at extremely low levels, the continued accumulation of debt in the public and private sectors could give rise to market concerns about fiscal sustainability and financial stability.  Chart 2.5 Global debt as a percentage of GDP  Another problem left behind involves the potential long-term economic losses or lasting scarring caused by the pandemic. For example, high uncertainty may cause companies to reduce investment, while workers plagued by prolonged unemployment may permanently exit the labour market, resulting in a substantial waste of human resources.  In East Asia, real GDP growth stabilised in the second half of 2020 after a sharp decline in the second quarter of 2020 (Chart 2.6). The momentum of the economic recovery came mainly from a rebound in exports, with export demand for electronics and technology equipment being the strongest. At the same time, the hardest-hit service industries (such as tourism and consumer services that require face-to-face contact with customers) continued to be in difficulty. Since the second half of last year, the region has attracted more bond fund inflows due to improved market sentiment and higher yields relative to bonds in advanced economies (Chart 2.7). As signs of economic recovery emerged and vaccine production programmes were rolled out, equity fund inflows into East Asia also accelerated in the final quarter of 2020. Regional currencies also appreciated accordingly on the back of portfolio fund inflows, causing the Bloomberg JPMorgan Asia Dollar Index to rebound by about 10% from its low in March last year. First, although the rollout of vaccines brings hope for the region's hardest-hit service industries and economies, competition around the world for early batches of vaccines has pushed up procurement costs, and vaccine distribution also poses challenges to the region's logistics and public health capacities. As a result, the region's slower-developing economies may achieve herd immunity later than advanced economies, and uneven vaccination across economies could prolong border closures and delay the recovery of tourism-related industries. Second, since investors' optimistic sentiment is largely driven by the vaccine rollout, if the progress or effectiveness of vaccination falls far short of expectations, the current capital inflows and the rebound in financial asset prices could come to an end. A sudden reduction in capital inflows could trigger another wave of market turmoil.  With COVID-19 successfully brought under control and consumption gradually recovering, the Mainland economy recovered rapidly in the second half of 2020. At the same time, benefiting from strong demand for pandemic-related products (such as medical supplies and high-tech products), exports also maintained growth (Chart 2.8). Over the course of 2020, despite the unprecedented shock to the economy from the COVID-19 pandemic, the Mainland's GDP still recorded growth of 2.3%. However, whether the economic recovery can be sustained still depends to some extent on the development of the pandemic. Although industrial production activity on the Mainland has already normalised, the service industry remained partly disrupted as the pandemic re-emerged in several northern provinces. In terms of the external environment, although exports resumed growth in the second half of 2020, global demand remains uncertain due to fresh waves of the pandemic breaking out in most developed economies. In addition, China-US tensions may not ease in the near term, but the recently signed Regional Comprehensive Economic Partnership and the concluded China-EU Comprehensive Agreement on Investment could help China integrate further with other economies, potentially partly offsetting the adverse impact of China-US decoupling on the economic recovery. Considering that the economic outlook remains full of uncertainties, the government announced at the Central Economic Work Conference in December 2020 that the existing policy stance would not change significantly in 2021, in order to support economic growth, while at the same time emphasising the importance of controlling systemic risks, such as maintaining the stability of macro leverage and the sustainability of local government debt. In addition, the latest Government Work Report set the 2021 growth target at above 6%. In the long run, the "14th Five-Year Plan" has set science and technology self-reliance and self-strengthening, as well as "dual circulation", as priority development directions, with the aim of raising per capita GDP to the level of moderately developed countries by 2035. As the COVID-19 pandemic raged, inbound tourism quickly fell into a slump, and the market was concerned that this crisis would have a scarring effect on the future recovery of the labour market. To this end, this Box empirically analyses the impact of a boom in inbound tourism on Hong Kong's labour market, in order to explore the potential impact of the current tourism slump. Since 2000, inbound tourism has experienced dramatic booms and busts (Chart B2.1). Specifically, the number of visitor arrivals declined during the 2003 SARS (Severe Acute Respiratory Syndrome) epidemic. Since the launch of the Individual Visit Scheme (commonly known as "free individual travel") in July of the same year, visitor arrivals began to surge. Under the original Individual Visit Scheme, Mainland residents could apply on an individual basis for one to two trips to Hong Kong per year, each lasting no more than seven days. The Individual Visit Scheme was expanded from April 2009 onwards, allowing eligible residents with Shenzhen household registration to apply for multiple-entry Individual Visit endorsements (the "multiple-entry permit" arrangement). Since then, the number of Mainland visitors has increased substantially. Driven by new cross-boundary infrastructure connecting the Chinese Mainland, the number of inbound visitor arrivals reached a record high between late 2018 and early 2019. Subsequent local social incidents halved visitor arrivals in the second half of 2019, and under the COVID-19 pandemic, inbound tourism has been at a standstill since late January 2020. Chart B2.1 Visitor arrivals and related policies. We take the tourism boom brought about by the Individual Visit Scheme as an example to explore the impact of inbound tourism on local employment and income. We consider the Individual Visit Scheme launched in 2003 to be akin to a random economic shock, as it was nearly exogenous in timing and its introduction could not have been anticipated by Hong Kong residents. Our main analytical data come from population data in the Hong Kong Population Census or By-census. Specifically, we use the 5% samples from the 1996, 2001, 2006, 2011 and 2016 Population Censuses or By-censuses. In addition, we define tourism-related industries as the food and beverage, retail, hotel and transport industries. First, we adopt the difference-in-differences approach as our analytical framework, comparing the differences in employment outcomes before and after the implementation of the Individual Visit Scheme between younger workers (aged 20–40) in the treatment group and older workers (aged 41–65) in the comparison group. We classify the younger cohort into the treatment group because they are still in the early stages of their careers and can more flexibly make significant changes to their employment choices in response to the exogenous growth in inbound tourism. As the impact of the tourism boom brought about by the Individual Visit Scheme on the labour market may change over time, we also adopt the event study approach to identify time-varying effects. Our empirical findings show that, compared with the older cohort, younger workers (especially women and those with only a secondary education) were more likely to enter tourism-related industries after the implementation of the Individual Visit Scheme. Among them, the impact of the Individual Visit Scheme on the probability of young women engaging in tourism-related industries was particularly significant and persistent, remaining at close to 5 percentage points from 2006 onwards (in terms of the average difference in entry probability relative to the older cohort) (Chart B2.2). We also use a similar approach to compare the income of those engaged in tourism-related industries (treatment group) with those in non-tourism-related industries (comparison group). The estimation results show that, following the implementation of the Individual Visit Scheme, the income growth of workers engaged in tourism-related industries was higher than that of employees in non-tourism-related industries. Moreover, compared with similar employees engaged in other industries, female workers and workers with lower educational attainment employed in tourism-related industries saw higher and rising income increases (3–20 percentage points) (Chart B2.3). Chart B2.2 Impact of the Individual Visit Scheme on female employment. Chart B2.3 Impact of the Individual Visit Scheme on the income of women and workers with lower educational attainment. The above results are broadly consistent with international experience, revealing that tourism is an important source of employment, especially for young people, women and workers with lower educational attainment. In the case of Hong Kong, our findings are also consistent with previous analyses, namely that the strong growth of inbound tourism increased market demand for lower-skilled workers and improved the resilience of the labour market for lower-skilled workers. As inbound tourism falls from its boom to a trough, these worker groups may be more affected, warranting close monitoring.

The Hong Kong dollar exchange rate continued to trade close to the strong-side Convertibility Undertaking, which was triggered multiple times between September and October 2020. The strong demand for Hong Kong dollars was driven mainly by equity-related funding needs, including those arising from vibrant Initial Public Offering (IPO) fundraising activities, as well as southbound fund inflows through the Shanghai-Hong Kong Stock Connect and Shenzhen-Hong Kong Stock Connect. As the Aggregate Balance increased to over HK$450 billion, Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rates (HIBORs) declined across the board. Although uncertainties related to the development of the COVID-19 pandemic, the pace of economic recovery, and continued tensions in China-US relations may intensify the volatility of fund flows, Hong Kong possesses ample foreign exchange reserves and a robust banking system, and is well positioned to withstand the pressures arising from fund flow volatility. The Hong Kong dollar exchange rate traded close to the strong-side Convertibility Undertaking, driven mainly by equity-related funding demand, including that from vibrant IPO fundraising activities, as well as southbound fund inflows through the Shanghai-Hong Kong Stock Connect and Shenzhen-Hong Kong Stock Connect (Chart 4.1). Although some of the proceeds raised through IPOs were remitted out, the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate traded within a narrow range of 7.7505 to 7.7544 in November and December, owing to buoyant sentiment in the local stock market and market expectations of rising funding demand towards the end of the year. As fundraising activities remained active in the first two months of 2021 (Chart 4.2), the Hong Kong dollar closed at 7.7568 against the US dollar on 26 February 2021. Overall, trading in the Hong Kong dollar remained smooth and orderly. During the review period, the strong-side Convertibility Undertaking was triggered multiple times, leading to an increase in the Aggregate Balance and reflecting significant fund inflows into the Hong Kong dollar. Between September and October 2020, the strong-side Convertibility Undertaking was triggered 47 times. Under the design of the Linked Exchange Rate System, the HKMA sold a total of HK$263.3 billion, increasing the Aggregate Balance from HK$193.1 billion at the end of August to HK$457.5 billion at the end of February (Chart 4.3). The strong-side Convertibility Undertaking was triggered a total of 85 times throughout 2020, with cumulative inflows of HK$383.5 billion. From a cross-border perspective, total deposits increased, indicating no signs of significant fund outflows from the local banking system. Meanwhile, the latest balance of payments figures showed that non-resident direct investment continued to flow into Hong Kong in the fourth quarter of 2020, with no signs of any abnormal fund movements. During the review period, the nominal effective exchange rate index of the Hong Kong dollar generally declined in tandem with the softening of the US dollar against major currencies (Chart 4.4). As the inflation differential between Hong Kong and its trading partners was small and had limited impact on the real effective exchange rate index of the Hong Kong dollar, the movement of the real effective exchange rate index broadly followed that of the nominal effective exchange rate index. As an international financial centre, Hong Kong hosts various fundraising activities (such as IPO fundraising), leading to significant fund inflows into and outflows from Hong Kong. On the one hand, such fundraising activities can attract international investors to move funds into Hong Kong. On the other hand, the funds raised by listed companies may subsequently be transferred out of Hong Kong to meet business needs. Hong Kong possesses ample foreign exchange reserves and a sound banking system, and is well positioned to withstand fund flow volatility without affecting financial stability. Amid continued fund inflows into the Hong Kong dollar, the local monetary environment remained accommodative in the second half of 2020 and in recent months. Over the eight months since the end of June 2020, the Hong Kong dollar Monetary Base increased by 20.8% (Chart 4.5). Analysed by component, the increase in the Monetary Base during this period reflected the increase in the Aggregate Balance resulting from the multiple triggering of the strong-side Convertibility Undertaking. On the other hand, other components, including Certificates of Indebtedness, government-issued notes and coins in circulation, and outstanding Exchange Fund Bills and Notes, remained relatively stable. During the review period, large-scale IPO fundraising activities led to an increase in Hong Kong dollar deposits arising from IPO subscription loans, and therefore Hong Kong dollar broad money (Hong Kong dollar M3) and its Hong Kong dollar deposit component rose notably during July to October 2020 and in January 2021 (Chart 4.6). As IPO fundraising activities concluded and customers repaid their IPO subscription loans, Hong Kong dollar deposits and broad money returned to normal levels at the end of 2020. The three-month CNH HIBOR followed onshore renminbi interest rates lower in late December, then rose again in late January, partly owing to tighter onshore liquidity and seasonal factors. As the recurrence of the COVID-19 pandemic led to a persistent economic recession, and coupled with the impact of a prolonged low interest rate environment, the profitability of retail banks in Hong Kong declined further in the second half of 2020, while asset quality also deteriorated slightly. Nevertheless, given that their capital and liquidity positions remained strong, the Hong Kong banking sector continued to be robust. During the review period, in order to continue supporting the overall economy in weathering the difficulties, the Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA) decided to extend a number of relief measures. Looking ahead, although the roll-out of vaccines may raise hopes that the global pandemic can be brought under control and economic activities can resume, the pace of economic recovery remains uncertain. The aforementioned uncertainties, together with persistent geopolitical tensions, will be unfavourable to business activities and continue to pose challenges to the local banking sector. In particular, as the pandemic weakens the repayment ability of corporates and households, the banking sector should still closely monitor the impact of relevant downside risk factors on its asset quality. In the second half of 2020, the overall pre-tax operating profit of retail banks fell by 38.5% compared with the same period in 2019. Correspondingly, the return on assets fell to 0.62% in the second half of 2020, compared with 1.13% in the same period in 2019 (Chart 5.1). The net interest margin of retail banks narrowed from 1.63% in the second half of 2019 to 1.01% in the same period in 2020 (Chart 5.2), causing net interest income to decline and outweighing the slight increase in non-interest income, which resulted in a drop in profitability. For the whole of 2020, the overall pre-tax operating profit of retail banks fell by 29.4%, and the return on assets declined from 1.19% in 2019 to 0.77%. Among them, the three-month HIBOR fell by 43 basis points in the second half of the year to 0.35% at the end of 2020 (the blue line in Chart 5.3). The decline in the composite interest rate mainly reflected a fall in interbank funding costs and a downward adjustment of time deposit rates by some major retail banks. The capital position of Hong Kong's banking sector remained sound and well above minimum international standards. The consolidated total capital ratio of locally incorporated authorized institutions stood at 20.7% at the end of December 2020, above the international minimum requirement of 8% (Chart 5.5). The HKMA's Opinion Survey on Credit Condition Outlook in December 2020 showed that the proportion of surveyed authorized institutions expecting an increase in loan demand over the next three months rose to 37%, while the proportion expecting a decrease in loan demand over the same period fell to 13% (Table 5.A). In addition, the pace of deterioration in loan quality also slowed in the second half of 2020. Entering 2022, the global economy performed weakly, but inflationary pressures continued to intensify in various regions, particularly the United States. Looking ahead, the outlook for the global economy faces significant uncertainties, including the risk of a large-scale outbreak of the pandemic, and the possibility that if US inflation proves more persistent and broad-based than expected, monetary policy could be tightened more forcefully than anticipated. Should the US Federal Reserve tighten monetary policy substantially and thereby lead to tighter global financial conditions, it would place pressure on the recovery of more vulnerable emerging market economies. Recently, the outbreak of military conflict between Russia and Ukraine could have a significant impact on the global economy through trade and financial channels, and further complicate the outlook for global monetary policy. During the review period, the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate softened, but trading remained smooth and orderly. Total deposits grew moderately during the review period, and there were no significant signs of funds flowing out of the Hong Kong banking system. For the full year of 2021, the growth of total bank lending accelerated somewhat. On the other hand, the residential property market has softened since mid-2021. Looking ahead, the rapid spread of the Omicron variant could pose a threat to the continued economic recovery, and coupled with the possibility that the pace of US monetary policy normalisation may be faster than expected, these risk factors will pose challenges to banks' credit risk management. Banks should remain vigilant and carefully assess the potential impact of relevant risk factors on the asset quality of their loan portfolios. The global economy began to slow in late 2021, with the weakness extending into 2022, owing to the spread of the highly contagious Omicron variant that led to increased restrictions on the movement of people globally, coupled with persistent supply bottlenecks weighing on production. At the same time, amid imbalances in supply and demand and labour shortages, global inflationary pressures continued to intensify and have spread to a broad range of goods and services in major advanced economies, particularly the United States. Recently, with the outbreak of military conflict between Russia and Ukraine, the sharp rise in commodity prices could further aggravate the threat of global inflation, while heightened financial market volatility may cause global financial conditions to tighten in an undesirable manner, further complicating the outlook for global monetary policy. Looking ahead, there are significant uncertainties in the outlook for the global economy. In the short term, if there is a large-scale outbreak of the pandemic, the reimposition of lockdown measures and renewed worsening of supply bottlenecks cannot be ruled out. In the United States, as the risk of inflation being more persistent and broad-based than expected has grown, the Federal Reserve's stance has turned hawkish, accelerating the timeline for tapering asset purchases and raising interest rates, and beginning to discuss reducing its balance sheet. If the Federal Reserve needs to tighten monetary policy substantially, global financial conditions may also tighten, leading to a deterioration in borrowers' debt-servicing capacity, while disorderly capital outflows would place pressure on the recovery of relatively vulnerable emerging market economies. Recently, the military conflict between Russia and Ukraine may expose global commodity prices to the risk of sustained increases, aggravate shortages in the supply of industrial goods, and increase financial market volatility. Heightened market volatility may also trigger redemption pressures on open-ended funds, increasing their liquidity risks. Feature Article 1 discusses whether swing pricing (a liquidity management tool for open-ended funds) can reduce the liquidity risks of these funds during periods of market stress, and discusses the potential limitations of this tool. In emerging Asia, the economy continued to recover in the second half of 2021, though the recovery momentum was temporarily slowed as some Southeast Asian economies reimposed stringent anti-epidemic measures in the third quarter, while the region's technology product exporting economies (South Korea and Singapore) continued to benefit from strong global demand for technology products. Although the market generally expects emerging Asia to recover broadly in 2022, the region's short-term economic outlook faces multiple headwinds. First, new variants remain a concern, especially for economies in the region with lower vaccination rates and stretched public health resources. Second, the Federal Reserve's accelerated policy normalisation could trigger capital outflows from the region and aggravate currency depreciation pressures; and for economies in the region that still need to maintain accommodative monetary policy to support economic recovery, the trade-off between curbing capital outflow pressures and supporting economic activity will become more difficult. Third, the slowdown in major economies, coupled with the possibility that demand may shift from goods to services as the global economy gradually reopens, will weigh on the prospects for trade growth. Fourth, the increase in the prices of various commodities triggered by the Russia-Ukraine conflict will be transmitted to inflation in the region while at the same time weakening consumption. Coupled with increased global economic uncertainty, the monetary policy normalisation decisions of central banks in the region will become more complicated. Central banks in some economies in the region with weaker growth momentum and inflation that is more sensitive to energy prices will face particularly difficult trade-offs. In the long run, in order to rebuild sustainable and robust growth models, investors need to place greater emphasis on environmental, social and governance (ESG) factors in their investment considerations. Feature Article 2 examines the sensitivity of equity returns to changes in climate risk, and how such sensitivity is affected by the environmental performance of firms. Economic growth in Mainland China slowed in the second half of 2021, affected by a new wave of the novel coronavirus outbreak, power rationing measures and tightening measures in the property market. Looking ahead, owing to the persistent slump in the property market and the outbreak of the Omicron variant, the Mainland economy may continue to face downward pressure in the short term. As a result, the Mainland authorities have made stabilising growth the top priority for this year and introduced a series of fiscal and monetary support measures. In the second half of 2021, both the total value of onshore bond defaults and onshore bond defaults by state-owned enterprises declined; Feature Article 3 discusses whether the pricing of SOE bonds has improved in recent years. Overall risks in the banking sector remain manageable, as Mainland banks (especially systemically important banks) have limited exposure to developer loans, and have a low non-performing loan ratio and a high provision coverage ratio. The Hong Kong economy continued to recover in the second half of 2021, but at a slower pace than in the first half. As merchandise exports and private consumption benefited from the continued recovery of the global economy, improved local labour market conditions and the government's launch of the Consumption Voucher Scheme, seasonally adjusted real gross domestic product grew moderately. Year on year, the economy grew by 5.1% in the second half of 2021, compared with 7.8% in the first half. For the full year of 2021, the economy grew by 6.4%, marking the first full-year positive growth since 2019. Entering 2022, a new wave of the local epidemic and the resultant tightening of social distancing measures placed pressure on Hong Kong's economic activity. The government launched the fifth and sixth rounds of the Anti-epidemic Fund, and introduced additional counter-cyclical measures under the 2022-23 Budget to support the economy. To support cash flow, the "100% Personal Loan Guarantee Scheme" and the various guarantee products under the "SME Financing Guarantee Scheme" will be enhanced, with the maximum loan amount raised and the application period and repayment period extended. The HKMA, together with the banking sector, will also extend the "Pre-approved Principal Payment Holiday Scheme" to the end of October 2022. The scheme also provides borrowers with a one-year partial principal repayment option, which is also applicable to loans under the "SME Financing Guarantee Scheme". Hong Kong's economy is expected to continue to recover for the full year of 2022, but the pace of growth will be slower than in 2021, partly reflecting the slowdown in global growth amid the ongoing pandemic and a higher base effect. Specifically, Hong Kong's merchandise exports will continue to benefit from the expansion of the global economy. The government's promotion of various capital works and infrastructure projects will also provide support to the economy. The government forecasts that real gross domestic product will grow by between 2.0% and 3.5% in 2022, while the average growth forecast of international organisations and private-sector analysts is 1.6%. However, the strength and pace of the economic recovery are affected by a number of uncertainties and risks discussed in the preceding sections, particularly the pandemic and the pace of US monetary policy normalisation. As the economy recovered, the labour market improved further in the second half of 2021, with the seasonally adjusted unemployment rate falling to 3.9% at the end of the year. Overall employment rebounded, but remained below the pre-pandemic level. In early 2022, official data showed that labour market pressures re-emerged amid a new wave of the local epidemic. In addition, the decline in the number of online job advertisements also reflected a reduction in new job vacancies. The new wave of the local epidemic and the tightening of anti-epidemic measures will place some pressure on the local labour market (especially industries involving face-to-face contact) in the short term. In the longer term, labour market conditions will depend on the development of the local epidemic and the pace of the local economic recovery. Local inflationary pressures broadly increased in recent months, but remained moderate. Year on year, the underlying consumer price inflation rate edged up to 1.1% and 1.2% in the third and fourth quarters of 2021 respectively, and remained at 1.2% in January 2022. The three-month-on-three-month annualised underlying inflation rate, which reflects inflation momentum, has also picked up in recent months, partly owing to rising prices for dining out and some energy-related items. Looking ahead, with rising import prices and pandemic-related disruptions to logistics, local inflation is expected to edge up in the short term. However, soft rentals and moderate local labour cost pressures should restrain overall price pressures. The market consensus forecasts that the headline inflation rate for 2022 will reach 2.4%, while the government forecasts a headline inflation rate of 2.1% and an underlying inflation rate of 2.0% for 2022. Since September 2021, amid risk-averse sentiment in the local stock market, the Hong Kong dollar has gradually softened against the US dollar. Although the Hong Kong dollar rebounded slightly in October 2021, its upward momentum subsequently faded, mainly owing to weak net southbound buying through the Shanghai-Hong Kong Stock Connect and the Shenzhen-Hong Kong Stock Connect, as well as market expectations that the US dollar would strengthen with the Federal Reserve's monetary policy normalisation. As the virus variants (Delta and Omicron) spread rapidly around the world and production bottlenecks persisted, the global economy slowed markedly in late 2021, and growth momentum remained weak entering 2022. Global inflationary pressures continued to intensify and had already spread to a broad range of goods and services in major advanced economies (especially the United States). Rising inflation concerns prompted the US Federal Reserve to shift its monetary policy stance towards a more hawkish position, heightening the risk that a premature tightening of global financial conditions could put pressure on currently elevated asset valuations, and would also be unfavourable to emerging markets where the recovery still generally lags behind. More recently, the conflict between Russia and Ukraine has pushed up energy and other commodity prices and triggered volatility in global financial markets, exacerbating some of the aforementioned risks. In emerging Asia, although the Delta variant had spread within the region, the economy continued to recover in the second half of 2021, and the region's major technology-product exporting economies continued to outperform other economies. While the Omicron variant is currently not expected to severely impede the region's economic recovery, any uncertainty related to new virus variants will continue to cast a shadow over the region's economic outlook. In addition, the normalisation of the Fed's policy may also trigger an adjustment in asset prices in the region, while slowing growth in major economies may also weigh on the region's merchandise export growth. On the one hand, the conflict between Russia and Ukraine has led to rising commodity prices and increased inflation risks; on the other hand, it will weaken consumption and increase global economic uncertainty, which will make the decision-making on monetary policy normalisation by the region's central banks more complicated. On the Mainland, economic growth slowed in the second half of 2021, affected by a fresh wave of COVID-19 outbreaks, power restrictions and tightening measures in the property market. Looking ahead, the Mainland economy may continue to face downward pressure from a cooling property market and the Omicron variant outbreak. In light of this, the government has set growth stabilisation as its top priority for this year, and macroeconomic policies will also provide greater support. The global economic recovery slowed markedly in the final quarter of 2021, as the highly contagious Omicron variant overlapped with the transmission of the Delta variant, triggering a fresh wave of infections and prompting the tightening of mobility restrictions around the world. In addition, supply chain problems (such as shipping bottlenecks and shortages of key production inputs like semiconductors) continued to weigh on production. Entering 2022, the International Monetary Fund (IMF) forecast in January that global GDP growth would slow from 5.9% in 2021 to 4.4% in 2022, reflecting the continued drag from the pandemic and supply constraints, reduced policy support in the United States and other major advanced economies, as well as slowing growth momentum in the Mainland offsetting the expected growth rebound in the rest of Asia (Chart 2.1). Chart 2.1 The IMF's real GDP growth forecasts. Alongside slowing global economic growth, inflationary pressures also continued to increase during the review period. Core inflation (excluding food and energy prices) rose significantly in major advanced economies, especially in the United States, which has adopted relatively large-scale policy stimulus since the onset of the pandemic. Amid supply bottlenecks, the release of pent-up demand and labour shortages, inflationary pressures have spread to a broad range of goods and services (Chart 2.2). In addition, the recent military conflict between Russia and Ukraine has pushed up the prices of various commodities, which may exacerbate the already elevated global inflationary pressures. Chart 2.2 Core Consumer Price Index inflation rates in selected economies. (1) The latest data for the United States, the United Kingdom and the euro area are for January 2022, while the rest are for December 2021. (2) "Advanced Asian economies" include Australia, New Zealand, Japan, South Korea, Hong Kong and Singapore. (3) "Emerging Asian market economies" include the Mainland, Indonesia, Malaysia, the Philippines and Thailand. Looking ahead, the global economic outlook faces significant uncertainties and elevated downside risks, and will hinge on the development of the pandemic and related supply chain disruptions, how the impact of geopolitical tensions on global trade, inflation and financial market sentiment evolves, and the policy responses of major central banks to inflation. On the pandemic front, most governments have so far adopted targeted measures in response to the recent surge in Omicron cases, focusing on restricting high-risk activities, encouraging remote working and promoting vaccination. Compared with previous lockdown policies, these more relaxed measures should help reduce supply chain disruptions, which have shown preliminary signs of improvement since late 2021 (Chart 2.3). However, should a large-scale outbreak occur, it cannot be ruled out that lockdown measures will be reimposed, thereby causing supply bottlenecks to worsen again. Chart 2.3 Purchasing Managers' Index – Suppliers' Delivery Times sub-index. Should the pandemic remain under control, supply bottlenecks are expected to gradually improve, providing some relief for goods inflation. However, several developments may make the current elevated global inflation more persistent than expected, including the risk that the military conflict between Russia and Ukraine and sanctions on energy imports from Russia will push up commodity prices, the lagged pass-through of rising production costs to final selling prices, the possibility that the earlier surge in global residential property prices may drive up rents going forward, the upside risk to wage growth posed by tight labour markets, and rising inflation expectations. In particular, given that US inflation recorded its largest increase in decades, the Fed shifted towards a more hawkish policy stance at the Federal Open Market Committee meeting in December 2021, no longer characterising high inflation as "transitory", and doubled the pace of asset purchase tapering from a monthly reduction of US$15 billion to US$30 billion, with a view to ending the asset purchase programme before March 2022 and beginning discussions on shrinking its balance sheet. Indeed, recent market pricing suggests that the Fed may raise interest rates multiple times during 2022. By contrast, given the euro area's closer trade and financial ties with Russia and Ukraine, the European Central Bank may face more significant policy trade-offs. Against this backdrop, coupled with global debt levels and asset valuations remaining persistently elevated under prolonged accommodative policies, should inflationary pressures persist and require the Fed to tighten policy faster than expected, borrowers' debt-servicing ability may face a heightened risk of deterioration, and financial market volatility may be triggered. Recently, as geopolitical tensions in Eastern Europe have escalated, risk-averse sentiment in financial markets has risen, and signs of US dollar shortages have emerged, including a widening of cross-currency swap spreads. Amid a premature tightening of global financial conditions, emerging market economies with weaker fundamentals and still affected by the pandemic may be vulnerable to a renewed growth slowdown, currency depreciation and capital outflow pressures. Increased market volatility may also trigger redemption pressures on open-ended funds, increasing their liquidity risk. Box 1 discusses whether swing pricing (a liquidity management tool for open-ended funds) can reduce the liquidity risk of these funds during periods of market stress, and discusses the potential limitations of this tool. In emerging Asia, the economic recovery continued in the second half of 2021, but the transmission of the Delta variant weakened growth momentum in the third quarter, especially in some Southeast Asian economies (Chart 2.4). At the same time, as major technology-product exporting locations in the region, South Korea and Singapore continued to benefit from strong global demand for technology products, which further widened the imbalance in the recovery across the region. In addition, inflationary pressures in several emerging Asian economies remained moderate. Chart 2.4 Manufacturing Purchasing Managers' Index. The market generally expects emerging Asian markets to recover broadly in 2022, but the region's near-term economic outlook faces multiple headwinds. First, although the Omicron variant has spread within the region since late 2021, the economic impact it has brought remains milder than previous waves of infection; however, some economies in the region where vaccination rates still lag and public health resources are relatively tight will continue to face the threat of the emergence of new virus variants. Second, the normalisation of the Fed's policy may trigger capital outflows and create depreciation pressures on the region's currencies. For economies in the region that still need to maintain accommodative monetary policy to support economic recovery, the trade-off between curbing capital outflow pressures and supporting economic activity will become more difficult. At the long end of the yield curve, given the high historical correlation between the two (Chart 2.5), the risk of a sudden surge in US long-term yields may also spread to long-term bond yields in emerging Asia, heightening the risk of an adjustment in the region's asset markets. Chart 2.5 Correlation between Asian ten-year sovereign bond yields and the corresponding US Treasury yields. Third, the region's merchandise trade outlook faces the uncertainty of a slowdown in major economies as well as the possibility that demand may shift from goods to services amid the gradual reopening of the global economy, and these factors may weaken the region's export growth. Chart 2.6 United States: imports from emerging Asia and real GDP. Fourth, although the region's economies have relatively limited trade and financial ties with Russia and Ukraine, the rise in commodity prices triggered by the conflict will be transmitted to inflation in the region while at the same time weakening consumption. Coupled with increased global economic uncertainty, the decision-making on monetary policy normalisation by the region's central banks will become more complicated. For some economies in the region with weaker growth momentum and inflation that is more sensitive to energy prices, their central banks will face particularly difficult trade-offs. The pandemic also serves as a reminder that the region's economies need, over the long term, to rebuild more sustainable and resilient growth models in order to prepare for other risks such as climate change. To this end, investors need to place greater emphasis on environmental, social and governance (ESG) factors in their investment considerations. Box 2 examines whether stock market returns are affected by changes in climate risk, and how such sensitivity is influenced by corporate environmental performance. The COVID-19 pandemic caused a huge shock to global financial markets in March 2020. During this period of market turmoil, some open-ended funds suffered substantial fund outflows (Chart B1.1), creating pressure on their liquidity management. Chart B1.1 Fund outflows from selected open-ended funds during the March 2020 episode. In addition to investors' liquidity needs, another reason for the substantial fund outflows may be that investors took advantage of the "first-mover advantage" by redeeming early, thereby avoiding bearing the redemption costs that may surge under market stress. To curb the fund outflows caused by the first-mover advantage, some open-ended funds adopt swing pricing — a pricing rule for open-ended funds that reduces investors' first-mover advantage. Although many open-ended funds used swing pricing during this episode, there has been no empirical research indicating whether swing pricing can effectively reduce outflows from open-ended funds. Against this backdrop, this Box conducts empirical research to understand whether swing pricing was able to reduce fund outflows from open-ended funds during the March 2020 episode, thereby lowering their liquidity risk. In addition, this Box also seeks to identify factors that may limit the effectiveness of swing pricing during periods of market stress. Based on these assessments, we put forward policy recommendations in relation to financial stability. The first-mover advantage refers to investors redeeming ahead of other investors, thereby passing the redemption costs on to them. With continued growth in goods exports and private consumption, Hong Kong's economy continued to recover in the second half of 2021, returning to positive full-year growth for the first time since 2019. Entering 2022, a new wave of local epidemic and the consequent tightening of social distancing measures weighed on local economic activity. It is expected that the overall economy will maintain its recovery for 2022 as a whole, though the strength and pace will be affected by uncertainties and risks such as the epidemic and the normalisation of US monetary policy. These adverse factors may also affect the outlook for the labour market following its significant improvement in 2021. Although local inflation may edge up slightly in the short term as import prices rise, soft local rentals and labour costs should restrain overall price pressures. Hong Kong's economy continued to recover in the second half of 2021. On a year-on-year basis, real Gross Domestic Product (GDP) grew further by 5.5% in the third quarter and by 4.8% in the fourth quarter (Table 3.A), but its growth pace slowed compared with the first half of the year. For 2021 as a whole, real GDP grew by 6.4%, marking the first positive full-year growth since 2019. Chart 3.1 Real GDP growth rate and contributions of major expenditure components. On a quarter-on-quarter basis, economic activity grew moderately by 0.6% and 0.2% in the third and fourth quarters of 2021 respectively (Chart 3.1). On the domestic front, improved labour market conditions, together with the Government's implementation of the Consumption Voucher Scheme, drove private consumption higher. However, overall investment expenditure declined in the final quarter after a strong rebound in the preceding two consecutive quarters. On the external front, as the global economy continued to recover, Hong Kong's merchandise trade performance remained strong, while services trade remained weak, partly because inbound tourism remained at a standstill (Chart 3.2). In net terms, external trade dragged on GDP in the third quarter but provided support to GDP growth in the fourth quarter. Chart 3.2 Import and export volumes. A new wave of local epidemic and the consequent tightening of social distancing measures weighed on local economic activity in early 2022. The Government launched the fifth and sixth rounds of the Anti-epidemic Fund and introduced additional counter-cyclical measures under the 2022-23 Budget to support the economy. To support cash flow, the "100% Personal Loan Guarantee Scheme" and various guarantee products under the "SME Financing Guarantee Scheme" will be enhanced, with the maximum loan amount raised and the application period and repayment period extended. The HKMA, together with the banking sector, will also extend the "Pre-approved Principal Payment Holiday Scheme" to the end of October 2022. The scheme will also provide borrowers with a one-year partial principal repayment option, which will also apply to loans under the "SME Financing Guarantee Scheme". Hong Kong's economy is expected to continue recovering for 2022 as a whole, but the pace of growth will be slower than in 2021, partly reflecting the slowdown in global economic growth amid the persistent epidemic and a higher base effect. Specifically, Hong Kong's goods exports will continue to benefit from the global economic expansion. The Government's advancement of various public works and infrastructure projects will also provide support to the economy. The Government forecasts real GDP growth in 2022 to range between 2.0% and 3.5%, while the average growth forecast by international organisations and private-sector analysts is 1.6%. However, the strength and pace of Hong Kong's economic recovery are subject to the numerous uncertainties and risks described in the preceding chapters. In particular, recent epidemic developments, the accelerated pace of US monetary policy normalisation, and heightened geopolitical concerns (such as the Russia-Ukraine situation) have cast a shadow over the near-term economic outlook for Hong Kong and the world at large. On the other hand, if Hong Kong resumes quarantine-free travel with Mainland China earlier than expected, it may stimulate local economic growth. As the economy recovered, the labour market improved further in the second half of 2021, with the seasonally adjusted unemployment rate falling to 3.9% by year-end (Chart 3.3). Total employment in December 2021 also rebounded by 2.0% from the recent low in February 2021, though it remained below the pre-epidemic level. In early 2022, official data showed that pressure on the labour market re-emerged amid the new wave of local epidemic. In addition, a decline in the number of online job advertisements also reflected a reduction in new job vacancies. Looking ahead, the new wave of local epidemic and the tightening of anti-epidemic measures will place some pressure on the local labour market in the short term, particularly in sectors involving face-to-face contact. In the longer term, labour market conditions will depend on the development of the local epidemic and the pace of the local economic recovery. Chart 3.3 Labour market conditions. Local inflationary pressures have generally increased in recent months, but remained mild. On a year-on-year basis, the underlying consumer price inflation rate edged up slightly to 1.1% and 1.2% in the third and fourth quarters of 2021 respectively, and remained at 1.2% in January 2022 (Chart 3.4). The three-month-on-three-month annualised underlying inflation rate, which reflects inflation momentum, has also picked up in recent months. Specifically, as local demand recovered and external prices rose (Chart 3.5), the prices of meals out and some energy-related items rose at a faster pace. At the same time, the housing rental component of the Composite Consumer Price Index continued to decline broadly, thereby restraining overall inflation momentum (Chart 3.6). Although real unit labour costs remained soft, they edged up slightly in recent quarters, partly due to an improvement in real average wages (Chart 3.7). Chart 3.4 Different indicators reflecting consumer price inflation. Chart 3.5 Hong Kong's import prices. Chart 3.6 Composite Consumer Price Index rental component and market rentals. Chart 3.7 Unit labour costs. Looking ahead, as import prices rise and the epidemic causes logistics disruptions, local inflation is expected to edge up slightly in the short term. However, soft rentals and mild local labour cost pressures should restrain overall price pressures. Market consensus forecasts the overall inflation rate for 2022 to reach 2.4%, while the Government forecasts the overall inflation rate for 2022 at 2.1% and the underlying inflation rate at 2.0%.

Amid risk-averse sentiment in the local stock market and concerns over the normalisation of US monetary policy, the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate softened during the review period. As Hong Kong dollar liquidity remained ample, the Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rate (HIBOR) continued to stay at low levels. Overall, trading in the Hong Kong dollar foreign exchange and money markets continued to be smooth and orderly. Looking ahead, although uncertainties surrounding US monetary policy, the pandemic, and escalating geopolitical tensions may intensify fund flow volatility, Hong Kong possesses ample foreign exchange reserves and a sound banking system, giving it the ability to withstand the shocks brought about by fund flow volatility. Overall, the Hong Kong dollar traded on the strong side of the Convertibility Zone for most of the time, and trading continued to be smooth and orderly. Since September 2021, the Hong Kong dollar has gradually softened against the US dollar amid risk-averse sentiment in the local stock market (Chart 4.1). Although the Hong Kong dollar rebounded slightly in October 2021 as market sentiment improved, its upward momentum subsequently faded, mainly due to weak net southbound buying flows through Shanghai-Hong Kong Stock Connect and Shenzhen-Hong Kong Stock Connect (Chart 4.2), as well as market expectations that the US dollar would strengthen as the US Federal Reserve's monetary policy outlook turned more hawkish. During the review period, new share fundraising activities continued to provide support for the Hong Kong dollar (Chart 4.3). Total deposits grew moderately during the review period, with no significant signs of funds flowing out of the local banking system. At the same time, the latest balance of payments figures showed that non-residents' direct investment continued to flow into Hong Kong in the second half of 2021, and there were no signs of abnormalities in cross-border fund flows. Chart 4.1 Hong Kong dollar exchange rate. Chart 4.2 Net southbound buying through Shanghai-Hong Kong Stock Connect and Shenzhen-Hong Kong Stock Connect. Chart 4.3 Equity funds raised on the Hong Kong Stock Exchange (HKEX). Although the US dollar strengthened during the review period, the nominal effective exchange rate index of the Hong Kong dollar remained stable due to the appreciation of the renminbi against the Hong Kong dollar (Chart 4.4). Given the small inflation differential between Hong Kong and its trading partners, the real effective exchange rate index of the Hong Kong dollar broadly tracked the movement of the nominal effective exchange rate index. Chart 4.4 Nominal and real effective exchange rates. Looking ahead, uncertainties surrounding US monetary policy, developments in the pandemic, and escalating geopolitical tensions may intensify fund flow volatility. As US dollar interest rates rise, under the normal operation of the Linked Exchange Rate System (LERS), outflows of Hong Kong dollar funds (the pace and scale of which will depend on prevailing market conditions at that time) could lead to a weakening of the Hong Kong dollar and trigger the weak-side Convertibility Undertaking. Hong Kong also possesses ample foreign exchange reserves and a sound banking system, giving it the ability to withstand fund flow volatility without affecting financial stability. During the review period, Hong Kong's monetary conditions remained accommodative. The Hong Kong dollar Monetary Base rose 1.4% over the eight months since the end of June 2021, mainly driven by an increase in Certificates of Indebtedness. Reflecting additional issuance made to meet banks' sustained demand for Exchange Fund Bills amid ample liquidity in the banking system, Exchange Fund Bills and Notes increased by HK$119.7 billion to HK$1,188.7 billion during the review period, with the Aggregate Balance (before discount window activities) correspondingly decreasing by HK$119.9 billion to HK$337.6 billion (Chart 4.5). Meanwhile, government-issued banknotes and coins remained relatively stable. Chart 4.5 Aggregate Balance and Exchange Fund Bills and Notes. Over the six months since the end of July 2021, total deposits with authorized institutions grew moderately by 4.5%, while Hong Kong dollar deposits rose slightly by 0.3%. However, it should be noted that monetary statistics may fluctuate due to various short-term factors (such as seasonal and IPO-related fund demand, as well as business and investment-related activities), so it is advisable to observe longer-term trends. For the whole of 2021, total deposits and Hong Kong dollar deposits grew by 4.6% and 1.4% respectively. Chart 4.6 Deposits with authorized institutions by currency. Overall, trading in Hong Kong's interbank market continued to be smooth and orderly. As liquidity in the banking system was ample, despite market concerns over the tightening of US monetary policy, HIBOR continued to stay at low levels (Chart 4.7). Partly reflecting market expectations of rising fund demand towards the year-end, HIBOR edged up slightly in December 2021. The average lending rate for new mortgages rose slightly from 1.48% in July 2021 to 1.56% in January 2022. On the other hand, the Best Lending Rates of major retail banks remained unchanged during the review period, ranging between 5.00% and 5.50%. Looking ahead, ample liquidity in the banking system can provide a sufficient buffer during large-scale capital market activities or when volatility occurs in financial markets. Chart 4.7 Hong Kong dollar and US dollar interbank offered rates. During the review period, the offshore renminbi interbank market continued to operate normally. Affected by seasonal liquidity demand towards the year-end, the overnight offshore renminbi Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rate (CNH HIBOR) experienced slight fluctuations in late December 2021, while the 3-month CNH HIBOR remained relatively stable, hovering around 3% throughout the review period (Chart 4.8). Chart 4.8 Overnight and 3-month CNH HIBOR fixings. In the second half of 2021, Hong Kong's offshore renminbi liquidity pool continued to grow steadily. Over the six months since the end of July 2021, the balance of renminbi customer deposits and certificates of deposit grew by 30.3%, reaching RMB1,113.5 billion at the end of January 2022 (Chart 4.9 and Table 4.A). Among these, renminbi customer deposits increased by 33.5%, mainly driven by corporate fund inflows, offsetting a 48.0% decline in the balance of certificates of deposit. Chart 4.9 Renminbi deposits and certificates of deposit in Hong Kong. Over the six-month period since July 2021, although the balance of renminbi loans decreased by 10.2% to RMB167.6 billion, Hong Kong's renminbi trade settlement continued to grow. Between the end of July 2021 and the end of January 2022, the transaction volume handled by local banks reached RMB3,763.0 billion (Chart 4.10), an increase of 18.3% from RMB3,181.0 billion in the same period last year. Hong Kong's large renminbi liquidity pool continued to support a substantial volume of renminbi payment and financing transactions. For the whole of 2021, the average daily turnover of the renminbi Real Time Gross Settlement system rose from RMB1,191.5 billion in 2020 to RMB1,522.6 billion. Chart 4.10 Renminbi trade settlement remittances. Looking ahead, with the establishment of the two-way northbound and southbound Shanghai-Hong Kong Stock Connect, Shenzhen-Hong Kong Stock Connect, Bond Connect and Cross-boundary Wealth Management Connect, the continued opening of the Mainland's capital account, increasing demand from international investors for renminbi assets, and the deepening of regional economic and financial cooperation under the "Belt and Road" and "Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macao Greater Bay Area" initiatives, Hong Kong's offshore renminbi business is expected to benefit. Major global stock markets continued to rise in the fourth quarter of 2021, but have consolidated since January 2022 amid growing market concerns over the tightening stance of major central banks in developed economies and the escalation of the conflict between Russia and Ukraine. The Hong Kong stock market remained sluggish in the fourth quarter of 2021, largely dragged down by a sharp decline in technology stocks. Uncertainties over global risks and developments in Hong Kong's pandemic situation drove the Hang Seng Index to a near two-year low at the end of February. Meanwhile, Hong Kong's offshore renminbi bond market continued to grow steadily in the second half of 2021. The residential property market has softened since mid-2021, partly affected by weakening sentiment in asset markets and a new local wave of the pandemic. Major global stock markets on the whole continued to rise in the final quarter of 2021, leading the MSCI World Index to hit an all-time high of 3,262 points on 4 January 2022 (Chart 4.11). Supported by government monetary and fiscal policy stimulus, the global economic recovery and strong corporate earnings underpinned the upward trend in major global stock markets, but the pandemic remained investors' main risk concern throughout the year. However, major global stock markets have consolidated since early January 2022, with growing market concerns over the tightening stance of major central banks in developed economies amid surging inflation risks, sharply rising commodity prices, and the escalation of the Russia-Ukraine conflict. By comparison, at the end of 2021, the Hong Kong stock market continued to lag behind other major global stock markets. The Hang Seng Index hovered between 24,000 and 26,500 points from September to mid-November, closing at 23,398 points at the end of 2021, down 14.1% from 2020. The profitability of retail banks in Hong Kong declined in the second half of 2021. The classified loan ratio edged up slightly in the second half of 2021, but it remained at a low level by both historical and international standards. Underpinned by robust capital and liquidity positions, the Hong Kong banking sector remained resilient. During the review period, in order to further help the economy weather this difficult period, the HKMA extended a number of support measures. Looking ahead, the rapid spread of the Omicron variant may pose a threat to the economic recovery, and, coupled with the risk that the pace of US monetary policy normalisation may be faster than expected, both will pose challenges to banks' credit risk management. Banks should remain vigilant and carefully assess the potential impact of the relevant risk factors on the asset quality of their loan portfolios. In the second half of 2021, the overall pre-tax operating profit of retail banks fell by 16.1% compared with the same period in 2020. The weak profitability was mainly attributable to a decrease in net interest and non-interest income and an increase in operating expenses. As a result, the return on assets dropped to 0.50% in the second half of 2021, compared with 0.61% in the same period in 2020 (Chart 5.1). For the whole of 2021, the overall pre-tax operating profit of retail banks decreased by 18.6% compared with 2020, while the return on assets fell from 0.77% to 0.59%.
