Although the normalisation of US monetary policy may signal an improvement in banks' profitability, the improvement in the short term may be partly offset by two factors. First, although the Federal Reserve has indicated that it would raise interest rates several times in 2022, past experience shows that changes in local interest rates may lag behind US rates (particularly when interbank liquidity in Hong Kong remains very ample). Therefore, an improvement in banks' net interest margin may take more time to materialise. In addition, the surge in Omicron variant cases may also introduce uncertainty to the pace of economic recovery, thereby exerting pressure on banks' asset quality and profitability. The capital position of Hong Kong's banking sector remained robust and well above the minimum international standards. During the period, the Tier 1 capital ratio and the Common Equity Tier 1 (CET1) capital ratio were 18.2% and 16.2% respectively. In addition, the leverage ratio of locally incorporated authorized institutions recorded a robust level of 7.9% at the end of 2021, exceeding the statutory minimum level of 3%. Climate change affects every aspect of life, and everyone has a responsibility to do their part to mitigate its impact. In this regard, the HKMA has devoted considerable effort to advancing Hong Kong's climate goals and to contributing to enhancing global climate resilience and sustainable development. Following our inclusion of our first sustainability report as a chapter in the HKMA Annual Report 2021 last year, this year we have, for the first time, published the Sustainability Report 2022 separately. I hope this report will give readers a deeper understanding of the HKMA's work strategies and priorities in strengthening the Hong Kong banking system's capacity to respond to climate change, building a green finance ecosystem, and how we put into practice our roles as a responsible investor and a sustainable organisation. During the year, we made significant progress in advancing sustainability work across the HKMA's major functions. In this report, you will learn about our concrete measures and work, with the following highlights:  Banks' day-to-day operations are exposed to climate risks. As the banking regulator, the HKMA has taken concrete measures to strengthen banks' capacity to respond to climate change. In 2022, we formulated a two-year plan to incorporate climate risk factors into the supervisory process, and studied how to harness the power of technology to help banks assess the impact of physical risks. As banks launch an increasing number of green and sustainable products, we have also shared with the industry good practices on how to properly manage these products, so as to promote banks' enhancement of their climate risk management capabilities.  The HKMA has actively participated in various collaborative initiatives on addressing climate risks and promoting the development of sustainable finance. On the local front, we are working with other financial regulators through the "Green and Sustainable Finance Cross-Agency Steering Group" (Steering Group) to develop a local green classification framework; the framework will increase the transparency of financial markets and make green finance policies more consistent. At the international level, we are actively participating in a number of different international organisations to help formulate policies to address climate change and to assess their impact on financial stability.  Hong Kong is well positioned to meet Asia's demand for green and sustainable financing. Although 2022 was a rather difficult year for the global bond market, the amount of green and sustainable debt issuance in Hong Kong continued to record strong growth of 42%, with total issuance increasing to US$80.5 billion, making Hong Kong the largest centre for arranging international green and sustainable bond issuance in Asia². Relevant issuers included the Shenzhen Municipal People's Government and the Hainan Provincial People's Government, whose issuances once again demonstrated Hong Kong's unique role in facilitating the flow of green and sustainable funds between the Mainland and the international market. The vibrant development of Hong Kong's green bond market can also be partly attributed to the Government Green Bond Programme. Since 2019, the HKMA has assisted the Government in issuing green bonds totalling nearly US$16 billion, with the proceeds raised allocated to more than 40 green government projects, including green buildings, waste management and resource recovery, and energy efficiency and conservation. We also assisted the Government in achieving two "firsts": in May 2022, we assisted the Government in issuing its first batch of government green retail bonds totalling HK$20 billion, which was the largest green retail bond issuance in the world at the time. In addition, we assisted the Government in issuing its first batch of tokenised green bonds in February 2023. These were the world's first tokenised green bonds issued by a government, and this issuance marked a milestone, as it represented our successful combination of our strengths in the bond market, green and sustainable finance, and financial technology.  Standards, data and talent are indispensable elements for driving the sound development of the climate finance ecosystem, and their establishment relies on the efforts and collaboration of different sectors. To this end, the HKMA works mainly through the Steering Group with other relevant government departments, regulators, academic institutions and the financial industry to develop the above elements. In addition to the development of the local green classification framework mentioned above, the Steering Group has also promoted skills training in the industry and improved Hong Kong's data resources through its established "Centre for Green and Sustainable Finance". Furthermore, the Steering Group has made good progress in other areas, such as mandatory disclosure of climate-related information and carbon market opportunities.  In 2022, the HKMA further strengthened the Exchange Fund's work on responsible investment, in particular by setting a target for the Exchange Fund's investment portfolio to achieve net-zero greenhouse gas emissions by 2050. At the same time, we also enhanced our risk management work to improve the Exchange Fund's climate resilience and risk-adjusted long-term returns. In addition, to fully capture the opportunities that climate change may bring, we are committed to promoting the Exchange Fund's sustainable investment, seeking out investment opportunities that help support the climate transition and mitigate climate change, so as to enhance the long-term returns of the investment portfolio. At the end of 2021, the weighted average carbon intensity of the Exchange Fund's equity portfolio had fallen by 43% compared with the 2017 level. In fact, the Exchange Fund's risk exposure to carbon-intensive assets has consistently been lower than the overall market. In the future, we will continue to move towards the net-zero emissions target by continuously strengthening the integration of environmental, social and governance (ESG) factors into the investment management process, actively exercising asset ownership, continuing to collaborate with various stakeholders, and focusing on the decarbonisation and transition of the investment portfolio.  At the HKMA, the "Corporate Social Responsibility and Sustainability Committee", which I chair, is responsible for formulating the HKMA's sustainability strategy. Our strategic direction is based on the three pillars of environment, staff and social responsibility. On the environmental front, we are committed to promoting a green working environment and promoting a more environmentally friendly market to the public; on the staff front, as a responsible and caring employer, we actively foster a healthy and inclusive working environment; and on the social responsibility front, we are committed to raising the public's level of financial literacy, promoting financial inclusion, and actively giving back to society. Compared with the level when we started tracking our carbon footprint in 2015, our per-capita greenhouse gas emissions, energy consumption and paper consumption in 2022 all achieved double-digit reductions. More importantly, we have formulated a roadmap to achieve net-zero emissions by 2050. In the short term, our target is to completely eliminate Scope 1 emissions and, using 2015 as the baseline, to reduce Scope 2 emissions by 63% by 2030.  Addressing climate change and promoting sustainable development require the sustained efforts and collaboration of many parties. On this important global issue, we understand that we must take action ourselves and lead by example, and work together with like-minded peers and international organisations. In the next section, we will outline the HKMA's short-term plans and work priorities in addressing climate change under each of its major functions. Achieving net-zero emissions by 2050 is a formidable task, and we will spare no effort in reaching this goal. We are confident that, through the joint efforts of all colleagues, the financial industry and the general public, we will be able to successfully meet the climate challenges of the future.  Eddie Yue Chief Executive

In 2023, the HKMA will continue to promote the sustainable development of Hong Kong's financial industry and fulfil its responsibilities as a responsible investor and a sustainable organisation. At the same time, through participation in international and regional organisations, the HKMA will also strive to promote the broad development and best practices of green and sustainable finance. As the regulator of the banking industry, we will endeavour to strengthen the climate resilience of the banking sector and further enhance our green finance ecosystem to support the green transition of banks. Specifically, the HKMA will communicate with banks to understand their progress in implementing the supervisory requirements on climate risk management, incorporate climate factors into our supervisory review process, and revise the "Green Benchmarking" common assessment framework for the banking industry. Meanwhile, the HKMA will support banks' efforts to enhance their climate resilience and risk management capabilities, for example by exploring various measures and technological solutions to help banks identify, quantify and monitor their climate risk exposures. The HKMA will also work with banks to launch the next round of climate risk stress testing, as part of the regular supervisor-led stress testing for 2023 to 2024. Participating banks will be required to assess their ability to cope with climate risks based on an enhanced stress testing framework, which covers various stress scenarios such as extreme climate conditions and adverse economic environments. To foster the healthy development of banks in providing green and sustainable investment products, the HKMA will keep abreast of local and international market and regulatory developments, maintain communication with the industry, and provide guidance on the sales process in a timely manner. We will also conduct off-site thematic assessments to gain a comprehensive understanding of the green and sustainable investment products offered by banks. At the same time, to strengthen the development of the green finance ecosystem in support of the green transition of the financial industry, the HKMA is planning to consult the industry on the structure and core elements of a local green classification framework. In terms of market development, to promote Hong Kong as a green and sustainable finance hub in the region, the HKMA will assist the Government in expanding the issuance scale of green bonds under the "Government Green Bond Programme" and broadening the scope of the programme to cover sustainability bonds; at the same time, it will attract more green financing activities to be conducted in Hong Kong through the "Green and Sustainable Finance Grant Scheme". The HKMA will also assist in implementing the government-funded "Pilot Green and Sustainable Finance Training Programme" to expand Hong Kong's talent pool in green finance. In addition, the HKMA will continue to encourage more Mainland local governments, institutions and enterprises to conduct green financing through Hong Kong, and explore the feasibility of combining green finance with technology. On the other hand, we will continue to work with other institutions and departments through the "Green and Sustainable Finance Cross-Agency Steering Group" on cross-sector topics such as skills training and data, green taxonomy, climate-related disclosures and sustainability reporting, and carbon market opportunities. Through the Alliance for Green Commercial Banks, the HKMA will jointly launch various dedicated programmes with the International Finance Corporation in the Asian region, including conducting green finance research, providing unique market analysis, offering targeted professional training for banks, and providing practical guidance to help banks formulate roadmaps to develop green finance into a core business. Looking ahead, the Alliance will work closely with its founding members, global partners and knowledge partners to launch a membership programme to expand the Alliance's influence in the Asian region. At the same time, the Alliance will also strengthen the professional capabilities of industry practitioners, promote the sharing of green finance knowledge, and lead the launch of projects in new areas. As a responsible investor, the HKMA has set a target of achieving net-zero emissions for the Exchange Fund's investment portfolio by 2050 or earlier, as its commitment to participating in global climate action and implementing the recommendations of the Task Force on Climate-related Financial Disclosures. Looking ahead, the HKMA will continue to incorporate environmental, social and governance factors into its investment management process, strive towards the net-zero emissions target, and fully support global climate action. As a responsible and sustainable organisation, the HKMA cares about both its staff and the general public as well as the surrounding environment. We have formulated a sustainability roadmap and set climate targets for our own operations, as our commitment to participating in global carbon reduction and climate action efforts. The HKMA will continue to prioritise the reduction of carbon emissions, and encourage staff to give their full support in saving energy and reducing waste. In addition, we will provide staff with further guidance on incorporating sustainability principles into the procurement process. To implement digital transformation and enhance operational flexibility, the HKMA will explore ways to modernise internal systems and applications, further improving work efficiency while minimising as far as possible the potential risks that may arise during the digital transformation process.

Climate change is a significant risk faced by the financial system. The HKMA has been committed to strengthening Hong Kong's financial system to build a greener and more sustainable future, contributing to Hong Kong's climate goals and the global sustainable development agenda. Banks face the impact of various sustainability- and climate-related matters in their day-to-day business operations. To continue performing their important function in the financial system and to channel more funds towards green and sustainable projects, banks must proactively manage climate risk. As the regulator of the banking industry, the HKMA places particular emphasis on building banks' capacity to respond to and manage climate risk, and on accelerating banks' efforts to support the transition to a low-carbon economy. The HKMA also supports banks in enhancing their capabilities in detecting environmental crimes, and participated in the recently published Hong Kong Money Laundering and Terrorist Financing Risk Assessment, which covers areas such as environmental crimes and illegal wildlife trafficking. In 2022, the Basel Committee on Banking Supervision (the Basel Committee)¹ issued the Principles for the Effective Management and Supervision of Climate-related Financial Risks, and responded to frequently asked questions, clarifying how the existing Basel framework covers the above risks. In response to these international developments, the HKMA will continue its efforts to incorporate climate-related factors into the regulatory framework. Following the issuance of the Supervisory Policy Manual module GS-1 "Climate Risk Management" in 2021, the HKMA has also maintained communication with banks, exchanging views on the expectations, progress, and challenges in implementing the relevant regulatory requirements. To further strengthen the supervision of banks' climate risk management, the HKMA has formulated a two-year plan to incorporate climate risk factors into the banking supervisory process, and communicated this to the banking industry in June. As part of the implementation of the two-year plan, the HKMA issued a revised Supervisory Policy Manual module SA-1 "Risk-based Supervisory Approach", and enhanced the CAMEL² rating system by incorporating climate risk into the risk-based supervisory process. At the same time, drawing on the experience gained from the 2021 pilot exercise, the HKMA refined the climate risk stress-testing scenarios and assessment framework. The HKMA has also formulated plans to incorporate the next round of climate risk stress testing into the regular supervisor-driven stress testing, so as to conduct a more comprehensive assessment of the banking sector's resilience under extreme climate scenarios. Under the two-year plan, the HKMA is also enhancing its green assessment framework for banks to reflect the latest developments in sustainability-related topics, including climate risk management and transition planning. Meanwhile, the HKMA is reviewing the supervisory review process used to assess and monitor banks' capital adequacy levels and to determine their Pillar 2 capital requirements, with the aim of encouraging banks to strengthen their risk management framework to address the risks related to climate change and the transition to carbon neutrality. In view of the growing prevalence of banks issuing green and sustainable products, the HKMA conducted a round of thematic review, primarily examining banks' development and ongoing management of these products. During the thematic review process, the HKMA identified some good practices, and issued a circular in December to share them with the industry, enabling banks to progressively strengthen their climate risk management capabilities. The application of technology can improve data availability and enhance banks' capacity to manage climate risk. The HKMA has begun developing a common platform for banks to assess the impact of physical risk on real estate. In addition, together with other central banks and regulators, the HKMA completed a project under the BIS Innovation Network, exploring how technological solutions can assist in conducting physical risk assessments. The HKMA also attaches great importance to promoting sustainable and world-leading anti-money laundering practices; this work adopts advanced analytics and regulatory technology, complemented by fully automated regulatory data collection. Over the past 12 months, the HKMA has streamlined the anti-money laundering regulatory data collection process to reduce banks' manual workload and paper usage. To enhance transparency across financial markets and to make green finance policies more consistent, the HKMA has collaborated with other financial regulators to establish a local green classification framework. The green classification framework, commonly referred to as a green taxonomy, classifies economic activities as green or sustainable, providing a reference for authorities and market participants to determine whether an activity or its related products are genuinely green or sustainable. To this end, the HKMA has maintained contact with the industry and other relevant stakeholders to explore in depth the features and challenges of the framework, and is preparing to make recommendations and conduct consultation on the structure and core elements of the framework in the first half of 2023. The HKMA is keenly aware that climate change may pose potential risks to the financial system, and has therefore incorporated a broader range of climate factors and scenarios into its financial risk analysis and research, so as to strengthen its ongoing monitoring efforts. In its continuous monitoring of financial stability risks, the HKMA takes climate change into account, and has incorporated analysis of climate-related risks into its various financial stability reports. Through active participation in the Scenario Design and Analysis Workstream under the Network of Central Banks and Supervisors for Greening the Financial System (NGFS), the HKMA has helped to further enrich climate scenarios, enabling central banks and supervisors to gain a clearer understanding of the macroeconomic and financial impacts of climate change. In terms of research work, in 2022 the HKMA conducted a number of applied research projects, exploring in depth two major topics, namely greenwashing behaviour in the corporate green bond market³, and the role of disclosure in mitigating climate risk exposures⁴. The above research findings help inform the formulation of policies and regulatory measures to address the impact of climate risk on financial stability. Locally, this research helps strengthen the HKMA's ongoing monitoring and assessment of the impact of climate risk on financial stability. Externally, the HKMA has shared its research findings with a wide range of stakeholders through various channels, including international central banking research conferences and the HKMA's Half-Yearly Monetary and Financial Stability Report. The HKMA's Liquidity Facilities Framework is a collateralised standby liquidity arrangement that provides timely liquidity support to banks in need. The HKMA is studying the incorporation of sustainability considerations when assessing eligible collateral under this framework. The HKMA actively participates in international and regional discussions on addressing climate risk and mainstreaming sustainable finance. Through such participation, the HKMA helps to facilitate international and regional policy dialogue on addressing climate change and its impact on financial stability, and draws on the insights gained to help strengthen the climate resilience of Hong Kong's financial system.

To consolidate Hong Kong's position as a regional hub for green and sustainable finance, the HKMA has stepped up its efforts to enhance market awareness and participation, provide the necessary infrastructure and enablers, and support international initiatives to align with global standards. The Green and Sustainable Finance Cross-Agency Steering Group (the Steering Group), co-chaired by the HKMA and the Securities and Futures Commission (SFC), is responsible for coordinating the financial sector's response to climate and environmental risks, accelerating the development of green and sustainable finance in Hong Kong, and supporting the Government's climate strategy1. The Steering Group's work is largely based on its strategic plan, which sets out six focus areas and five action points to strengthen Hong Kong's financial ecosystem and jointly build a greener and more sustainable future (Chart 1). Strengthening climate-related financial risk management and consolidating Hong Kong's position as a global risk management centre; promoting the flow of climate-related information at all levels to facilitate risk management, capital allocation and investor protection; enhancing the relevant skills of industry practitioners and raising public awareness and understanding; encouraging product innovation and research measures to channel funds towards green and sustainable projects; capturing the business opportunities brought by the Mainland and developing Hong Kong into a green finance centre for the Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macao Greater Bay Area (the Greater Bay Area); and strengthening regional and international cooperation. Actions taken so far to advance the development of sustainable finance in Hong Kong: The Steering Group has made good progress since its establishment. The Steering Group's current work priorities include skills training and data collection under the Centre for Green and Sustainable Finance (see below), the green taxonomy (see the section "Establishing a green taxonomy framework to facilitate green fund flows" in the chapter "Building a Sustainable Financial System" on page 9), climate-related disclosures and sustainability reporting, as well as carbon market opportunities. Specifically, the Steering Group announced in March a preliminary feasibility assessment of Hong Kong's carbon market opportunities, and will support Hong Kong's development into a regional carbon trading centre, including developing an international high-quality voluntary carbon market and capturing opportunities arising from cooperation in the Greater Bay Area. In December, the Steering Group announced its collaboration with CDP2 to enhance data availability in Hong Kong and strengthen sustainability reporting. As part of this collaboration, the two parties developed a climate and environmental risk questionnaire targeting unlisted companies and small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs), which not only facilitates companies in conducting sustainability reporting but also helps financial institutions collect and analyse company-level data for use in risk assessment and related business decisions. This is an important step for the Steering Group in expanding the coverage of its data work to include SMEs, an important economic segment that has previously been harder to reach. The Steering Group established the Centre for Green and Sustainable Finance in July 2021, which is responsible for coordinating the work of financial regulators, government departments, industry stakeholders and academic institutions on training and policy formulation, and for building resource and databases. In the first half of 2022, the Centre for Green and Sustainable Finance launched three information repositories on data, training information and internship opportunities respectively, to help the financial industry and other sectors obtain green and sustainable finance-related data and learning resources. The resource repository provides data sources for assessing Hong Kong's physical risks. To support the training of industry talent, the Centre assisted the Government in December in launching the "Pilot Green and Sustainable Finance Capacity Building Support Scheme", which provides subsidies for practitioners, students and graduates participating in green and sustainable finance-related training and skills enhancement. Other measures to promote skills training include launching the "Sustainable Finance Internship Initiative" to create more internship opportunities for students, as well as developing a new "Green and Sustainable Finance" module under the HKMA's "Enhanced Competency Framework for Banking Practitioners"3. "Pilot Green and Sustainable Finance Capacity Building Support Scheme". The HKMA has also been actively supporting the development of green and sustainable finance in the region. In November 2020, the International Finance Corporation and the HKMA launched the "Alliance for Green Commercial Banks"4, bringing together financial institutions, banking industry organisations, research institutions and innovative technology providers in the region to jointly develop a cooperation platform for green commercial banks. The Alliance aims to enable commercial banks and other financial institutions to fully realise their potential, develop green finance into a mainstream core business, and promote the financial system's participation in global climate change-related activities. It operates by providing financial institutions with a one-stop mutual learning platform to acquire the necessary knowledge, tools and information to develop their own green finance roadmaps and transform into credible green financial institutions; bringing together green finance leaders and connecting green financial institutions across different emerging markets to facilitate communication and explore cutting-edge issues; and advancing the global green finance agenda to unlock endless green and climate-related investment opportunities. In June, five globally leading financial institutions5 became founding members of the Alliance and worked closely with the International Finance Corporation and the HKMA to encourage clients to adopt green strategies, promote best practices for green products and services, and unlock new business opportunities that help achieve the transition to a green economy. In addition, three global partners and one knowledge partner6 committed in 2022 to providing climate expertise in areas ranging from innovation and standardisation to academic research. Details of the Alliance and its membership structure are set out on the relevant webpage (English version): founding members, and the signing of the Memorandum of Understanding by the International Finance Corporation and the HKMA. On the other hand, since March 2021, the Alliance has held 18 training events and roundtable meetings, attracting more than 6,000 participants from around the world, including the Asia-Pacific region, Europe, the Middle East, Africa and the Americas. In addition, in June 2022 the Alliance, together with the Hong Kong Institute for Monetary and Financial Research (the Institute)7, published its first cutting-edge research report titled "Climate Risk: Definition, Measurement, Current Practices and Regulation". The HKMA has been promoting green and sustainable debt issuance and building up the ecosystem of related professional services locally. The total amount of green and sustainable debt (including bonds and loans) issued in Hong Kong in 2022 reached US$80.5 billion, an increase of 42%. +42% green and sustainable debt issuance (US$80.5 billion). To demonstrate the Government's determination to tackle climate change, promote green finance and strive to develop Hong Kong into a more sustainable and liveable city, the Government launched the "Government Green Bond Programme" in 2018, with the HKMA assisting in the implementation of the related green bond issuance. To date, the Government has issued green institutional and retail bonds equivalent to nearly US$16 billion, with the proceeds allocated to more than 40 green government projects, including green buildings, waste management and resource recovery, energy efficiency and energy conservation. To enhance the transparency and accountability of the programme, the Government publishes an annual "Green Bond Report", which sets out in detail the allocation of the proceeds raised from the green bonds and their expected environmental benefits. To enable the public to participate in Hong Kong's sustainable development through investment and share in the results it brings, the first batch of green retail bonds with a total value of HK$20 billion was issued in May, receiving enthusiastic support from the public and becoming the world's largest green retail bond issuance at the time. This issuance also expanded the range of green and sustainable finance products in Hong Kong and consolidated Hong Kong's position as a premier green finance hub in the region and internationally. The Government also continued its regular green institutional bond issuance work in the 2022-23 financial year, and issued green bonds equivalent to US$5.75 billion in January 2023. This tri-currency issuance covered US dollars, euros and renminbi, with tenors ranging from 2 to 30 years, continuing to provide an important benchmark for potential issuers in Hong Kong and the region. The issuance was widely welcomed by the global investment community and successfully attracted new investors who had not participated in the Government's previous green bond issuances, reflecting investors' confidence in Hong Kong's long-term credit profile and economic fundamentals. In response to investor demand, the Government doubled the issuance size of the renminbi bond to RMB10 billion. The share of international investors and Mainland investors participating in the issuance through the "Southbound Trading" of Bond Connect also increased, demonstrating Hong Kong's position as a premier offshore renminbi business hub and further consolidating Hong Kong's leading position as an international financial centre. In February 2023, the HKMA also assisted the Government in issuing a tokenised green institutional bond to test the use of distributed ledger technology for bond issuance and settlement. This was the world's first tokenised green bond issued by a government. This primary issuance was settled on a T+1 basis on a private blockchain network, and the subsequent processes (including coupon payment, secondary market trading settlement and redemption at maturity) were also digitalised. The experience of this Government issuance can serve as a reference for market participants interested in conducting similar bond issuances in the future. To provide the industry with credible and convenient market information, the HKMA continued to collaborate with the Climate Bonds Initiative and the International Capital Market Association to publish annual reports on the green debt markets in Hong Kong and the region respectively. The International Capital Market Association's report showed that in 2022 Hong Kong became the largest hub in Asia for arranging the issuance of international green and sustainable bonds, with the total amount of bonds arranged through Hong Kong reaching US$27.8 billion, accounting for over one-third of the regional total. The largest hub for arranging the issuance of international green and sustainable bonds in Asia, US$27.8 billion. Following its first issuance in 2021, the Shenzhen Municipal People's Government issued another RMB5 billion of offshore local government bonds in Hong Kong in November 2022, including RMB2.6 billion of green and blue bonds8. In the same month, the Hainan Provincial People's Government also issued RMB5 billion of offshore bonds in Hong Kong for the first time, including blue and sustainable bonds. The above bond issuance activities once again highlight Hong Kong's unique role in facilitating green and sustainable fund flows between the Mainland and the rest of the world, as well as its enduring status as a premier fundraising platform in the region. The HKMA continued to promote and implement the "Green and Sustainable Finance Grant Scheme" launched in 2021, and used the scheme to attract more relevant professional service providers (including financial institutions, green advisory firms and external review institutions) to establish and expand their operations in Hong Kong. The scheme has been widely welcomed by the industry. As at the end of 2022, the scheme had covered the pre-issuance, post-issuance or both external review service expenses of more than 180 issuers of green and sustainable debt instruments, helping issuers ensure and demonstrate strict adherence to market best practices and international standards. From March, the scheme was enhanced by lowering the minimum loan size threshold for applying for external review fee subsidies from HK$200 million to HK$100 million, helping smaller enterprises obtain green financing. Following the successful completion of the proof-of-concept for tokenised retail green bonds under Project Genesis in 2021, the HKMA collaborated again with the BIS Innovation Hub Hong Kong Centre under Genesis 2.0 to explore the technical feasibility of digitalised carbon forwards (also known as mitigation outcome interests, or MOIs), thereby enhancing the transparency, objectivity and environmental integrity of the green bond market. The project was completed in October 2022, successfully developing two prototypes that use blockchain and other related technologies to track, deliver and transfer digitalised MOIs.

As one of the world's largest asset owners and managers, the HKMA plays an important role in promoting the development of green and sustainable finance to support the global climate change agenda. The HKMA is also a pioneer in responsible investment. As early as 2015, it took the lead in investing in green and sustainable assets, requiring its external investment managers to adopt the Principles of Responsible Ownership issued by the Securities and Futures Commission, and integrating environmental, social and governance factors into the investment management of the Exchange Fund. The HKMA invests prudently in accordance with the principle of "capital preservation first, long-term value creation", believing that placing importance on environmental, social and governance (ESG) factors can unlock long-term sustainable value for investments and mitigate related risks. In the face of increasingly severe climate change challenges, the HKMA continues to advance on its responsible investment journey, including setting the "Net Zero by 2050" target in 2022 and enhancing its risk management strategy, thereby improving the resilience of its asset portfolio so as to strive for more favourable risk-adjusted long-term returns for the Exchange Fund. The HKMA also actively participates in building a green and sustainable finance ecosystem, partnering with like-minded investors and regulators to jointly promote responsible investment, and collaborating with international organisations to formulate ESG investment standards. Transparency of climate-related information plays a pivotal role in managing climate risks. To fulfil its commitment to support the Glasgow Declaration issued by the Network of Central Banks and Supervisors for Greening the Financial System (NGFS) at the 2021 United Nations Climate Change Conference and to greening the global financial system, the HKMA makes climate-related disclosures for the Exchange Fund in accordance with the recommendations of the Task Force on Climate-related Financial Disclosures (TCFD) under the Financial Stability Board. a. FCLTGlobal — Focusing Capital on the Long Term b. PRI — Principles for Responsible Investment c. NGFS — Network of Central Banks and Supervisors for Greening the Financial System d. TCFD — Task Force on Climate-related Financial Disclosures. The Exchange Fund Advisory Committee, chaired by the Financial Secretary, sets the responsible investment framework and guiding principles, which are implemented by the Exchange Fund Investment Office in the investment management of the Exchange Fund. The foremost guiding principle is that the HKMA gives priority to ESG investments whose risk-adjusted long-term returns are comparable to those of other projects, so as to fulfil the investment objectives of the Exchange Fund. Details of the HKMA's responsible investment framework are set out on the HKMA website. The Investment Sub-Committee under the Exchange Fund Advisory Committee, chaired by the Chief Executive of the HKMA, is responsible for overseeing the ESG and climate-related risks involved in the Exchange Fund's investments. The Investment Sub-Committee reviews the responsible investment framework and risk management approach, and monitors the progress of investments that integrate ESG factors as well as the ESG position of the Exchange Fund through regular meeting reports from the Risk Management and Compliance Department of the Exchange Fund Investment Office. As shown in Figure 1, the ESG Committee established under the Exchange Fund Investment Office, chaired by the Chief Risk Officer, is responsible for coordinating and overseeing the various ESG initiatives of the Exchange Fund Investment Office. The motions and work progress discussed at each meeting of the ESG Committee are reported to the Chief Executive Officer of the Exchange Fund Investment Office. Monitoring and governance structure of responsible investment: The dedicated team of the Risk Management and Compliance Department works closely with the various investment teams of the Exchange Fund Investment Office on integrating ESG factors, and assists the senior management of the Exchange Fund Investment Office in managing the ESG and climate-related risks and opportunities of various investment projects. Public market investments: The Credit, Regulation and Compliance Committee, composed of the senior management of the Exchange Fund Investment Office, monitors the ESG position of the fixed income portfolio through regular reports from the Risk Management and Compliance Department. In addition, the Risk Management and Compliance Department also participates from an ESG perspective in the selection, appointment and monitoring process of external investment managers for the equity portfolio (see the section "Striving to Actively Exercise Ownership" under the "Risk Management" section on page 27). Private market investments: The Investment Sub-Committee, chaired by the Chief Executive of the HKMA, considers the ESG-related assessments made by the Risk Management and Compliance Department and the private market investment team on each investment proposal. Concrete evidence² continues to show that the impact of climate change and related risks is significant. According to the latest report³ of the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (the UNFCCC), even assuming that the "Nationally Determined Contributions" targets announced by various regions are fully fulfilled, the global temperature rise by 2100 is still estimated to reach as high as 2.1 to 2.4 degrees Celsius, making it difficult to achieve the Paris Agreement's target of limiting the increase in the global average temperature to well below 2 degrees Celsius above pre-industrial levels. Should various regions adopt more aggressive policy measures to close the temperature gap, the resulting transition risks⁴, along with the repricing of assets by the market based on anticipated future trends, coupled with inherent physical risks, would all intensify the pressure on asset valuations. In view of updates to the global warming trajectory and model assumptions, the HKMA, leveraging the expertise of external consultants, further assessed the resilience of the Exchange Fund "investment portfolio" under a "rapid transition" scenario (Figure 2) beyond the scenarios assessed in 2021. The "rapid transition" scenario incorporates higher transition risk factors in the short, medium and long term, assuming that policy changes and technological developments jointly drive a rapid decline in carbon emissions, while various assets are subject to sudden divestment in order to keep the average temperature rise within 1.5 degrees Celsius before 2100. This scenario broadly aligns with the disorderly scenario recommended by the NGFS for forward-looking climate impact assessments. The "investment portfolio" is able to remain robust in the medium to long term, as a larger proportion of its asset allocation consists of sovereign bonds that are less sensitive to transition impacts. Sector distribution is key. Low-carbon electricity and renewable energy assets can benefit from the relevant transition. Transition risks and asset repricing may, in the short term, impact performance (especially equity assets). The "investment portfolio" as a whole will be increasingly affected by physical risks that gradually materialise over time. Energy and traditional utilities remain the sectors most vulnerable to impacts. Climate scenarios, like other model approaches, have their limitations. The relevant analysis is based on the market benchmark sector distribution at the strategic asset allocation level, and does not take into account the effect of actively selecting specific securities within a particular sector. More in-depth research shows that, compared with the market benchmark of the strategic asset allocation, the investments within the "investment portfolio" are generally more resistant to transition shocks or suffer relatively milder impacts. This result once again affirms that the HKMA's responsible investment focusing on combating climate change can enhance the resilience of the asset portfolio. The trajectory of climate change remains uncertain, and scenario analysis methods will continue to evolve as data quality improves and policies develop. The HKMA will regularly review relevant scenarios and refine its assessments in order to more clearly ascertain the Exchange Fund's resilience in the face of climate change. As a long-term investor, the HKMA fully understands the risks and opportunities that climate change can bring. The HKMA is committed to further expanding sustainable investments, and to seizing opportunities related to climate transition, mitigating climate risks and enhancing the long-term returns of the asset portfolio. In 2022, the HKMA continued its good momentum by further increasing its holdings of green, social and sustainable bonds by 50%. In terms of equity investments, the HKMA invested in a governance-themed active equity portfolio, and adopted a decarbonisation strategy favouring low-carbon-emitting companies for its passive equity portfolio. In addition, the HKMA is exploring with the dedicated general partners of the Exchange Fund's "Long-Term Growth Portfolio" the establishment of a dedicated private equity portfolio to promote green and sustainable development in the Asian region (Figure 3). Figure 3: Continuing to implement measures to increase ESG investments. The HKMA has invested in a pan-African wind farm operator. In addition to producing clean energy, this operator also attaches great importance to social and biodiversity factors. Before the wind farm was established, local villagers used poisoned bait to prevent predatory animals from preying on their livestock, but this inadvertently endangered certain vultures that are endangered species. Livestock is an important asset for local villagers. To help villagers protect their livestock, the operator built livestock shelters within the wind farm to protect the livestock from natural predators. In addition, the operator employed a bird monitoring team to issue warnings when vultures were found attracted by animal carcasses occasionally left behind by predators, so as to shut down the wind turbines and prevent the vultures from being struck by the blades. Reducing livestock predation creates a win-win situation: on the one hand, it safeguards the livelihoods of villagers, and on the other hand, it reduces cases of vultures being killed by wind turbines, thereby protecting endangered species. Good ESG practices can bring more business opportunities and open up revenue streams for enterprises, and the supply-chain-related operations described below are one such example. The investee company is an integrated logistics and warehousing operator in Mainland China, specialising in cold-chain pharmaceutical, chemical products and high-end consumer goods logistics services. The company faces continuously rising ESG operating standards, mainly stemming from multinational enterprise clients requiring their service providers to meet high decarbonisation targets consistent with the Paris Agreement. In response to such demand, the company engaged external consultants to help formulate a "Three-Year ESG Plan" to reduce carbon emission intensity by 50% on or before 2030. This comprehensive decarbonisation plan already yielded significant results in 2021 alone. The above ESG measures earned the company the "Low-Carbon Green Management Case" award from the China Federation of Logistics and Purchasing. These achievements and commendations enabled the company to gain considerable business opportunities from consumer and chemical product multinational clients that particularly value ESG practices. The growth of ESG investments is closely linked to the development of the green and sustainable finance ecosystem. The HKMA actively collaborates with like-minded investors and partners to promote responsible investment and enhance industry skills. In 2022, the HKMA successfully held its 4th annual ESG workshop, exchanging good ESG practices with 9 participating private market institutions (including dedicated general partners, limited partners and enterprises) and promoting sustainable investment opportunities in the Asia-Pacific region and the Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macao Greater Bay Area. In the public market, the HKMA urged its trading counterparties (mainly investment banks) to expand their ESG manpower and research capabilities, particularly in Hong Kong. Mr Clement Li, Chief Executive Officer of the Exchange Fund Investment Office, delivered the opening remarks at the HKMA's 2022 ESG Workshop.
